mem.t: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

sat.d: Prepare a “welcome-home feast” together as a family: the children help wash the vegetables and set the table, and the parents cook a dish everyone loves. Before the meal, Mom or Dad briefly tells the story of the prodigal son. Then each person writes on a slip of paper one unhappy thing they want to let go of and puts it in an envelope. After praying together, tear the slips up and throw them away. During the meal, take turns saying, “Thank you for forgiving me” or “I choose to forgive you.” At the end, say the Lord’s Prayer together, pause at the line “forgive us our debts,” and hug one another.

sun: What did “forgiveness” look like in the home you grew up in? Were you told to say “it’s okay,” or were you truly forgiven?
This week, in what matter did you forgive your child, or teach your child to forgive? What was hardest about it?
The Discipline and Forgiveness unit has ended. Which change will you carry into the days ahead, and whom would you like to invite to practice it with you?

lessons.title: As the Lord Forgave You
lessons.theme: The source of forgiveness is that we were forgiven first

v: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.

lessons.still: Read slowly: “even as Christ forgave you.” Think of how many times God has forgiven you. There is no need to count; just let the feeling of being forgiven fill you, and then say to the Lord, “Thank you.”
teach: Paul says, “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” The standard of forgiveness is not “does he deserve it?” but “how did the Lord forgive me?” Home is the place where complaints come most easily, because we are together every day and see one another at our most real, and our least attractive.

Forgiveness is often misunderstood. Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened, and it does not cancel boundaries: a child who breaks something can be forgiven and still needs to learn responsibility. Nor does forgiveness mean all trust is restored at once; trust takes time to rebuild. Forgiveness is handing the right to collect the debt over to God, and no longer using the matter to punish the other person. If there is violence or harm in your home, forgiving does not mean staying in danger; seek help from your pastor and from professionals.

Paul first says, “God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved,” and only then calls for a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility and perseverance. It is like a garment: only when you know you are loved can you put on forgiveness. Parents need to teach children to forgive and also to forgive their children, but both begin in the same place: we have first been forgiven by the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: First with God, then with yourself, then with others. Being forgiven by God is the relationship with God; accepting the forgiven self is the relationship with yourself; and only then do we have the strength to forgive family. A self-emptied person no longer clutches at “I am right,” but lets Christ live in him and loves others with his forgiveness.
q: Who is God? — The Lord has forgiven us and does not count up our wrongs. For which time of being forgiven do you most want to thank him today?
Who am I? — What are my misunderstandings about forgiveness? Do I treat it as pretending nothing happened, or as canceling boundaries?
How should I respond? — To which family member will I hand back the “right to collect the debt” to God today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was nailed to the cross, in terrible pain and bearing every humiliation, he said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” In his deepest pain, he still chose to forgive. We can forgive others because we were first forgiven by such a love.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for forgiving me on the cross, and for forgiving me again and again. I confess that I often keep accounts against my family, and want them to pay in full before I will forgive. Let me remember how you forgave me. Give me a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, and teach me to bear with one another and forgive one another at home. Amen.
acts: Write down three things God has forgiven you, and thank him for each.
Think of one matter for which you are still “keeping accounts” against your child, and lay it down before God.
Today when your child makes a mistake, after you have dealt with the consequence, add: “That’s over now. I forgive you.”
lessons.noon: “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” — Lord, thank you for forgiving me; let your forgiveness flow from me to my family. Amen.

fam.key: Jesus forgives me, and I forgive others.

lamb.do: After your child has grabbed your hair or thrown food on the floor, deal with it calmly, then hold him close and rock him gently.
lamb.say: It’s all right. Mommy still loves you so much.

sprout.story: Kitten Mimi tore her little sister’s picture, and her sister cried. Mimi felt awful and ran to say, “I’m sorry I tore your picture.” Her sister was still very sad, but she remembered that yesterday she had lost Mimi’s ball, and Mimi had forgiven her. She wiped her tears and said, “I forgive you. Shall we draw another one together?” The two kittens drew an even bigger picture.
sprout.ask: When someone forgives you, how does it feel inside?
sprout.do: Practice saying together, “I’m sorry, I…” and “I forgive you.” Give a high five each time you finish.

soldier.story: Jiaming and Jiale from Johor are brothers. Jiale accidentally dropped and broke Jiaming’s favorite model. Jiaming was furious. “I will never forgive you!” That evening Dad sat with Jiaming and asked, “Do you remember when you dropped Dad’s phone in the water?” Jiaming bowed his head. Dad said, “I forgave you then, not because you deserved it, but because I love you.” The next day Jiaming said to Jiale, “I forgive you, but next time you have to ask me before you take it.”
ask: Jiaming said, “I forgive you, but next time ask me first.” Do those two sentences conflict? Why?
After you forgive someone, can there still be rules?
soldier.do: Make a poster, “Forgiveness is not…”, and write together: forgiving is not pretending nothing happened, not having no rules, and not being instantly not sad. Stick it up at home.

youth.talk: I am still learning about forgiveness myself. Some people hurt me, and even now it hurts when I think of it. So I don’t want to just tell you, “Hurry up and forgive,” as if it were simple. But I am slowly finding that forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened, and not letting the other person keep hurting me. It is no longer letting that thing keep me tied up. God did this for me first.
ask: What do you think is the biggest difference between forgiving and “pretending nothing happened”?
Is there something you find very hard to forgive? Would you be willing to talk about it?
youth.do: The parent shares a true experience of learning to forgive (choosing a fitting part), then invites the child to name something he is struggling with, and prays together, without rushing him.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for forgiving us the things we do wrong. Help us to forgive other people too, so that our home is full of love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Am I Still Keeping Accounts?
lessons.theme: Seeing the old ledger in my heart

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to open the “ledger” in your heart: the times your child let you down, embarrassed you or made you angry. How many do you still remember? Don’t rush to tear it up; first look honestly.
teach: Peter asked Jesus, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” He thought he was being very generous. Jesus said, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” It doesn’t mean you may stop forgiving once you reach four hundred and ninety; it means stop counting altogether. A person who forgives carries no calculator.

Parents easily keep accounts on their children: “You did the same last time,” “I’ve told you hundreds of times,” “Ever since you were small, you…” Every “again,” “every time” and “always” is an old account being turned over. What the child hears is: in your eyes, I am forever the one who messes up. Love “takes no account of evil,” but dredging up the past keeps every mistake on file.

Jesus went on to tell a parable: a servant who had been released from a debt of ten thousand talents went out and grabbed by the throat a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii. The master said, “Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” What we owe before God is far more than what our children owe us. Only when we see how much we have been forgiven can we put down the little ledger in our hand.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled parent remembers every one of the child’s wrongs, because what he cares about is that he has been offended; the self-emptied parent remembers every one of God’s mercies, because his focus is on Jesus. Pride makes people judges; humility brings them back to the place of sinners who have received grace.
q: Who is God? — God forgave a debt we could never repay. When did you last feel deeply what it is to be “released from a debt”?
Who am I? — In which matters do I most often say “again,” “every time” and “always” to my child?
How should I respond? — Which old ledger am I willing to tear up before God today?
lessons.jesus: People brought Jesus a woman who had sinned, wanting him to condemn her. Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” He did not turn over her old accounts, but gave her a new start. Jesus’ forgiveness is not indulgence; it lets a person set out afresh.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving a debt I could never repay. I confess that in my heart there is a ledger on my children, recording their failures and my disappointments. I often use “again,” “every time” and “always” to remind them of past mistakes. Forgive me. Today I hand this ledger to you. Let me be like you, taking no account of evil, and give my children a new start. Amen.
acts: Notice how many times today you say “again,” “every time” or “always,” and write it down.
On a sheet of paper write one old matter you have been holding against your child, pray over it, and tear the paper up.
Say to a child, “That thing that happened before, I won’t bring it up again.”
lessons.noon: “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” — Lord, let me stop counting and simply forgive. Amen.

fam.key: To forgive is to stop bringing up old wrongs.

lamb.do: Play “gone!” with your child: cover a little toy with a hankie, take the hankie away, say “all gone,” and then hug him.
lamb.say: All gone! Mommy only remembers how lovable you are.

sprout.story: Little Elephant had a big notebook. Each time a friend made him angry, he wrote it down: “Monkey took my banana,” “Rabbit stepped on my foot”… The notebook got heavier and heavier, and walking became tiring for Little Elephant. Grandma Elephant said, “Would you like to try throwing it away?” Little Elephant threw the notebook into the river. His body felt so light, and he could play with everyone again.
sprout.ask: If we keep remembering other people’s mistakes, how does that feel inside?
sprout.do: Put a few books in a small backpack and let your child carry it round once. Then take out the books one by one, saying each time, “I forgive you!”, and feel how the bag gets lighter.

soldier.story: Peter asked Jesus, “When someone wrongs me, how many times must I forgive him? Is seven enough?” Jesus said, “Not seven times, but seventy times seven!” Peter must have been startled. Then Jesus told a story: a servant owed the king a huge, huge amount of money, and the king canceled all of it. But the servant went out, saw a friend who owed him a tiny amount, and grabbed him by the throat to make him pay. Jesus said that God has forgiven us so much, so we must forgive others too.
ask: What did that servant do wrong?
Do you have a “ledger” in your heart where you write down other people’s mistakes? What is written in it?
soldier.do: Each person takes a sheet of paper as a “ledger” and writes down one wrong of someone else they still remember. After the whole family has prayed, tear up the papers and throw them away.

youth.talk: I want to admit something: I am very good at turning over your old accounts. Every time you make a mistake, I say, “You did this last time too,” as if I keep all your mistakes on file, ready to pull out at any moment. I don’t know how tiring that has been for you. Jesus said to forgive seventy times seven, and I think he is saying: stop counting. From today I want to stop bringing up things that are already past.
ask: Which old account do I turn over most often? How do you feel when you hear it?
Do you think you keep accounts against anyone in the family?
youth.do: The parent says one specific sentence to the child: “That matter of ___ from before, I have let it go, and I won’t bring it up again,” and truly keeps to it this week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving us so many, many times. Help us not to keep remembering other people’s mistakes, but to forgive often, just as you forgive us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: The Prodigal’s Father
lessons.theme: I believe: my home will always keep a light on for my child

v: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.

lessons.still: Picture the father standing at the roadside, gazing into the distance every day. Today you are the child he sees. Quietly let your heavenly Father run to you and hold you.
teach: The prodigal son took his inheritance and wasted it all in a far country, until he was so low he was fighting the pigs for food, and then he remembered his father’s house. All the way home he rehearsed his apology, ready to say, “Make me as one of your hired servants.” But “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” In that age, for a respected elder to hitch up his robe and run down the road was undignified. This father cared more about his son than about his dignity.

Before the son had even finished speaking, the father ordered the robe, the ring and the sandals: the robe to restore honor, the ring to restore standing, the sandals to show he was a son and not a servant. The father did not say, “Prove you have changed first, and then I will accept you.” He restored the relationship first, and then they walked the road ahead together. Forgiveness is not a prize given after the child has behaved well enough; it is the starting point from which a child can begin again.

The change of viewpoint is from “my child has let me down, so I withdraw my love” to “however far my child goes, the door of home stays open.” This does not mean there are no boundaries; the prodigal still had to face the loss of his inheritance. But the door of the relationship is not shut. Today write your “I believe” declaration: I believe my home will always keep a light on for my child.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Turn from an earthly viewpoint to a heavenly one, from the temporary to the eternal. A child’s failure in this season does not define his whole life; the heavenly Father sees us as children who “were dead and are alive again, lost and found.” If a parent is first embraced by such a Father’s love, he can embrace his child in the same way.
q: Who is God? — The Father saw the prodigal, was moved with compassion, and ran to embrace him. Is the heavenly Father in your heart one who would run to you?
Who am I? — When my child lets me down, am I more like the father who runs to him, or the father who stands at the door waiting for him to confess first?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe the Father runs to me, so I will… ; I believe my child…
lessons.jesus: Jesus told this parable because the Pharisees murmured that he welcomed sinners. Jesus himself is the heart of the father who runs to the prodigal. He said, “the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.” Jesus did not sit waiting for sinners to come back; he went out himself to look for them.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that when I was still far off you saw me, ran to me and held me. I believe you have never shut the door of home on me. Let me become this kind of parent too: when my child goes far away, I will keep watch for him, and when he returns I will run to him. Let my forgiveness be the starting point for my child to begin again, and not a prize he receives once he has behaved well enough. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences: I believe the Father runs to me; I believe my child’s failure is not his definition; I believe the door of my home is always open to my child.
Today, after your child makes a mistake or lets you down, take the first step toward him and give him a hug.
Think: what “robe, ring and sandals” could you prepare for your child, to restore his dignity?
lessons.noon: “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” — Father, thank you for running to me; let me run to my children in the same way. Amen.

fam.key: However far I go, home waits for me.

lamb.do: Play “run over for a hug” with your child: stand at the other end of the room with your arms open, and when he crawls or walks over, go to meet him and pick him up.
lamb.say: You’re back! I missed you so much. I love you so much.

sprout.story: A young son left home and went to a faraway place, spent all his money and was so hungry that he had to feed pigs. He thought, “I will go home and tell Dad I’m sorry.” He walked and walked, and while he was still a long way from home, his father saw him! Dad ran to him, hugged him tight, and kissed him again and again, gave him new clothes and a ring, and held a big party.
sprout.ask: When Dad saw his son coming back, what do you think he felt inside?
sprout.do: Play “coming home”: the child hides at the other end of the room, Mom and Dad call, “You’re back!”, and the child runs over, and they open their arms, hug him and spin him round.

soldier.story: Jesus told a story: the younger son took his father’s money, went off to a far country and wasted it, until he had nothing left and even wanted to eat what the pigs ate. He decided to go home, ready to say, “I am not worthy to be called your son. Let me be a worker.” But his father saw him from far away, ran to him, hugged him, and gave him a robe, a ring and sandals. The robe stands for honor, the ring for still belonging to the family, and the sandals for being a son and not a servant.
ask: Why didn’t the father scold his son first?
If you had done something very wrong, how would you want Mom and Dad to treat you?
soldier.do: As a family, write a card, “The door of our home is always open,” and let everyone sign it. Stick it on the inside of the front door.

youth.talk: I have read the story of the prodigal son many times, but lately I have been reading it as a parent. I wonder what that father was thinking as he stood at the roadside every day waiting. I want to tell you: whatever choices you make in the future, and wherever you go, even if we disagree, the door of this home will be open to you. I may disagree with you, but I will never stop loving you.
ask: Have you ever been afraid that if you did something very wrong, you would not dare come home, or dare tell us?
What kind of response from us would make you still dare to come back and tell us after you have done wrong?
youth.do: The parent writes the child a short letter: “However far you go, the door of home is open to you,” with one specific promise, for example, “Call me at any time and I will come and get you.”

fam.pray: Daddy in heaven, thank you for being like that father, always waiting for us to come home. Help our family to forgive one another, so that everyone feels home is the warmest place. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Forgive Us Our Debts
lessons.theme: Practice the Lord’s Prayer at home and teach your children to forgive

v: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.

lessons.still: Slowly pray the Lord’s Prayer once, and pause at the line, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Ask the Lord, “Today, whose debt do I need to forgive?”
teach: The Lord’s Prayer is the prayer Jesus taught us, and in the middle is the line, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” This line ties together our relationship with God and our relationship with people. Jesus goes on to say, “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” Forgiveness is not an elective; it is the daily homework of a disciple.

Many parents teach children to forgive with just one sentence: “Quick, say it’s okay!” But “it’s okay” is often not true, and the child is still hurting inside. A better way has four steps. One: name the hurt: “He took my toy and I’m angry.” Two: choose to let go: “I decide not to get back at him.” Three: hand it to God: “God, I give this to you.” Four: make up, as long as it is safe: “Let’s play together.” The one who was wronged can say “I forgive you,” rather than being pushed to say “it’s okay.”

Tonight at bedtime, the whole family can say the Lord’s Prayer together and pause at “forgive us our debts.” Each person quietly thinks: who made me sad today? Am I willing to forgive him? And also: whom did I make sad today? Then take turns saying one sentence, “I forgive…” or “I’m sorry…” Let forgiveness become your family’s bedtime habit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit; don’t use the head and rely on yourself. Forgiveness is not done by gritting your teeth and willpower, but by asking the Holy Spirit for strength. When parents first forgive in front of their children, the children learn to forgive. This is the most natural multiplication in a family: life influencing life.
q: Who is God? — Jesus put “forgive us our debts” into our daily prayer. Why does he take forgiveness so seriously?
Who am I? — When I teach my child to forgive, do I push him to say “it’s okay,” or walk with him through the hurt?
How should I respond? — Tonight, how will I lead my whole family to practice forgiveness through the Lord’s Prayer?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus knew perfectly well who would betray him, yet he stooped down and washed the feet of all his disciples, Judas included. Before he was hurt, he had already chosen love. Jesus taught us to pray, and he lived out the forgiveness he taught.
lessons.pray: Our Father in heaven, forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Lord, I confess that I often tell my children to hurry up and say “it’s okay,” while I have not truly forgiven myself. Today help me walk with my child through his hurt and learn true forgiveness. And let the Lord’s Prayer become the nightly rhythm of our home, so that forgiveness takes root among us. Amen.
acts: Tonight at bedtime, lead the whole family in the Lord’s Prayer, pause at “forgive us our debts,” and take turns saying “I forgive…” or “I’m sorry…”
The next time the children have a conflict, use the four steps in place of “quick, say it’s okay”: name the hurt, choose to let go, hand it to God, make up.
Parents go first, naming one small matter today that they chose to forgive.
lessons.noon: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” — Lord, today I will forgive debts too; give me strength. Amen.

fam.key: Forgive us our debts, and we forgive others.

lamb.do: At bedtime, hold your child in your arms and slowly say the Lord’s Prayer, gently patting his chest at “forgive us our debts.”
lamb.say: God forgives us, and we forgive others. Good night, my darling.

sprout.story: Her little brother snapped Xiaoqi’s crayon, and Xiaoqi was very cross. Mom said, “You can tell your brother that you are angry.” Xiaoqi said, “You broke my crayon, and I’m angry!” Her brother said, “I’m sorry.” Mom asked, “Will you forgive your brother?” Xiaoqi thought, then said, “I forgive you, but you have to be careful.” That night they said the Lord’s Prayer together, and when they got to “forgive us our debts,” they both smiled.
sprout.ask: When you are angry, how can you tell someone?
sprout.do: Teach your child to do the Lord’s Prayer with hand actions: at “forgive us our debts,” open both hands and push them outwards to show “letting go.”

soldier.story: Jesus taught his disciples to pray, and one line is: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” It means: ask God to forgive us, just as we also forgive other people. It is as if the line says: if we are unwilling to forgive others, it is hard to truly understand how great God’s forgiveness is. So forgiving others is not only good for them; it also brings us closer to God.
ask: Why are forgiving others and God forgiving us joined together?
Did anyone make you sad today? Are you willing to forgive them?
soldier.do: Tonight the whole family says the Lord’s Prayer together, pauses at “forgive us our debts,” and each person says one sentence, “Today I forgive…” or “Today I want to say sorry to…”

youth.talk: When you were small and quarreled with your brothers and sisters, I often told you to “hurry and say sorry, hurry and say it’s okay,” so that it would be over quickly. Thinking back, that may have made you feel your feelings didn’t matter. Forgiveness actually takes time, and it takes honesty. The Lord’s Prayer says “forgive us our debts,” and I think we can really practice it together, not just make up on the surface.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “it’s okay” and “I forgive you”?
Was there ever a time you were made to say “it’s okay” when you were still upset inside?
youth.do: Invite your child to say the Lord’s Prayer together at bedtime this week, pausing at “forgive us our debts,” and each pray quietly for a minute, with no need to say what you prayed.

fam.pray: Our Father in heaven, thank you for forgiving us. Help us today to forgive others too, and to go to sleep with peace in our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

lessons.title: Don’t Let the Sun Go Down on Your Anger
lessons.theme: Review and adjust: making up as a family habit

v: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
and don’t give place to the devil.
And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.

lessons.still: Look back over this week, and over these five weeks of the Discipline and Forgiveness journey. Which picture makes you most thankful? Which still makes your heart ache? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you.
teach: Paul says, “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil. Anger itself is not necessarily sin, but taking it to bed is like leaving a seed in the soil: by tomorrow a bitter shoot will have grown. In many families, distance does not come from one big fight but from many nights when people fell asleep without making up.

Peter says, “above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.” To cover is not to hide or pretend; it is like a cloak laid over another’s weakness, not announced around, not turned over and over. A home can have quarrels, but if there is making up every day, love grows thicker and thicker.

In these five weeks we have learned: discipline is love; don’t provoke your children; boundaries and natural consequences; parents apologize first; forgiveness and mending. Today is not about giving yourself a score, but about honest review and humble adjustment. You may still raise your voice and still keep accounts, but you now know the road back. Review, adjustment, repetition: it is in this rhythm that life is changed.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last of the eight steps for changing beliefs is multiplication. When children have experienced love within discipline and mending after a break at home, they will treat their friends, spouses and children the same way in future. A parent’s making up today is preparing a healthier home for the next generation.
q: Who is God? — God’s love covers a multitude of sins. Where have you experienced this love of God in these five weeks?
Who am I? — In these five weeks, what has been my biggest change in discipline and forgiveness? Where do I still need to keep adjusting?
How should I respond? — What kind of “make up before sunset” habit will our family build?
lessons.jesus: On the evening of the resurrection, the disciples who had run away and denied the Lord were hiding behind closed doors. Jesus came and stood among them, and his first words were, “Peace be to you.” He did not rebuke them. He brought peace first, and then sent them out. This is Jesus’ way of making up.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us through these five weeks. I confess that I still often get angry and still keep accounts, but thank you for giving me the way back again and again. Help our family not to let the sun go down on our anger, and let love cover a multitude of sins. And let what we have learned in discipline and forgiveness become a blessing for our children when they build their own families. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for fifteen minutes: what has been the biggest change in our home in these five weeks? What shall we keep adjusting next?
Ask your child, “In these weeks, have Mom and Dad been more like Jesus? Where do we still need to change?” Just listen, and say thank you.
As a family, set up a “make up before sunset” habit, for example saying to one another at bedtime, “Is there anything today we need to make up?”
lessons.noon: “And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.” — Lord, cover our family’s weaknesses today with your love. Amen.

fam.key: Before we go to sleep, we make up.

lamb.do: Every night at bedtime, hold your child, kiss his forehead, and say a short blessing prayer for him.
lamb.say: Today is all over, and tomorrow is a new day. Mommy and Daddy love you.

sprout.story: Little Chick Chirpy and Mother Hen quarreled today, because Chirpy didn’t want a bath. At bedtime, Grandfather Sun was slowly going down. Mother Hen said, “Chirpy, the sun is going down. Shall we make up?” Chirpy nodded. “I’m sorry, Mommy.” Mother Hen said, “I’m sorry too. I was too loud just now.” The two chickens cuddled together, watched the sun set, and fell sweetly asleep.
sprout.ask: What shall we say in our family before we go to sleep?
sprout.do: Tonight at bedtime, sit in a circle, and each person says, “Today, thank you for…” and “Today, I’m sorry for…” Then say together, “We’ve made up!”

soldier.story: The Bible says, “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath.” It means: when you are angry, don’t keep it inside overnight. It is like trash: if you take it out every day, the house stays clean; if you leave it piled up, it starts to smell and breed bugs. Anger is the same. Deal with it every day and your heart feels light; leave it, and it turns into dislike and hatred. So every night in our family we ask: is there anything today that we need to make up?
ask: Have you ever gone to sleep angry? How did you feel the next day?
How do you think our family could make up before bed?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares “the change I liked most in these weeks” and “one thing I want to keep practicing next week,” and then together agree on a way to make up before bed.

youth.talk: These weeks we have talked a lot about discipline, apologies and forgiveness. I want you to know I understand I still have many things I haven’t done well; sometimes I still raise my voice, and still turn over old accounts. But I hope we can have a habit between us: however fierce the quarrel during the day, we can say one word before bed. It doesn’t have to solve every problem right away, but at least the other person knows the relationship is still there.
ask: In these weeks, have you felt anything different in our home?
What kind of “making up before bed” would not feel too awkward for you?
youth.do: Agree with your child on a simple way of making up before bed, such as a goodnight message, a hug or a gesture, and do it every day this week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us a new beginning every day. Help us to make up every day before we sleep, so that our home is full of love and peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

40.memT: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

mem.t: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!

sat.d: Set up three challenges that one person cannot do alone but two can: carrying a ball together on a towel, one child blindfolded while the other gives directions across the living room, and building a paper-cup tower together. A child without siblings can invite cousins or friends from church. After each challenge, say “Thank you for helping me.” At the end, sit together and let everyone name one thing they admire about their brother or sister (or family member). Then the parents bless the children with Psalm 133.

sun: How is your relationship with your own brothers and sisters? How does it shape the way you see your children getting along today?
What is the most common tension between your children? Have you ever shown favouritism or made comparisons without meaning to?
What one concrete step will you take next week to help your children become companions rather than rivals? You might also invite the group to pray for each family’s sibling relationships.

lessons.title: Brothers Living Together in Unity
lessons.theme: Siblings are a child’s first companions, given by God

v: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!
It is like the precious oil on the head, that ran down on the beard, even Aaron’s beard, that came down on the edge of his robes,
like the dew of Hermon, that comes down on the hills of Zion; for there the LORD gives the blessing, even life forever more.

lessons.still: Picture your children as they are today: laughing together, grabbing toys from each other. Quietly bring each child’s name to the Lord and say, “Lord, help them live together in unity.”
teach: Psalm 133 is a song of ascents, sung by Israelites as they traveled to Jerusalem for the festivals. People from different tribes and clans walked the same road, and the psalmist marveled, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” This goodness is tested first, and most truly, at home: brothers and sisters under one roof.

The psalmist gives two pictures: precious oil poured on Aaron’s head, running down his beard and onto his robes, and the dew of Hermon falling on the hills of Zion. Oil flows from the head downward. Peace at home often flows the same way, from the top down. How parents treat each other, and how they treat each child, runs all the way down into how the children treat one another.

Proverbs says, “A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.” Siblings are a child’s first companions, and often the longest relationship of a lifetime, outlasting even parents. Today’s squabbles over toys and seats are God’s first classroom for learning to love. A child with no siblings can learn the same lesson among cousins and spiritual companions at church.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In the 920 vision, brothers and sisters are the closest “2” in a child’s life. As children learn to lay themselves down before their siblings and live out the “0”, the nine fruits of the Spirit begin to grow at home. Peace in the home flows down from the parents and bears fruit between the children.
q: Who is God? — God has commanded his blessing where brothers live in unity. Where have you seen that blessing?
Who am I? — How is the way my spouse and I treat each other “flowing down” into my children’s relationships?
How should I respond? — What can I do today to help my children see one another as companions?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for his disciples, “that they may all be one.” Among them were fishermen, a tax collector and a zealot, all very different in character, yet Jesus placed them on one team. He prayed for unity, and he gave his own life to make it real.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for giving our children to one another as companions. Help them live together in unity, like precious oil and the dew of Hermon. I confess that the discord in our home sometimes flows down from us adults. Let peace begin first between my spouse and me, and then flow to each child, so that our home becomes a place where you command your blessing. Amen.
acts: Pray for each child by name today, asking God to help them love one another
Notice a moment when your children cooperate or help each other, and praise it specifically
Say a word of thanks to your spouse where the children can see
lessons.noon: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” — Lord, help the children in our home to love one another.

fam.key: Brothers and sisters are friends God gave us.

lamb.do: Let an older brother or sister gently touch the baby’s hand, or sit two children on your lap together and give everyone a big hug.
lamb.say: This is your big brother (sister). God gave you to each other.

sprout.story: Three bunny siblings lived in one burrow. The big brother was good at digging, the middle sister was good at finding carrots, and the little sister sang the best songs. One rainy day the burrow entrance was about to cave in. Big Brother dug, Middle Sister carried, and Little Sister sang to cheer everyone on. Together they fixed it. Mother Bunny said, “When you are together, you are wonderful!” God puts brothers and sisters in one family so we can help each other.
sprout.ask: What is your brother or sister (or best friend) really good at?
sprout.do: Hold hands in a circle and say together, “Brothers and sisters are great!” Each time you say it, take one step around, then give each other a hug.

soldier.story: Every year the Israelites traveled to Jerusalem for the festivals. People from all over walked the same road, singing as they went. One of their songs says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” It is like dew after rain, refreshing dry hills. It is the same in our home. When brothers and sisters make peace, the whole house feels good. When they quarrel, it feels as if the whole house has dried up.
ask: When does our family feel most like “how good and how pleasant”?
How can brothers and sisters (or family members) help each other?
soldier.do: Finish a job together with your brother or sister (or family): tidy a room, make a snack, or draw a picture. Take a photo when you are done.

youth.talk: You may find your younger brother or sister (or older one) annoying, and sometimes the noise of your arguing gives me a headache too. But I want you to know that when we are old, the person who has been with you longest will probably be your sibling. I have things with my own brothers and sisters that I have not sorted out, so I am not lecturing you. I am still learning too.
ask: What are the best and the hardest moments between you and your brothers and sisters?
What do you hope your relationship will look like ten years from now?
youth.do: A parent shares a true story about their own relationship with a sibling, good or hard, and then invites each child to describe the sibling relationship they would love to have.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for our brothers and sisters and our family. Help us love and help one another so that our home is good and pleasant. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Am I Playing Favorites?
lessons.theme: Seeing a parent’s comparing and favoring in the light

v: The boys grew. Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob was a quiet man, living in tents.
Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a tunic of many colors.
His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him.

lessons.still: Be still before the Lord and call to mind each child’s face in turn. Ask yourself: which child makes me smile more easily? Which one makes me sigh more easily? Ask the Holy Spirit to shine gently into your heart.
teach: The Bible honestly records favouritism in one family: “Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.” Each parent had a favorite, and the two brothers were rivals from then on. In the next generation Jacob repeated the pattern: “Israel loved Joseph more than all his children,” and made him a tunic of many colors. The result: “His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him.” Favouritism passes from generation to generation.

Favouritism is not always about bigger presents. More often it hides in everyday words: “Look how sensible your brother is,” “Your sister is so well behaved, unlike you.” It shows when the high achiever is the one we always introduce to guests, or when we are strict with the eldest and lenient with the youngest. Children are very sensitive to this, and they keep a quiet tally in their hearts: who is loved more?

Fair does not mean identical. A three-year-old and a thirteen-year-old need different things, and so do an introvert and an extrovert. Fairness means every child knows for certain that they are loved just as deeply, and each receives what they need. God shows no favouritism, yet he knows every sheep by name.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled parent often favors the child who “makes me look good” or “is most like me”, keeping the focus on personal preference. The self-emptied parent sees each child through God’s eyes: each is a treasure entrusted by God, with a unique design.
q: Who is God? — God shows no partiality and does not favor one person over another. How does that challenge the way you see your children?
Who am I? — Do I compare my children, knowingly or not, or favor one of them? What would they say?
How should I respond? — Which child do I need to tell, “I have not shown you enough of my love”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus dealt with each disciple differently. To doubting Thomas he said, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands.” To Peter, who had failed, he gave a fresh commission three times. Jesus did not use one mold for everyone, yet each person knew for certain they were loved.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light into my heart. I confess that sometimes I compare my children and favor the one who is more obedient, more like me, or who makes me look good. Forgive me, and heal the child who feels less loved. Teach me to see each child through your eyes, so that every one of them knows they are deeply loved. Amen.
acts: Write down the comparing phrases you often use, such as “Why can’t you be like your brother…”, and decide not to say them this week
Think about which child has had the least of your attention lately, and give that child fifteen minutes of your undivided time today
Ask your spouse, “Do you think I favor one of our children?”
lessons.noon: “His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him” — Lord, keep favouritism from planting bitterness in our home.

fam.key: Mom and Dad love every child.

lamb.do: Hold each child in turn, say their name, and kiss their forehead.
lamb.say: [Name], you are Mom and Dad’s one and only treasure.

sprout.story: Mommy had three children: Big Bao, Middle Bao and Little Bao. Little Bao asked, “Mommy, who do you love best?” Mommy took out a candle and lit it. “This is my love,” she said. She used it to light a second candle, then a third, then a fourth. “See?” said Mommy. “I gave my love to Big Bao, Middle Bao and Little Bao. Did my flame get smaller?” “No!” said Little Bao. “That’s right. My love never gets divided. Everyone gets all of it.”
sprout.ask: Why do you think Mommy’s love does not get smaller?
sprout.do: With a grown-up helping, light a few small candles or switch on a few flashlights one at a time. As you light each one, say a family member’s name: “Mommy loves you with all her heart!”

soldier.story: Jacob had twelve sons, but he loved Joseph most and gave him a beautiful coat of many colors. None of the other sons had one. His brothers saw it and felt hurt. They grew to dislike Joseph more and more, and would not even speak kindly to him. Their father’s favouritism opened a deep crack between the brothers. Later, many sad things happened in that family. The Bible shows us that favouritism pulls family members apart.
ask: If you were one of Joseph’s brothers and saw that coat, what would you be thinking?
Have you ever felt that Mom or Dad loved someone else more? Can you tell us about it?
soldier.do: Each child writes or draws a picture of “a time I felt loved by Mom and Dad” and gives it to the parents. The parents write each child a note: “What I love most about you.”

youth.talk: I want to ask you a question that might feel a bit awkward: do you think I play favorites? When I was young, I often felt that the grown-ups preferred one of my brothers or sisters, and I still remember how that felt. I am afraid I might be repeating it without noticing. You can tell me honestly. I will not be angry, and I will not repeat it to your brothers and sisters.
ask: In what ways do you feel I treat you differently? Which differences seem reasonable, and which feel unfair?
Do you think “fair” means everyone gets the same, or that everyone gets what they need?
youth.do: Each parent arranges a one-to-one outing with each child and asks, “When do you feel most loved by me?” Just listen and take notes.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for loving each one of us equally. Help Mom and Dad not to play favorites, and help us brothers and sisters not to compare ourselves with each other, but to love one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Am I My Brother’s Keeper?
lessons.theme: I believe: siblings are companions, not rivals

v: The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?
If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
The LORD said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”

lessons.still: Read slowly what God said to Cain: “Why are you angry?” Imagine God asking your child, and you, in the same gentle way. Be still and listen for his voice.
teach: The first pair of brothers in the Bible ended in tragedy. God accepted Abel’s offering, and Cain became angry and downcast. But before the tragedy happened, God came to Cain and asked, “Why are you angry?” Then he warned him: “Sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” God saw jealousy sprouting in Cain’s heart and warned him early. Jealousy between siblings is real. Parents need not be shocked, but they should pay attention early.

After Cain’s sin, God asked, “Where is Abel, your brother?” Cain answered, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” It was an attempt to dodge responsibility, yet it asked a good question. The Bible’s answer is yes: we are to look after one another. John writes, “he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” Loving God and loving family cannot be separated.

A change of viewpoint: from a human angle, siblings are rivals competing for parents’ attention, toys and resources. From God’s angle, siblings are companions he placed beside us to look after one another and grow together. Parents can help children put jealousy and anger into words, not only say “You mustn’t be angry.” And let your children know, “You are your brother’s and sister’s keeper.” Today, write down your own “I believe” declaration.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Changing your beliefs changes your life. When parents are convinced that siblings are companions, they stop motivating children through comparison and start nurturing them through cooperation. Parents must first lay down their own comparing of their children with other families’ children, and then their children can learn to lay down comparing themselves with their siblings.
q: Who is God? — God cared about Cain’s anger before Cain sinned. What kind of heart do you see in God?
Who am I? — Am I motivating my children through comparison and competition, and unintentionally turning them into rivals?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe my children are…; I believe God wants to…
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the Son of God, yet he is not ashamed to call us brothers. He does not compete with us. He gave his life for us, so that we could become children in God’s family. Jesus is the best big brother of all, and he watched over his brothers and sisters all the way to the cross.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for caring about Cain when anger first stirred in his heart. Please also watch over the jealousy and sense of unfairness in my children’s hearts. I believe my children are companions to one another, not rivals. I believe you placed them together so that they would look after each other. Help me stop motivating them by comparison and instead bind them together with love. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” sentences: I believe my children are companions; I believe jealousy can be spoken about and healed; I believe they are to look after one another
When a child shows jealousy today, help them name the feeling: “Do you feel that I care more about your brother?”
Give a child a “caring” task, such as an older brother preparing his younger brother’s water bottle, and praise him for it
lessons.noon: “This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother.” — Lord, help the children in our home to look after one another.

fam.key: I will take care of my brothers and sisters.

lamb.do: Let the older child help with the baby’s bottle or diaper, or sing the baby a song. Stand nearby and praise them for being a good big brother or sister.
lamb.say: You are taking care of your little brother (sister). Well done!

sprout.story: Little Lamb Mia had a baby brother who followed her everywhere, and she found it so annoying. One day her brother got lost in the meadow and cried loudly. Mia heard him, ran to find him, and led him home by the hand. Mama Sheep said, “Thank you for looking after your brother!” “Because he’s my brother!” said Mia. From that day on, Mia did not find her brother annoying any more, because she was his keeper.
sprout.ask: How can you look after your brothers and sisters or friends?
sprout.do: Play the “keeper” game: one person closes their eyes while the other leads them slowly around the living room so they don’t bump into anything. Then swap.

soldier.story: Cain and Abel were the first brothers in the Bible. God was pleased with Abel’s gift, and Cain became very angry and jealous. God came and asked Cain, “Why are you angry?” God reminded him to master the anger in his heart. But Cain did not listen, and later he did something terrible and hurt his brother. God asked him, “Where is Abel, your brother?” Cain said, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” He meant, “He is not my business!” But God meant: you should look after your brother.
ask: Why did God come and ask Cain “Why are you angry?” before he did anything wrong?
What can you do when you feel jealous of a brother, sister or friend?
soldier.do: Each person writes a card that says “I am [name]’s keeper”, adds one caring thing they will do for that person this week, and gives it to them.

youth.talk: Cain asked God, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” I think many people think that way today: everyone lives their own life and owes nobody anything. But the Bible says that those who love God must love their brothers and sisters too. I also admit that sometimes I compare you with your brothers and sisters, which makes you feel more like competitors. That is not your fault. It is something I need to change.
ask: Are you and your brothers and sisters more like teammates or rivals? Why?
Is there any jealousy or sense of unfairness in your heart toward a brother or sister? Would you like to talk about it?
youth.do: Parent and child think of one thing an older sibling can do to help a younger one (or the other way round), such as teaching homework or exercising together, and try it once this week.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for my brothers, sisters and friends. Help me not to be jealous, and teach me to take care of them, just as Jesus takes care of us. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Be Tenderly Affectionate, Prefer One Another
lessons.theme: Start today making your children teammates

v: In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

lessons.still: Think about where your children are likely to clash today: the TV remote, the seat in the car, the last chicken wing? Ask the Lord to help you prepare a “teammate” plan before it happens.
teach: Paul says, “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another.” He also says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.” Among siblings, the hard part is often not weeping together but rejoicing together: when one wins a prize, the other feels a pang; when a sister gets a birthday present, her sibling sulks. Learning to be glad for a brother or sister is a lifelong lesson.

Parents can deliberately turn children into teammates. First, give them shared tasks: wash the car together or prepare breakfast together, rather than “see who finishes first.” Second, let them praise each other: at dinner, take turns saying one thing “I appreciate about you.” Third, give each child one-to-one time. When a child’s “love tank” is full, they have less need to fight their siblings for attention.

Avoid creating opposition as well. Don’t say “Whoever finishes eating first wins,” don’t praise one child in front of another, and don’t make the older child always give way to the younger. Work out turn-taking with your children, such as the elder chooses on odd days and the younger on even days, so that fairness can be seen. Start today with one small team task.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than things, and relationships matter more than possessions. Remotes, seats and toys are only “things”, but siblings are a lifetime relationship. When parents teach children to give up things for the sake of relationships, they are teaching them the self-emptied life: let others go first, and keep the focus on Jesus.
q: Who is God? — God delights when brothers are tenderly affectionate and prefer one another. What does that show you of his hope for the family?
Who am I? — Without noticing, am I leading my children to cooperate or to compete?
How should I respond? — What shared task will I give my children today?
lessons.jesus: After meeting Jesus, Andrew “first found his own brother, Simon,” and said, “We have found the Messiah!” Then he brought him to Jesus. The loveliest thing siblings can do is lead one another to Jesus. These two brothers later became disciples of Jesus together.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for letting Andrew bring his brother to you. Make the children in our home teammates for one another, tenderly affectionate and ready to prefer each other, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep. Give me wisdom to arrange cooperation instead of competition, and to watch over each child’s heart. Amen.
acts: Arrange a shared task for your children today, and celebrate together when it is done
At dinner, let each child say one thing they appreciate about a brother or sister
Work out with the children a turn-taking rule for something they often argue about
lessons.noon: “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,” — Lord, help our children be each other’s teammates today.

fam.key: We are all on the same team!

lamb.do: Let two children clap together or roll a ball to each other, and cheer each time they catch it.
lamb.say: You are great teammates. Playing together is so much fun!

sprout.story: Big Brother and Little Sister both wanted the window seat. “I want it!” said Brother. “I want it!” said Sister. Dad said, “Today is an odd day, so Brother sits by the window. Tomorrow is an even day, so Sister will.” Brother thought for a moment and said, “Sister, you go first. You look like you really want to see the view today.” Sister was so happy that when they got out of the car, she shared her little cookies with Brother.
sprout.ask: What would you be willing to let a brother, sister or friend have?
sprout.do: Play the “After you” game with the whole family: set out a plate of fruit, and before anyone takes a piece they must say, “After you,” and let someone else go first.

soldier.story: Jiaxin and her brother Haoran in Hong Kong were always arguing over whose turn it was to wash the dishes. One day Mom said, “From today you are the Dishwashing Team. One washes, one dries, and when you finish you choose a song for the whole family to sing.” On the first day they still bickered. By the third day Haoran was trying to out-joke his sister, and Jiaxin laughed as she washed. Mom noticed that when the children shared a goal, they argued less.
ask: Why did Jiaxin and Haoran argue less once it became “the Dishwashing Team” instead of “whose turn”?
What kind of “team” could you form with your brothers and sisters (or family)?
soldier.do: Form a “sibling team” (or parent-and-child team) and take charge of one household job this week. Choose your own team name, and report to the family at the weekend.

youth.talk: When you argue, I often act as referee, and then both of you feel I am being unfair. I want to try something different. Instead of deciding who is right and wrong, I want to find ways for you to do things together and enjoy each other. You are older now, and you have real influence among your brothers and sisters. If you are willing, I would like you to help me think about it.
ask: What do you most enjoy doing together with your brothers and sisters?
When a brother or sister has good news, what do you honestly feel inside?
youth.do: Invite your child to plan a small surprise for a sibling, such as an encouragement card before an exam, or a little celebration on their birthday.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for making us all one team. Help us give way to each other, encourage each other, and be happy together. Amen.

lessons.title: From Cain and Abel to Joseph’s Reconciliation
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: God can mend broken sibling relationships

v: Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.

lessons.still: Look back over this week and picture your children together: cooperating, arguing, making up. Remember your own story with your brothers and sisters too. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and believe that he can mend.
teach: Genesis begins with Cain killing Abel, goes on to the rivalry between Esau and Jacob, and then to Joseph sold into Egypt by his brothers. The wounds between brothers grow heavier with each generation. But the story does not end in brokenness. Years later Joseph says to his brothers, “I am Joseph, your brother,” and then, “Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.”

Joseph “fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept,” and “kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.” Remember how, years earlier, his brothers “couldn’t speak peaceably to him”? Now they could finally talk. Even earlier than this, Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him, and the two of them wept. God can mend sibling relationships that look beyond repair.

This week we have learned that siblings are companions God gave us; that parents must not play favorites; that jealousy should be spoken about early; and that children can be teammates. Today, review honestly: have I compared or favored? Have there been better moments between the children? Perhaps you also have something unresolved with your own brothers and sisters. Ask God to begin the mending in you, so that your children can see an example of reconciliation.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parent first, then the children. If a parent still has unresolved hurt with their own brothers and sisters, the children will see it, and they will learn from it. Review, adjust, repeat: when parents take the first step toward reconciliation, they give the next generation the best example. That is the multiplication of life.
q: Who is God? — God turned the hurt in Joseph’s family into grace that preserved life. Do you believe he can do the same in your home?
Who am I? — Have I compared or favored this week? Is there a relationship with my own brothers and sisters that needs mending?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I adjust next week, and how exactly will I do it?
lessons.jesus: While Jesus was teaching, even his own brothers did not believe in him. But after his resurrection and ascension, the Bible records that his brothers joined the disciples, praying with one accord. Jesus, who was not understood by his own siblings, finally saw his family change. This brings hope to every family with a broken sibling relationship.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for mending Joseph’s family, and for being able to mend ours. This week I saw that I compared and favored. Forgive me, and heal the sense of unfairness in my children’s hearts. If there is still hurt between me and my own brothers and sisters, give me courage to take the first step. Let the children in our home grow up in reconciliation and love one another all their lives. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse: what was the loveliest moment between the children this week? Did we compare or favor without meaning to?
Ask your children, “This week, were Mom and Dad more like Jesus? Did anything feel unfair to you?” Just listen, and say thank you
Write down next week’s adjustment. If you have a relationship with your own brother or sister that needs mending, pray about it and consider making a phone call
lessons.noon: “He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.” — Lord, mend every sibling relationship in our home.

fam.key: God can make brothers and sisters friends again.

lamb.do: After two children have quarreled, hold them together in your arms and let their little hands touch.
lamb.say: We’re friends again. You are each other’s good friends.

sprout.story: Joseph’s brothers had been very unkind to him and sold him far away. Many years later Joseph was a great ruler in Egypt, and his brothers came to buy grain but did not recognize him. Joseph said, “I am your brother Joseph!” The brothers were terrified. But Joseph was not angry. He hugged his brothers, cried, and forgave them. From that day they were a family again.
sprout.ask: Why was Joseph able to forgive his brothers?
sprout.do: Act out Joseph’s story together: one person is Joseph and the others are his brothers. When Joseph says, “I am your brother Joseph,” everyone hugs.

soldier.story: When Joseph was young, his brothers sold him as a slave in Egypt, and he suffered a great deal. Later God made him the ruler of Egypt, second only to Pharaoh. When famine came, his brothers traveled to Egypt to buy grain, and Joseph recognized them. He could have taken revenge, but he chose to forgive. He told his brothers not to blame themselves, because God had sent him ahead to save their lives. He cried as he hugged his brother Benjamin, and then he hugged his other brothers and cried. Brothers who had not spoken kindly for many years finally started talking again.
ask: Joseph had the power to take revenge. Why did he choose to forgive?
Is there anything that needs to be put right between you and a brother, sister or friend?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person shares one thing they are thankful for about a brother or sister (or family member) this week, and one thing they would like to do together next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: I have read the story of Joseph and his brothers many times, and this time it touched me in a special way. I have things with my own brothers and sisters that have gone unsaid for years. I don’t want that to happen to you when you grow up. This week we talked about favouritism and comparing. I want to admit that I have not done well in this area, and I would like you to give me a chance to change.
ask: Have you noticed any small change in how we brothers and sisters get along this week?
If there is something between you and a brother or sister that needs mending, what might the first step be?
youth.do: If a parent has a sibling relationship that needs mending, share with your children how you plan to take the first step (for example, a phone call), so they can see an example of reconciliation.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for bringing Joseph and his brothers back together. Help the brothers and sisters in our family forgive each other, love each other, and be good friends all our lives. In Jesus’ name, amen.

41.memT: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!

mem.t: If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

sat.t: Family Day: The Great Teamwork Challenge
sat.d: Set up three games that no one can do alone: a three-legged walk across the living room, stacking ten paper cups using only one hand each from two people, and carrying a balloon on a towel through an obstacle course as a whole family. Deliberately put the two children who quarrel most on the same team. After each game, ask, “How did you disagree just now? How did you sort it out?” Finish with a snack together, and let each child say to a sibling, “Thank you for helping me.” Then hold hands and bless one another.

sun: What do your children quarrel about most this week? Do you usually act as judge, police officer, or peacemaker?
“If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” Who is hardest for you to be at peace with? How does that affect the way you handle your children’s conflicts?
Which step of making peace would you like to teach your children next week? How could you share it with another family struggling with sibling conflict?

lessons.title: Be at Peace with All, as Much as It Is Up to You
lessons.theme: Peace does not mean no conflict, but being able to make up after conflict

v: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

lessons.still: Recall the last time your children quarreled: the crying, the accusations, the slammed door. Don't analyze who was right. Just say to the Lord, “Lord, our home needs your peace.” Be quiet for a moment and let his peace enter your heart first.
teach: It is Saturday morning, and war has broken out again in the Lins’ living room in Taipei. The older brother and the younger brother are fighting over the remote. “He grabbed it first!” “He’s been watching for ages!” Mom rushes out of the kitchen wanting only one thing: quiet. Many parents know this. Sibling conflict is like the weather: it comes every day, and often when you are most tired. We cannot help sighing: why can’t a family just get along?

Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” That is honest. “If it is possible” admits that peace cannot always be achieved, because what the other person does is not in our hands. But “as much as it is up to you” means our own part must not be left undone. Paul then gives concrete direction: repay no one evil for evil, don’t take revenge, overcome evil with good. These are exactly the three things siblings most need to learn: don’t hit back, don’t get even, and take the first step with something kind.

Conflict is like a fire. Revenge adds firewood; overcoming evil with good pours on water. A parent’s most important task is not to put out the fire for the children every time, but to teach them to pick up the bucket themselves. A peaceful home is not one that never quarrels, but one that knows how to turn back and make up afterward. This week we will learn to move from being a referee to being a peacemaker, teaching our children to walk the road of reconciliation themselves.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The root of sibling conflict is often the self-ruled life that says, “I want to win, I want to be king.” When parents first live the self-emptied life and refuse to repay evil for evil, children can see what peace looks like. People matter more than things. Don't hurt a brother over a remote control.
q: Who is God? — God is the just God who says, “Vengeance belongs to me,” and the God of peace who calls us to overcome evil with good. What reassurance does that bring you?
Who am I? — When my children fight, do I overcome evil with good, or repay evil for evil with a louder voice?
How should I respond? — When my children clash today, what will I do first to “pour water” rather than “add firewood”?
lessons.jesus: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” On the cross he prayed for those who nailed him there, overcoming the greatest evil with the greatest good. Jesus not only taught peace; he became the way for us to be reconciled with God and with one another.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, I confess that I often just want the house to be quiet, and I lack the patience to teach my children to make peace. Sometimes I repay evil with evil myself, shouting back when I am shouted at. Fill me first with your peace, so that I become someone who pours water on my children's conflicts. Give me wisdom to teach them, step by step, to overcome evil with good. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” and stick it where the children quarrel most
When the children clash, take three deep breaths before you speak
At bedtime ask your children, “Did anyone be kind to you today? Were you kind to anyone?”
lessons.noon: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Lord, today at home help me answer every unpleasant moment with kindness.

fam.key: Don’t hit back. Answer with love.

lamb.do: When two children grab the same toy, crouch down and give each a hug, then bring out a second toy and gently help their hands touch.
lamb.say: We don't grab. We take turns. God likes it when we play nicely.

sprout.story: Two little goats met in the middle of a very narrow log bridge. White Goat said, “I'm going first!” Black Goat said, “No, I'm going first!” They pushed and butted each other, and splash! Both tumbled into the river and got soaking wet. The next day the two goats met on the bridge again. This time one said, “I'll lie down, and you can walk over my back!” Both crossed safely. The Bible says: do all you can to live at peace with everyone.
sprout.ask: If you were a goat, what would you do?
sprout.do: Act out the two goats with your child: once butting each other, once saying “You go first.” Ask which way felt happier.

soldier.story: Paul wrote to the Christians in Rome, “Repay no one evil for evil.” It means that when someone treats you badly, you shouldn't pay them back in the same way. That is hard! When your brother wrecks your project, you want to wreck something of his. When your sister shouts at you, you want to shout louder. But Paul says to “overcome evil with good”: beat a bad action with a good one. That is not weakness. It is a braver kind of strength than revenge. It is like chess: a real master doesn't try to capture a piece with every move, but knows how to make the whole game go well.
ask: Has there been a time lately when you really wanted to repay evil with evil? What happened?
To overcome evil with good, what could you do for the person you quarrel with most?
soldier.do: This week each person chooses one family member and secretly does something kind for them. On Friday evening at dinner, reveal “Who was my secret angel?”

youth.talk: To be honest, the way Mom and Dad handle your arguments is often not very fair. Sometimes we only listen to whoever cries the loudest, and sometimes we just want it to be over. Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” He admits not every relationship can be perfect, but we must do our part. This is not only about brothers and sisters. At school and in group chats we all meet moments when we badly want to hit back.
ask: Do you think “overcoming evil with good” works in real life? Can you give an example?
When we deal with conflict between you and your siblings, what feels most unfair to you?
youth.do: This week, find time to listen to each child alone about “what feels unfair to me.” Only ask and listen, and finish by saying, “Thank you for telling me.”

fam.pray: Dear Father, help each one of us not to hit, not to shout, and not to take revenge, but to answer with love and kind actions. Let our home have your peace. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Who Made Me a Judge over You?
lessons.theme: A parent is not a judge, but one who leads children back to the heart

v: One of the multitude said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?”
Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to take you back to your reaction the last time your children clashed. What did you say? What was your tone? What did you most want in your heart? Don't rush to give yourself a grade. Just let him gently shine his light: “Lord, what kind of parent was I then?”
teach: Someone in the crowd called out, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” It was a classic quarrel between brothers over property. He wanted Jesus to be the judge and rule in his favor. But Jesus answered, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?” Then, instead of dividing the estate, he pointed to a deeper problem: covetousness. Jesus did not get caught up in a verdict about who was right. He led the man to see his own heart.

When children fight, parents tend to play certain roles. The Judge is busy investigating who hit first and deciding who must apologize. The Police Officer shouts louder to crush it: “All of you, go to your rooms!” The Avoider puts on headphones and pretends not to hear. The Favorite-Picker always says, “You're the older one. Give way.” Each can stop the fight for now, but none teaches the children to reconcile, and each may plant the seed in their hearts: “Mom and Dad aren't fair.”

James asks, “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” The answer is desires in the heart: I want, I can't have, so I fight. A child grabs a toy, but what he is really fighting for is “I want to be seen, I want to win.” Parents are the same. We are quick to pass judgment often because we are tired, want quiet, or want control. Today, ask yourself honestly: in my children’s conflict, what do I want most, their peace or my own peace and quiet?
lessons.light: 321 Light: Deal with the parent's heart first, then the child's behavior. When parents sit on the judge's seat as king, children learn to take their complaints to the king. When parents humbly return to the place of steward and let Jesus be king of the home, children learn to bring their conflicts to Jesus.
q: Who is God? — Jesus did not rush to judge, but saw through to the covetousness in the heart. How does he see the quarrels in our home?
Who am I? — When my children fight, am I more like a judge, a police officer, an avoider, or a favorite-picker? What do I really want in my heart?
How should I respond? — Next time my children quarrel, will I ask less “who started it?” and more about what is going on in their hearts?
lessons.jesus: Jesus refused to be the judge of the inheritance, not because he did not care about fairness, but because he saw that what the man needed most was not to win his case but to have his heart healed. With the words, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness,” he brought the man back to the real issue. He wants to lead our children just as gently.
