lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I confess that when my children fight, I am often quick to play the judge, or to make everyone be quiet by shouting, and sometimes I have favored one child. What I want is often my own quiet rather than their reconciliation. Forgive me, and help me, like you, to see the hearts behind my children’s quarrels and gently lead them back to you. Amen.
acts: Write down the role you most often play in your children's conflicts, and a one-sentence confession to God
When your children quarrel today, try asking first, “What do you want most in your heart?”
If you have favored one child, find a chance today to say to the other, privately, “Last time I didn’t listen to you properly. I’m sorry.”
lessons.noon: “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?” — Lord, help me not to rush to judge but to lead my children back to you.

fam.key: When we fight, look at our hearts first.

lamb.do: When your child cries from anger, put a hand on their chest and breathe slowly with them. When they settle, give them a hug.
lamb.say: You're very angry. Mommy knows. Let's breathe in and out slowly together.

sprout.story: Xiaole and his little sister both wanted the window seat, and they were arguing loudly in the car. Xiaole shouted, “Dad, say it's mine!” Dad pulled over, turned around and said, “I'm not going to be the judge. I want to ask about your hearts first. Why do you want the window seat so much?” Xiaole said, “Because I want to see airplanes.” His sister said, “I want to see puppies.” Dad smiled. “Then let's think how both of you can see.”
sprout.ask: When you argue with someone, what do you want most in your heart?
sprout.do: Draw a big heart and ask your child, “When you're fighting, what feeling lives in your heart?” Let them draw or color it in.

soldier.story: A man ran up to Jesus and said, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me!” He thought Jesus would be the judge and rule in his favor. But Jesus said, “Who made me a judge over you?” Then he warned everyone to be careful about greed. Jesus knew the real problem when brothers fight is not how the property gets divided but the wanting more in their hearts. James also says fights come from the “I want” in our hearts. What we grab may be a tablet or the last chicken wing, but behind it is often “I want to win.”
ask: The last time you argued with a brother or sister, what were you fighting over on the surface? What did you really want inside?
Why didn't Jesus just divide the inheritance for that man?
soldier.do: Make a “heart detective card”. Next time you argue, first ask yourself, “What do I want in my heart?” Write it on the card, then go and talk to Mom, Dad or your sibling.

youth.talk: There is a passage that makes Mom and Dad a bit embarrassed. Someone asked Jesus to be judge over an inheritance, and Jesus refused and pointed to the man’s greed instead. When you argue, we often jump into the judge’s seat very quickly. Sometimes we judge unfairly, and sometimes we just want quiet. We want to admit that first. We also want to learn from Jesus: not just who is right and wrong, but the real need behind the conflict.
ask: When you have a conflict with your brothers or sisters, what role do you want Mom and Dad to play?
How much of the conflict between siblings do you think is really not about the thing itself?
youth.do: Agree on a “help signal” with your child: they use it only when they need a parent to step in. At other times the parent steps back and lets them try to sort it out themselves.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, you know our hearts. When we feel like fighting, help us see what we want in our hearts, and teach us to stop first and speak with love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Blessed Are the Peacemakers
lessons.theme: I believe: conflict is God’s school for learning to make peace

v: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

lessons.still: Imagine you are standing in a field with a handful of seeds. The Lord asks, “What will you sow in your home?” Be quiet for a moment, and tell him, “Lord, I want to sow seeds of peace.”
teach: Many parents hold a hidden belief: if my children fight, I have failed as a parent. So when we hear a quarrel, we feel anxious and angry and rush to make it vanish. But Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers.” He did not say, “Blessed are those who have no conflict.” Where there is conflict, peacemakers are needed; where there is a tear, we can see the mender. God has not promised us a home without friction, but he has promised to be with those willing to make peace.

In Kuala Lumpur, Mrs. Chen has three daughters less than five years apart, and there is almost daily warfare at home. One day she changed her angle: “Perhaps God put three such different daughters together so they could learn to make peace at home from childhood.” From then on, she no longer just called a halt. After each quarrel she sat them down to practice naming feelings, saying sorry, and saying “I forgive you.” Her home became a training ground for peace.

James says the wisdom from above is “first pure, then peaceful,” and “the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” Peace is a seed to be planted, not a fruit that appears overnight. Each gentle response from a parent, each time you walk a child through making up, is sowing. Today let us move from “conflict is a nuisance” to “conflict is a school,” from “I must settle this quickly” to “I will sow peace,” and declare: I believe.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint. From the human view, conflict is failure; from God's view, conflict is a chance to grow. The short-term view wants only today’s quiet; the eternal view sees the character a child will carry in getting along with others for life. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on the noisy surroundings.
q: Who is God? — Jesus calls the peacemakers children of God. God himself is the Father who reconciled us to himself. How have you experienced his reconciling love?
Who am I? — Do I see my children's conflicts as my own failure, and so become more anxious and controlling?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe sibling conflict is…; I believe my children can…; I believe God wants to use me to…
lessons.jesus: Paul says, “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation.” Jesus did not come into the world to avoid conflict. He stepped into the brokenness between people and God, and between people and one another, and made peace with his own body. He is the greatest peacemaker and the source of peace in our home.
lessons.pray: Father, I believe you are the God of peace. I believe my children's conflicts are not our family's failure but your school for learning to make peace. Give me the wisdom from above, first pure, then peaceful, gentle and full of mercy. Let me sow peace in our home, and one day see my children bear the fruit of righteousness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations and share them with your spouse or a spiritual companion
After your children quarrel today, don't dig into it. Simply help them say “I'm sorry” and “I forgive you”
Pray for each child: “Lord, make him a peacemaker.”
lessons.noon: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” — Lord, make me a peacemaker in my home today.

fam.key: We are peacemakers.

lamb.do: When two children make up or play together, clap right away and gather them both into a hug.
lamb.say: You're playing together. That's wonderful! God is so happy.

sprout.story: In the forest, Little Rabbit and Squirrel were arguing over one apple, and neither would give way. Then Tortoise crawled slowly over and said, “Please don't fight. Shall we think of a way together?” Squirrel said, “We could cut the apple in half!” Rabbit said, “And I can share my carrot with you!” In the end they all sat together and enjoyed a snack. Jesus said that people who help others make peace are blessed!
sprout.ask: How can you be a Tortoise who helps everyone make up?
sprout.do: Use two soft toys to act out an argument, and let your child be the “peace helper”, thinking of ways to help them make up.

soldier.story: On the mountainside, Jesus taught his disciples, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” Why “children of God”? Because God himself is the greatest peacemaker. Sin once stood between people and God, but God sent Jesus so we could come back to him. When you help two friends make up, or give way first at home, you are doing what God loves to do, and others will see the Father in you. A peacemaker is like a bridge, joining people on both sides.
ask: What is the difference between “making peace” and “ignoring other people’s fights”?
At school or at home, where can you be a “bridge of peace”?
soldier.do: The whole family writes “I believe” cards. Each person writes one sentence beginning “I believe that after a fight we can…” Stick them on the fridge.

youth.talk: Sometimes we think a good Christian family should never argue. That is not true. Mom and Dad argue too, and so do you and your brothers and sisters. Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers.” He did not say there would be no conflict. He said we need people willing to step up and reconnect what is broken. We want to learn this with you, seeing conflict as a chance to learn rather than a disaster.
ask: What is the difference between peace and pretending everything is fine?
Among your friends, is there anyone who needs a peacemaker?
youth.do: A parent shares a true experience of making up after a conflict with someone (or with each other), including what they got wrong, and then invites the child to share.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for sending Jesus so that we could be reconciled to you. Make each person in our family a peacemaker. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Four Steps to Making Up: Stop, Speak, Listen, Reconcile
lessons.theme: Teach your children to walk the road of reconciliation themselves

v: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

lessons.still: Be quiet for a moment and ask the Lord to show you: which relationship at home most needs reconciliation today? Is it between two of the children, or between you and one of them? Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I will go first.”
teach: Jesus gave very concrete guidance on reconciliation: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone.” And when you are offering your gift and remember that your brother has something against you, “first be reconciled to your brother.” Whether I have wronged someone or someone has wronged me, Jesus wants us to take the initiative to “go”, privately, directly and with a heart for reconciliation, not telling tales behind someone’s back or shaming them in public.

From these principles we can teach children four steps. One, Stop: stop hands and mouths and calm down separately, perhaps with a drink of water or a hug with a cushion. Two, Speak: say “I feel… because…” rather than “You always…”. Three, Listen: repeat what the other said: “You're saying you're angry because I took your pen without asking?” Four, Reconcile: say sorry, say “I forgive you,” and think together of a plan for next time.

Here the parent is a coach, not a player. Mr. Huang, a single dad in Singapore, put two small chairs in a corner of the living room and called it the “Making-Up Corner”. When his two sons argued, he would just say, “Go to the Making-Up Corner, do the four steps, and call me if you need me.” At first he had to sit beside them and prompt them. Three months later the brothers often walked over and sat down by themselves. A swimming teacher cannot swim for the child, but can stand at the pool’s edge until the child can swim on their own.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is the key step in changing beliefs. Relationships matter more than things, and people matter more than issues. Teaching the four steps is not only solving today’s conflict but building a lifelong order of relationships in the child’s heart: first reconciled with God, then with oneself and others.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says, “you have gained back your brother.” What he values is winning back the relationship, not winning the argument.
Who am I? — When I have conflict with someone, do I take the initiative to “go”, or wait for the other person to bow first?
How should I respond? — How will I teach my children “stop, speak, listen, reconcile” today, and model it myself first?
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, Jesus prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias for Peter, who had denied him. He did not wait for Peter to apologize first. He went to him, asking three times, “Do you love me?” so that three denials were healed by three expressions of love. He is our example of taking the first step to make peace.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming to me first so that I could be reconciled to God. I confess that I often wait for others to bow first, and I often settle my children's conflicts for them without teaching them to make peace themselves. Today help me to model it first and to teach my children patiently: stop, speak, listen, reconcile. Make our home a place that learns to make up. Amen.
acts: Set up a “Making-Up Corner” with your children: two chairs and a card with the four steps
Model the four steps once today with someone at home you have friction with
When the children quarrel, step back as coach, only reminding them of the steps and not speaking for them
lessons.noon: “If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” — Lord, today help our family win each other back, not win arguments.

fam.key: Stop, speak, listen, reconcile. We can make up.

lamb.do: If your child pushes someone or is pushed, pick them up, help them stroke the other child’s arm, say “sorry” for them, and clap together.
lamb.say: Ouch! Let's rub it better. Say sorry. We're still friends.

sprout.story: Xiaoan grabbed his little brother's building blocks, and his brother cried. Mom said, “Let's play the Making-Up Game! Step one: Stop!” They both put their hands on their heads. “Step two: Speak!” His brother said, “I'm sad because you took my blocks.” “Step three: Listen!” Xiaoan said, “You're sad because I took your blocks.” “Step four: Make up!” Xiaoan said, “I'm sorry.” His brother said, “I forgive you!” They gave each other a hug, then happily built a house together.
sprout.ask: Which of the four steps do you think is hardest?
sprout.do: Make four hand-sign cards: Stop (hands on head), Speak (point to mouth), Listen (touch ears), Make up (hug). Practice together as a family.

soldier.story: Jesus said that if a brother wrongs you, you should go to him privately and tell him what was wrong, and if you remember that someone is unhappy with you, you should go and make peace first. This tells us making up is not waiting for others to come to you but going yourself. We can use four steps: Stop: calm down first. Speak: say how you feel using “I feel…”. Listen: say back what the other person said. Reconcile: say sorry, forgive, and plan for next time. When soccer players argue, a good coach doesn't play for them but teaches them how to work together again.
ask: Why did Jesus say to go “between you and him alone”?
How does “I feel…” sound different from “You always…”?
soldier.do: Role-play as a family. Draw a “conflict card” (for example: your brother used your felt pens without asking), then in pairs act out making up using the four steps.

youth.talk: Jesus said that when a brother sins against you, go and talk “between you and him alone”. That's the opposite of what is common today: we complain in group chats, talk behind backs, even post hints online. Mom and Dad make this mistake too, complaining about people in front of you. Making up takes courage: to speak privately, directly and gently. We want to practice this with you, and we are willing to start with ourselves.
ask: What do you think would be different between talking face to face privately and talking in a group chat?
Is there a relationship right now that you feel you need to “go” and mend? How can we help?
youth.do: A parent first chooses a relationship to repair (it might be with a child), uses the four steps privately this week, and then shares the experience with the child.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching us how to make up. Help us stop when we're angry, and be willing to speak, to listen and to make peace. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Let There Be No Strife Between You and Me
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: we are family, so we would rather give way

v: Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.
Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.”

lessons.still: Replay this past week’s conflicts and reconciliations at home, as if watching a recording. Ask the Holy Spirit to watch with you: where was there peace? Where was there tension? You don’t need to score yourself. Just see honestly.
teach: Abram's herdsmen quarreled with those of his nephew Lot. There were too many flocks and not enough land. As the elder, Abram could have said, “I choose first.” Instead he said, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.” He let Lot choose first: “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.” Abram valued the relationship more than the land, because he believed his real inheritance was in God's hands.

This week we learned to do all we can to be at peace with all, not to play judge, to believe conflict is a school, and the four steps of making up. Today we look back: has conflict at home decreased? Or, when conflict happens, are we making up faster? Peace is not a straight line. It is like learning to ride a bicycle: you fall and scrape your knees, but each time you get up, you are a little closer to balance.

In your review, also look at yourself and your spouse. Children often learn how to fight by watching their parents fight. If there is a cold war or sarcasm between husband and wife, the children will copy it. When parents first model giving way and reconciling in front of their children, it speaks louder than any lecture. Children may not remember what we said, but they will remember how we made up. Next week, choose one thing to adjust, and begin by giving way yourself.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to your proper place. Abram, though the elder, gave way first. That is the self-emptied life. Review, adjust and repeat are the necessary path of change. Humility draws out humility: when parents give way first, children learn to give way, and the family moves from both sides losing to both sides winning.
q: Who is God? — Right after Abram gave way, God said to him, “lift up your eyes, and look.” How does God care for those who are willing to give way?
Who am I? — This week at home, was I the one who gave way first, or the one who insisted on choosing first?
How should I respond? — What is the one thing I will adjust next week? Which family member will I give way to first?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” He is the greatest one who gave way: to be reconciled with us, he gave up the glory of heaven. His giving way was not loss; it was gaining us.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for walking with us through a week of learning peace. I confess that sometimes I only want quiet, sometimes I rush to be the judge, and sometimes I am unwilling to give way myself. Thank you also for letting us see moments when our children made up. Those were all your grace. Make me like Abram, valuing family above gain or loss, and keep sowing peace at home next week. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: which of this week’s conflicts did we handle well? Which need adjusting?
Ask each child, “This week, was Dad/Mom more like Jesus when handling your arguments?” Only listen, and don’t defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as, “When the children fight, I'll ask about feelings first, not who started it”
lessons.noon: “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.” — Lord, today help me value my family more than my own gain or loss.

fam.key: We're family. We can give way first.

lamb.do: Break a cookie in half. Give one half to your child and one half to another family member, and say “for you” together.
lamb.say: We share. We're family.

sprout.story: Grandpa Abram lived together with his nephew Lot. They had so many sheep that their shepherds often argued. Abram said, “We're family. Let's not fight! You choose first where you want to go. If you go left, I'll go right.” Lot chose a beautiful green land. Abram was not angry, because he knew God would take care of him. Later, God really did give Abram many, many blessings!
sprout.ask: Did you let someone choose first this week? How did it feel?
sprout.do: Play the “You choose first” game. Put out two snacks, and take turns letting someone else choose first. Each time, the one who gives way says, “You choose first. We're family.”

soldier.story: Abram and Lot both had large flocks, and their shepherds often argued over pasture and wells. Abram was the elder and could have picked the best land first, but he said, “We are family. Let's not quarrel. You choose first!” Lot chose the Jordan plain that looked the most fertile. Abram didn't complain, and God said to him, “Look in every direction. I will give you all this land.” Giving way looks like losing, but in God’s eyes, the one who is willing to give way and values family is the real winner.
ask: This week, was there a time you gave way to someone in the family? Was there a time you wanted to give way but didn't?
What do you want to practice “You choose first” on next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person shares one thing that went well in making up this week and one thing they want to improve next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All week we have been learning about peace. Honestly, there are still arguments at home, and Mom and Dad sometimes handle them badly. Abram was the elder, yet he let Lot choose first, because he valued the relationship more than gain or loss. We want to admit first that sometimes we refuse to give way in front of you, and often lean toward one side when dealing with conflict. Was there a moment this week when you felt we really changed?
ask: How has the way Mom and Dad handled conflict this week been better than before? What still needs to change?
Where do you think the line is between giving way and being bullied?
youth.do: A parent first apologizes to the children for one time this week they handled a conflict badly, and then together they make a family “peace agreement”, write it down and sign it.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for making us a family. This week we argued, and we made up. Help us be more willing to give way and to love one another next week. In Jesus’ name, amen.

42.memT: If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

mem.t: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.

sat.d: Invite the grandparents to your home, or connect by video call. Prepare snacks and a few old photographs, and let the children be “little reporters”, taking turns to ask: “Where did you live when you were little? What is the most unforgettable thing that happened? How has God helped you?” If an older relative does not yet know the Lord, ask them to share what they are most thankful for in life. Record it on a phone. At the end, ask the grandparents to bless the grandchildren, and let the children pray for the grandparents. Save the recording as “Our Family Story”.

sun: What story about God, or about life, did you receive from your parents or grandparents? How has it shaped you?
What is your biggest tension in living with, or being helped by, older generations in raising children? What light did God shine on it this week?
Which of God’s works in your family will you tell your children next week? How could you encourage another family to begin recording their family testimony too?

lessons.title: Tell the Next Generation
lessons.theme: Faith is a relay across three generations

v: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.
For he established a covenant in Jacob, and appointed a teaching in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children;
that the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children,
that they might set their hope in God, and not forget God’s deeds, but keep his commandments,

lessons.still: Think of an older person who shaped your faith: perhaps a grandmother’s prayers, a father’s word, or an elder at church. Thank God for them in your heart, and then say to the Lord, “Lord, I want to be that person on my children’s faith journey.”
teach: Asaph, the author of Psalm 78, begins by saying that what he will tell is what “we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.” Then he resolves: “We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.” Faith here is like a relay baton: our ancestors pass it to us, we pass it to our children, and our children pass it to theirs.

Look closely at verses 5 to 7 and you will find at least four generations: the fathers who were commanded, us who have heard, the generation yet to come, and their children after them. God’s heart is not to save just one generation, but that each one should “set their hope in God, and not forget God’s deeds.” In a relay race the baton is rarely dropped on the track; it is dropped at the handover. Many families do not lose their faith through persecution. They lose it through busyness, because nobody handed on the baton.

The way to hand it on is simple: tell. Not a lesson, but a story: how God provided when Grandpa lost his job, how he kept Mom safe in childbirth, how he led this family to a new city. Children may not remember our teaching, but they will remember our stories. This week we will see the place of grandparents in this relay, and learn to be united across three generations in telling God's works to the next.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Building what belongs to God is not the work of one generation but of three, four and more. The “3” in 235 is spiritual parents and children: we are our children’s spiritual parents, and grandparents are our spiritual elders. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means every generation tells of his works, not their own achievements.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who works wonders from generation to generation. What event in your family history shows you his faithfulness?
Who am I? — In this faith relay, am I the one who receives the baton, or the one who holds on to it and never hands it on?
How should I respond? — Which of God’s works can I tell my children this week?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples, and “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” He strung together generation after generation of Israel's history so they could see that the center of all these stories was himself. Our family stories must also point to Jesus.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you for the wonders you have done in the generation before me and in my own life. I confess that I am often too busy to tell them, and my children see only my busyness and do not hear your works. Help me to tell the next generation your praises and your strength, and make our family one in heart across three generations as we look to you together. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write down three things God has done in your family’s history, and tell your children one of them tonight
Phone your parents or in-laws and ask, “What is the one thing in your life you are most thankful for?”
Pray one sentence for your children's future children
lessons.noon: “telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.” — Lord, today let my mouth tell of your works.

fam.key: God’s story is passed down from one generation to the next.

lamb.do: Let your child look at photos of Grandpa and Grandma, point to each person and say their name, and then kiss the photo.
lamb.say: This is Grandpa and Grandma. They love you so much, and God loves you so much.

sprout.story: Enen asked Grandma, “Grandma, did you know Jesus when you were little?” Grandma stroked her head and said, “When I was little, our family was very poor. Once there was a flood and our house was under water. The church uncles and aunties brought us food and prayed for us. That's when I got to know Jesus. Later I told your mom, and now it's my turn to tell you.” Enen said, “Then when I grow up, I'll tell my children too!”
sprout.ask: Which story about Jesus would you like to tell your own children one day?
sprout.do: Play “Pass It On”: Dad whispers, “God loves our family,” and each person whispers it to the next. See whether the last person has it right.

soldier.story: Long ago, the Israelites had a habit: parents told their children what God had done, and when the children grew up, they told their own children. Psalm 78 says we will not hide these things, but will tell the next generation about God’s wondrous deeds. Why? Because if one generation doesn't tell, the next will forget God. It is like a relay race. However fast you run, if the baton is dropped at the handover, the whole team loses. The faith stories you hear now are meant to be handed on to someone else one day.
ask: Do you know a story of how God helped our family?
If you had to hand your faith on to the next generation, what would you most want to tell them?
soldier.do: Make a book called “Our Family’s Wonders”. Tonight ask Mom and Dad to tell one way God has helped our family, and you write or draw it as page one.

youth.talk: Sometimes you may find it tiresome when Mom and Dad or Grandpa and Grandma talk about the old days. We felt the same once. But when we grew up we found that those stories hold clues to how God has led our family. The psalm says to tell the generation to come. We want to admit that we have told too little, or turned it into lecturing. This week we would like to try telling it differently.
ask: Which story about God in our family has made the deepest impression on you?
Why do you think so many young people today don't catch the faith of the older generation?
youth.do: A parent and a child go for a one-to-one walk. The parent shares how they came to faith, or the lowest point in their faith, and the child is free to ask questions.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for all the wonderful things you have done in Grandpa and Grandma, in Mom and Dad, and in us. Help us to remember them and to tell others your story. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Am I a Wall or a Bridge?
lessons.theme: Seeing your own heart in the tension of multi-generational parenting

v: Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.

lessons.still: Think of the last time you disagreed with your parents or in-laws about raising the children. What feeling rose up in you? Hurt, anger, guilt, or helplessness? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and say, “Lord, let me see myself.”
teach: Moses was a leader God used greatly, yet he sat alone from morning to evening judging the people, and he was nearly worn out. His father-in-law Jethro saw it and said plainly, “The thing that you do is not good.” For a great leader, that is not an easy thing to hear. But Jethro went on to explain why, offered a solution, and added a blessing: “God be with you.” More remarkably, “Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.” Between the two generations, one spoke with tact and the other listened with humility.

Three-generation families today are often stuck in parenting tension. In Penang, the Huangs, a two-income couple, leave their two children with Grandma. She dotes on her grandchildren and offers candy, tablets and chasing after them with spoonfuls of rice, and when Mom gets home and sees it, she is furious. Other families are the opposite: the older generation is very strict and quick to scold, and the young parents ache for their children but dare not speak. Some grandparents live overseas, and the children have only seen them on video calls.

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine a light: in this relationship, what kind of parent am I? The Defensive type, who feels criticized the moment an older person opens their mouth; the Dependent type, who hands the children over entirely but complains the grandparents do a poor job; the Confrontational type, who argues with the older generation in front of the children and leaves them stuck in the middle; or the Grateful Partner, willing to listen, willing to speak, and willing to work things out together. Am I a wall between my children and their grandparents, or a bridge?
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled parent thinks, “These are my children, and I have the final say.” The self-emptied parent remembers that children are God’s inheritance and that both they and the elders are stewards. Pride provokes pride, and all three generations are hurt; humility draws out humility, and all three are blessed. Align with God first, then talk to the elders.
q: Who is God? — God helped Moses through Jethro’s words. Might he also remind me through the words of an older person?
Who am I? — In the parenting tension with my parents or in-laws, am I more Defensive, Dependent, Confrontational, or a Grateful Partner?
How should I respond? — Is there something an older person has said that I need to humbly hear again?
lessons.jesus: At twelve, Jesus was found in the temple “sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions.” He was the Son of God, yet he humbly learned from the elders, and afterward he went back to Nazareth and was obedient to his parents. Jesus showed an attitude that was neither servile nor proud: a clear identity, and a humble ear.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that with my parents or in-laws I am sometimes defensive, sometimes dependent, sometimes confrontational, and often I have neither listened well nor spoken well. Forgive me. Give me a teachable heart like Moses, and wisdom to say what I think with respect and love. Make me a bridge between my children and their grandparents, not a wall. Amen.
acts: Write down the parenting issue that most often causes conflict between you and an older relative, and pray about it
Think of one thing the older generation does well, and thank them for it specifically today
Avoid criticizing the grandparents in front of the children. If you disagree, find a time to talk gently in private
lessons.noon: “So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.” — Lord, give me a teachable heart.

fam.key: We respect our elders, and we learn together.

lamb.do: When Grandpa and Grandma come, welcome them with your child in your arms, and help the child wave and blow a kiss.
lamb.say: Grandpa and Grandma are here! We are so happy. We love them.

sprout.story: Little Bear lived with Papa Bear, Mama Bear and Grandpa Bear. Grandpa said, “Winter is coming. We need to store more honey.” Papa Bear was about to say, “I know already!” But then he thought, Grandpa has lived a long time and knows many things. So he said, “Thank you for reminding me, Dad. Can you teach me how to store it?” Grandpa was delighted. They stored lots of honey together, and no one went hungry all winter.
sprout.ask: What skill have your grandparents taught you?
sprout.do: Phone or video call Grandpa and Grandma, and ask them to teach you a nursery rhyme or a little game.

soldier.story: Moses was the great leader who led the Israelites out of Egypt. Every day, from morning till night, he settled people’s disputes, and he was exhausted. His father-in-law Jethro came to see him and said, “What you are doing is not good. You will wear yourself out.” Then he taught Moses to find capable, God-fearing people to share the work. Moses didn't say, “I'm the leader, so mind your own business.” He listened to his father-in-law’s advice, and everyone's load became much lighter. Even very capable people need to listen to the wisdom of their elders.
ask: Why was Moses willing to listen to his father-in-law? What would have happened if he hadn't?
What good advice have your grandparents given you?
soldier.do: Write a “Thank you for teaching me” card to an older relative, naming one thing they taught you that has helped you.

youth.talk: You may have noticed that Mom and Dad and Grandpa and Grandma think differently about some things: how to eat meals, whether you can use a phone, whether you need extra tutoring. Sometimes we haven't handled it well and have left you stuck in the middle, which is hard. We want to say sorry first. We are learning to be like Moses, willing to listen to our elders, and also learning to say what we think clearly and with respect.
ask: When Mom and Dad and Grandpa and Grandma disagree, how do you feel inside?
What strengths do you see in your grandparents that Mom and Dad should learn from?
youth.do: This week parents sit down privately with the grandparents, thank them first, and then talk through one parenting issue. Afterward, tell the child how it went and what came of it.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for giving us grandparents. Help us respect them, and bring our whole family together to know you and love you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: One Generation Will Commend Your Works to Another
lessons.theme: I believe: our family can be a link in the chain of faith

v: One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.
God, you have taught me from my youth. Until now, I have declared your wondrous works.
Yes, even when I am old and gray-haired, God, don’t forsake me, until I have declared your strength to the next generation, your might to everyone who is to come.

lessons.still: Picture your family as a great tree: the roots are the generation before, you are the trunk, your children are the branches, and your grandchildren are the fruit to come. Quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, let every part of this tree know your name.”
teach: “One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.” This is not a suggestion but the way God’s people live. In Psalm 71, a gray-haired man prays, “Even when I am old and gray-haired, God, don’t forsake me, until I have declared your strength to the next generation.” He did not retire because he was old. He saw his later years as a mission of handing on. Grandparents are not minor characters in a family. They are an essential leg of the faith relay.

But some parents' hearts sink: “My parents don't yet believe,” “No one in my family has ever followed Jesus,” “What my upbringing gave me was not faith but scars.” Mr. Xu in Taichung was the first Christian in his family. His grandfather held ancestral rites every year, and he often felt he stood in a place with no inheritance. Then he understood: every line of inheritance has a first generation. Abraham's father worshiped idols, yet God began a genealogy of faith with him.

Today, shift from the human viewpoint to God’s. From “My family has no spiritual tradition” to “God will begin with my generation.” From “The older ones are already old” to “Their later years still carry a mission to tell.” From “Faith is a personal matter” to “Faith is a relay across three generations.” Wherever you stand in the chain, God can use you. And write your declaration: I believe.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the temporary to the eternal. We are not just raising a child; we are building a spiritual family line. Building what belongs to God begins with one home, with the conviction of one generation. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on the family's past, but on the new thing God will do.
q: Who is God? — God is the God to whom “one generation will commend your works to another”, and his work is never broken by one generation's weakness.
Who am I? — What is my place in my family line? Am I the generation that receives a tradition, or the first generation God is using to begin a new one?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe our family's faith is…; I believe my parents/elders…; I believe my children will one day…
lessons.jesus: Matthew records the genealogy of Jesus, which includes foreign women such as Rahab and Ruth, as well as the story of David's sin. Jesus' family tree was not perfect, but it shows God's faithfulness: in a broken family history he worked out salvation, generation after generation. Our imperfect families are in his hands too.
lessons.pray: Father, I believe you are faithful from generation to generation. I believe the faith of our family does not stop with me but is meant to pass to my children and grandchildren. If my family has not yet come to know you, begin with my generation. If my parents are old, let them still declare your works when they are gray-haired. Let us praise you together across three generations. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations and pray for your parents
If your elders are Christians, ask them to tell your children about one experience of faith; if not, write a one-sentence prayer for their salvation
Draw a family tree and write beside it, “One generation will commend your works to another”
lessons.noon: “One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.” — Lord, let our generation tell the next about you.

fam.key: Our family will praise God, generation after generation.

lamb.do: Take out the family photo. Point from Grandpa and Grandma to Mom and Dad and then to the child, giving a gentle clap for each person.
lamb.say: One, and one, and one. Everyone is God’s treasure.

sprout.story: Little Apple Tree asked Old Apple Tree, “Grandpa, why can I grow apples?” Old Apple Tree said, “Long ago someone planted me. I grew up and bore apples, and the seeds from my apples fell to the ground and grew into your father, and your father grew you.” Little Apple Tree said, “Then I'll bear lots of apples too, so more little trees can grow!” Our family is like that. We pass on Jesus' love from one generation to the next.
sprout.ask: Who would you like to share Jesus' love with?
sprout.do: Draw a tree on paper. Write Grandpa and Grandma on the roots, Mom and Dad on the trunk, and the children’s names on the branches. Pray for each person together.

soldier.story: Psalm 71 is a prayer written by an old man. He says, “God, you have taught me from my youth. Now I am old and my hair is gray. Don't forsake me, so I can tell the next generation of your power.” He didn't say, “I'm old and useless.” He felt he still had an important task: to tell the children God's story. So grandparents aren't only people who help look after us. They are teachers and witnesses on our faith journey.
ask: What life lesson do you think your grandparents most want to tell you?
When you are old, what would you want to tell your grandchildren?
soldier.do: Everyone in the family writes one “I believe” sentence, for example, “I believe God will always take care of our family”, and adds a sentence of prayer for Grandpa and Grandma. Stick them beside the family photos.

youth.talk: In some families faith has been handed down for generations, and in others it began with Dad or Mom. Either way, it is nothing to boast about. Sometimes you may feel that faith belongs to Mom and Dad and not to you. That is normal, because faith cannot be inherited. Every generation has to meet God for themselves. But we believe God is the God to whom “one generation will commend your works to another”, and he wants you to have your own story with him.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “Mom and Dad's faith” and “my own faith”?
In our family line, what do you think God most wants to begin changing with our generation?
youth.do: Parent and child each write a short letter to “our family twenty years from now”, describing their faith and hopes today. Seal the letters and keep them safe.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for loving Grandpa and Grandma, and Mom and Dad, and us. Let our family know you and praise you, generation after generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Set Up the Stones as a Memorial
lessons.theme: Remember God’s works together as a family

v: that this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’

then you shall tell them, ‘Because the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the LORD’s covenant. When it crossed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. These stones shall be for a memorial to the children of Israel forever.’”

lessons.still: Remember one thing God has done in your home: a healing, a provision, a reconciliation, a protection. Let the picture rest in your heart for a moment, and then say to the Lord, “Lord, I don't want to forget.”
teach: When the Israelites crossed the Jordan, the water was cut off before the ark, and the people crossed on dry ground. God told Joshua to take twelve stones from the river and set them up at Gilgal. Why? “When your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’” parents can tell them what God did. God knows that people forget easily, and that children are curious and ask questions. A memorial stone gives children a place to start asking.

Our homes need memorial stones too. The Zhous in Vancouver have grandparents in Taiwan, and the children see them only once a year. Mrs. Zhou placed a glass jar in the living room. Whenever God did something in the family, she wrote it on a small stone and dropped it in: “Grandma’s surgery went well,” “Dad found a job,” “Little sister prayed by herself for the first time.” On every video call, the children rush to show the stones to Grandpa and Grandma, and three generations give thanks together across the screen.

Start today. A memorial doesn’t have to be a stone. It can be a photo album, a wall of pictures or a voice recording. What matters is that God’s works are seen and spoken about. Invite the grandparents to join in as well, and ask them to share the “memorial stones” in their own lives. When the stories of three generations are in the same jar, children will understand that God is not only our family's God but Grandpa and Grandma's God, and the God of the grandchildren to come.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice turns belief into life. Setting up stones turns unseen faith into visible signs and makes one generation’s experience a treasure shared by three. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means every stone points to him, not to our effort.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who opened a way through the Jordan, and who opens a way in our homes. What is the “Jordan” in your family?
Who am I? — Am I someone who often remembers God's works, or one who quickly forgets and remembers only the problems?
How should I respond? — What memorial stone will our family set up today? How will we invite the grandparents to take part?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper Jesus took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “Do this in memory of me.” He turned the giving of his life into a memorial that could be repeated from generation to generation. Every time we take communion, the church is telling of his works, and every family's memorial stones must also point to the Lord who gave his life for us.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for everything you have done in our home. I confess that I often remember the problems and forget your grace. Today help our whole family set up memorial stones, so that the children will ask and we will tell, and so that the grandparents’ stories will be heard. May our home be a home that remembers your works. Amen.
acts: Prepare a jar or a notebook as your family's “memorial stones”
Tonight write down with your children three things God has done in our family and put them in
Phone or video call the grandparents and ask them for one thing in life they are most thankful for, and add it to the memorial stones
lessons.noon: “These stones shall be for a memorial to the children of Israel forever.” — Lord, today help our family set up a stone to remember you.

fam.key: We remember what God has done for our family.

lamb.do: Put a few small stones (or building blocks) into a box with your child, saying “Thank you, God” each time you put one in.
lamb.say: Thank you, God! God loves our family so much.

sprout.story: The Israelites had to cross a big river, but the water was deep and fast. God said, “Let the men carrying the ark step in first!” As soon as their feet touched the water, the river stopped, and everyone crossed on dry ground! God told them to pick up twelve big stones from the river and pile them on the bank. Later, when the children saw the stones and asked, “What are these?” Mom and Dad would say, “These are the sign that God helped us cross the river!”
sprout.ask: If our family were to pile up stones, which thing God did would you want to remember?
sprout.do: Go to the park or garden and pick up some small stones. At home, draw pictures on them with colored pens and put them in the “memorial jar”.

soldier.story: When Joshua led the Israelites across the Jordan, God made the river stop and the people crossed on dry ground. God told twelve men, one from each tribe, to carry a big stone from the middle of the river and pile them up as a monument. God said that when children later asked, “What do these stones mean?”, they were to tell them what God had done. The monument is like a three-dimensional history book, so that every generation remembers that God once opened a way for us.
ask: If our family set up a monument, which three things God has done would you want written on it?
Why did God use stones to remind people? What could we use to remind ourselves?
soldier.do: Make a “memorial jar” together. Each person writes or draws one thing God has done in our family and sticks it on a stone. Ask Grandpa and Grandma for one, and put them in the jar together.

youth.talk: After the Israelites crossed the Jordan, God told them to set up stones so that later generations would ask, “What do these stones mean?” Our family has been through some “Jordans” too: moving house, illness, money problems, relationships that broke and were mended. We just seldom stop to say, “God did this.” Mom and Dad often remember the problems and forget to give thanks. Today we'd like to look back with you.
ask: Which difficult time in our family do you remember? How did you feel then?
Looking back, where did you see God's help?
youth.do: Put together a cloud photo album or short video with your child, titled “Our Family’s Memorial Stones”. Choose five moments of God's leading, add captions, and share it with the grandparents.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for all you have done for our family. Help us not to forget, and help us to tell Grandpa and Grandma and our friends about your works. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Children’s Children Are the Crown of Old Men
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: three generations of one heart, glory to one another

v: Children’s children are the crown of old men; the glory of children is their parents.
The women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you today without a near kinsman. Let his name be famous in Israel.
He shall be to you a restorer of life and sustain you in your old age; for your daughter-in-law, who loves you, who is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him.”
Naomi took the child, laid him in her bosom, and became nurse to him.

lessons.still: Think back on this week's interactions with your parents and with your children, like turning the pages of a family album. Some photos are warm, and some are blurred or hard to look at. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, without rushing to conclusions.
teach: “Children’s children are the crown of old men; the glory of children is their parents.” This proverb paints a lovely cycle across three generations: grandchildren are a crown for the grandparents, and parents are the glory of their children. It is not one generation pressing down on another, or one resenting another, but each becoming the other's splendor. It is like a cord of three strands: each strand needs the other two to bear the load. Grandparents' experience, parents’ strength and children’s laughter, woven together, are the strongest support a family has.

The end of the book of Ruth is exactly this picture. Naomi lost her husband and both sons, and once said to call her Mara, “bitter”. But when her daughter-in-law Ruth gave birth to Obed, the women said to Naomi, “He shall be to you a restorer of life and sustain you in your old age.” Naomi took the child, laid him in her bosom, and became nurse to him. This grandmother and child were not even related by blood, yet he became part of King David's family line. God healed a grandmother’s heart across three generations.

This week we have learned to tell the next generation, to see ourselves in the tension between generations, to believe in the relay of three generations, and to set up memorial stones. Today review honestly: have I respected my elders more? Have I spoken well of them in front of my children? Have I given my children more chances to be close to their grandparents? If there is tension, have I dealt with my own heart first? Review is not for condemnation, but to make the next step steadier.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God first, then myself, then others. Unity of three generations is not a matter of technique but of each generation returning to God first. Humility draws out humility: when parents first respect the grandparents, children learn to respect their parents. Review, adjust, repeat, and the family becomes more like Jesus with each generation.
q: Who is God? — God healed Naomi’s bitterness and gave her hope again through a grandson. How is he working among the three generations in your family?
Who am I? — This week, was I someone who drew three generations closer, or one who pushed them further apart?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I adjust in the three-generation relationship next week? How exactly will I do it?
lessons.jesus: When the baby Jesus was brought to the temple, old Simeon “received him into his arms and blessed God,” and Anna, a prophetess in her eighties, also gave thanks to God. God let two elderly people be the first to welcome the Savior and bless him. In Jesus, the old and the young meet, and the crown joins with hope.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for the grace of having three generations together. I confess that this week I sometimes did not respect my elders, and sometimes widened the distance between my children and their grandparents. Forgive me, and heal the gaps between the generations. May our children be a crown to their grandparents, and may we be the glory of our children. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what was the loveliest moment in our three-generation relationships this week? What most needs adjusting?
Ask your children, “This week, was Dad/Mom more like Jesus in how they treated Grandpa and Grandma?” Only listen, and don't defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as a regular weekly call with the grandparents
lessons.noon: “Children’s children are the crown of old men; the glory of children is their parents.” — Lord, let our three generations be glory to each other and not a burden.

fam.key: We are Grandpa and Grandma’s crown.

lamb.do: Make a small paper crown for your child to wear, then carry them to show Grandpa and Grandma, or take a photo and send it to them.
lamb.say: You are Grandpa and Grandma's precious crown!

sprout.story: Grandma Naomi's family had all passed away, and she was so sad that she often cried. Later her daughter-in-law Ruth had a baby boy named Obed. Grandma Naomi held the baby in her arms, so happy, so happy, and there was a smile on her face again! Everyone said, “God has not forgotten Naomi!” The little baby made Grandma happy again. You are Grandpa and Grandma's happy treasure too!
sprout.ask: What can you do to make Grandpa and Grandma happy?
sprout.do: Make a paper crown together and write on it, “I am Grandpa and Grandma's crown.” Take a photo or give it to them.

soldier.story: Proverbs says, “Children’s children are the crown of old men.” A crown is what a king wears on his head, a sign of glory. The Bible says grandchildren are their grandparents’ crown! Naomi once suffered terribly. She lost her husband and sons and felt her life was too bitter to bear. But when her grandson Obed was born, she found joy and hope again. Obed's grandson was the famous King David. A greeting, a drawing or a phone call from you may light up your grandparents' hearts again.
ask: This week, did you make Grandpa and Grandma feel you were their “crown”?
What would you like to do for Grandpa and Grandma next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person shares one thing they are thankful for in the three generations this week, and one thing they want to do for the older generation next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: All week we have been talking about three generations. Honestly, Mom and Dad also have many unspoken feelings about our own parents: gratitude, a sense of debt, and some tension too. What you see may not always be harmony. We want to admit that sometimes we have not been respectful enough to the older generation in front of you, or have left you stuck in the middle. We want to learn together how to help the three generations build one another up more.
ask: This week, where did you see change between Mom and Dad and Grandpa and Grandma? Where does it still need to change?
What kind of relationship do you want with your grandparents? How can we help?
youth.do: As a family, choose one “three-generation activity” for next week, such as a meal together, a walk or a video call, with the child in charge of planning it.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for our grandparents. Keep them healthy and safe, and help us show them more love and respect this week. In Jesus’ name, amen.

43.memT: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.

mem.t: Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.

sat.t: Family Day: A Day to Honor and Thank Our Parents
sat.d: Prepare something together for the older generation: cook the dishes Grandpa and Grandma love, take them for a walk, or post a box of handmade cards and snacks to relatives far away. At the meal, let each child say, “Thank you for what you did for our family…” If an elder has passed away, look at old photos together, talk about the good things they left this family, and thank God for those blessings. Finish by praying together as a family, asking God to bless the generation before us.

sun: What is the easiest part, and what is the hardest part, of honoring your parents?
What blessing from your family of origin do you want to pass on? What pattern do you ask God to stop with your generation?
Looking back over weeks 31 to 44, what is the biggest change in your family? What will you adjust first next week, and how could you walk another family through a family health check?

lessons.title: The First Commandment with a Promise
lessons.theme: Honoring parents is God’s road of blessing for the family

v: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.
Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
“Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise:
“that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.”

lessons.still: Think of your parents, whether they are still living or not, whether you are close or distant. Let the first picture that comes rest for a moment, without judging it. Say to the Lord, “Lord, teach me to see my parents through your eyes.”
teach: The first four of the Ten Commandments are about our relationship with God. Then the fifth turns to the home: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.” In Ephesians Paul points out, “which is the first commandment with a promise.” God places our attitude toward our parents first among our attitudes toward our neighbors, because the first place anyone learns to get along with people is at home.

The word “honor” carries the sense of “giving weight”: giving your parents the standing they deserve. That doesn’t mean blind obedience in everything, and it is not a tool of pressure. Grown children no longer obey as they did when small, but they can still honor their parents: thank them for what they gave, care about their needs, and speak to them with respect. Jesus also rebuked those who used religious excuses to avoid supporting their parents.

For parents raising children, this commandment works in two ways. We are still to honor the generation above us, and our children are watching how we treat our own parents. Mr. Wang in Singapore once spoke impatiently to his mother on the phone. When he hung up, his six-year-old daughter said, “Daddy, you sounded so cross just now.” He suddenly realized that children learn honor not from our demands but from our example.
lessons.light: 321 Light: To honor is to let people be people and God be God. Parents are not God. We need neither to idolize them nor to demonize them. We honor them because God values this relationship. The focus is on Jesus: we honor not because our parents are perfect but because we obey the God who designed the family.
q: Who is God? — God put honoring parents among the commandments and attached a promise to it. Why does he value this relationship so highly?
Who am I? — How do I treat my own parents now? What are my children learning from me, honor or going through the motions?
How should I respond? — What one concrete action can I take today so my parents feel “honored”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for using “Corban”, calling their possessions given to God, as an excuse not to support their parents. Jesus would not let anyone escape the duty of honoring their parents with spiritual language. He himself was obedient to his parents after he was twelve, and on the cross he still cared for his mother. He is the perfect example of honoring parents.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for giving me my parents, and for this commandment with a promise. I confess that sometimes I have been dismissive or impatient with my parents, and even criticized them in front of my children. Forgive me, and teach me to honor them through your eyes. Make me an example to my children, so that they learn honor from me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Phone or message your parents today and thank them specifically for one thing they did for you
Think: the last time I mentioned my parents in front of my children, what tone did I use?
Write a one-sentence prayer for your parents' health, hearts and salvation
lessons.noon: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.” — Lord, teach me to value my parents today.

fam.key: Honor your parents, and God will bless you.

lamb.do: Take your child's little hand and pass a cup of water or a tissue to Grandpa, Grandma or Mom and Dad, then clap together.
lamb.say: Here you are! We love you.

sprout.story: The little ducklings were playing by the pond. Mother Duck had swum all day and was so tired. The smallest duckling, Quack, saw her, ran off, and brought back a big leaf to shade Mother from the sun. Mother Duck was so touched. “Thank you, Quack!” she said. The other ducklings came too. Some rubbed Mother’s back, and some sang to her. The Bible says: honor your mom and dad, and God will bless you!
sprout.ask: How can you be like Quack and help Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Today let your child do one small thing for Mom or Dad: fetch slippers, pass a towel, or sing a song. When it's done, say together, “Honoring Mom and Dad makes God happy!”

soldier.story: On Mount Sinai, God gave the Israelites ten commandments. The fifth one is: “Honor your father and your mother.” Paul said this is the first commandment “with a promise”, meaning God added a blessing to it: that it may be well with you and you may live long. Honoring is not only obeying. It is treating your parents as very important: speaking respectfully, remembering to say thank you, and helping when they are tired. Just as a tree sends nutrients back to its roots, in a healthy family the children turn round and care for and respect their parents.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “obeying” and “honoring”?
Has there been a time lately when you made Mom or Dad feel respected?
soldier.do: Every day this week, do one “honoring task” for Mom or Dad without being asked. Write it on a little card, and on Friday count how many you did.

youth.talk: In Chinese culture, the words “honor your parents” are sometimes used very heavily, as if parents are always right and children can only obey. But the honor the Bible speaks of is “giving weight”: respect, gratitude and care, not blind obedience. Honestly, Mom and Dad haven't done well at this with our own parents either, and sometimes complain about them in front of you. We would like to learn again with you what honoring means.
ask: What do you think is the difference between filial obedience and honor?
What have you learned from watching how we treat Grandpa and Grandma? You can tell us the good and the not so good.
youth.do: Parents honestly ask the child, “Which of our expectations of you seem like reasonable respect, and which make you feel pressured?” Only listen, don't defend, and talk about it again next week.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for my mom and dad and my grandparents. Help me honor them, speak to them gently, and help them with my actions. Please bless our whole family. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Handed Down from Our Fathers, and the Blood of Christ
lessons.theme: Seeing the blessings and the bondages we bring from our family of origin

v: knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers,
but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ,

lessons.still: This lesson may touch deeper places in your heart. Breathe slowly first, and remember that you do not face this alone. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I believe your love is bigger than my past. Gently show me only as much as I can bear, and shine your light there.”
teach: Peter says that we were redeemed “from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers”, not with silver or gold but “with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ.” Everyone brings something from their family of origin. Some of it is precious: diligence, thrift, loyalty, reverence for faith. Some of it is heavy: solving problems by shouting, expressing displeasure with the silent treatment, rarely saying “I love you”, treating grades as worth. Often these things have been “handed down” through generations without our noticing.

The moment we most often notice is when we hear our parents' words come out of our own mouths in front of our children. Mr. Zhang in Ipoh was compared with his cousin by his father all his childhood, and swore he would never do that to his children. One day his son failed an exam, and he blurted out, “Look at your cousin…” The moment it left his mouth, he froze. That sentence had been living in him all along. That night he apologized to his son, and for the first time wept before God over the hurt he had suffered as a child.

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: from my family of origin, what blessings have I brought? What patterns have I brought that are replaying in my home? Seeing is not for blaming our parents, but for bringing these things to the cross. If you experienced violence, abuse or deep trauma while growing up, please don't carry it alone. Seeking professional counseling and the company of your church pastor is both brave and wise.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The second step in changing beliefs is revelation: letting the Holy Spirit light up the places we cannot see. The self-ruled person says, “That's how I was brought up.” The self-emptied person says, “Lord, I am willing to be renewed by you.” Deal with the parent's own heart first, and only then can we stop passing hurt on to the next generation.
q: Who is God? — God redeemed us from the useless way of life handed down from our fathers, not with silver or gold, but with the blood of Christ. What does the price he paid tell us?
Who am I? — From my family of origin, what blessing do I want to pass on? What pattern do I not want to repeat?
How should I respond? — Which inherited pattern am I willing to bring to Jesus today?
lessons.jesus: Paul says, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.” On the cross Jesus bore all brokenness and the consequences of sin. His precious blood is stronger than any family's past. He does not deny our wounds. He carries them, and gives us a new beginning.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for redeeming me with your blood. I bring my family of origin to you. Thank you for the blessings you gave me through my parents, and I give you the hurts and patterns that were handed down. Shine on what I still cannot see, heal the wounds in my heart, and let the unhealthy patterns stop with my generation. Amen.
acts: Draw two columns: on the left, “blessings from my family of origin that I want to pass on”; on the right, “patterns I want to stop with my generation”
Choose one item on the right, entrust it to God in prayer, and tell your spouse or a trusted spiritual companion
If it touches deep pain, contact your church pastor or a professional counselor this week and arrange a conversation
lessons.noon: “knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers,” — Lord, let your blood break every bondage in me that is not from you.

fam.key: Jesus’ love lets us start again.

lamb.do: After your child has finished crying, hold them close, sing a quiet hymn in a gentle voice, and pat their back.
lamb.say: It's all right. Jesus loves you. We can start again.

sprout.story: The elephant family all walked very hard, stomp, stomp, stomp, and trampled the little flowers. Little Elephant learned to stomp too. One day he saw a flattened flower and cried. He was so sad that he asked Mama, “Can I stop walking this way?” Mama said, “Of course. Let's learn to walk gently together!” From that day Little Elephant learned to tiptoe softly, and the flowers bloomed all over the meadow again. Jesus can help us change our bad habits.
sprout.ask: Is there a bad habit you would like to ask Jesus to help you change?
sprout.do: Play “Elephant Walk” with your child: first stomp hard, then walk softly and carefully. Talk about which way is better.

soldier.story: Peter wrote to Christians, saying you have been rescued from a meaningless way of life handed down from your ancestors, not with gold or silver but with the precious blood of Jesus. Every family hands down some habits. Some are good, like being tidy, punctual or loving to read. Others are not, like shouting whenever you're angry, or never saying sorry. It's like programs on a computer: some are useful software and some are viruses. Jesus' salvation is like the strongest antivirus program. It helps us keep the good and clear out the bad.
ask: Which good habit in our family do you think should always be passed on?
Is there a bad habit you wish our whole family would change together?
soldier.do: As a family, make a “family treasure list”: write three good habits to pass on and one bad habit to change together, and stick it on the fridge.

youth.talk: Sometimes Mom and Dad see our own parents in ourselves: the tone of voice, the way we get angry, the anxiety about grades. Some of it is good, and some we don't want to pass on to you. You may have noticed that we sometimes say the very things we hate hearing. Peter says the blood of Christ redeems us from the useless way of life “handed down from your fathers”. We want to face this honestly, and ask for your help.
ask: What patterns do you think get passed down in our family? Which are good, and which would you like to change?
When you see us repeating a bad pattern, how would you like to remind us?
youth.do: A parent honestly shares one pattern from their own family of origin that they are working to change, and asks the child to remind them gently with an agreed signal when they see it.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for loving our family. Help us keep the good habits and change the bad ones, so that our family becomes more and more like you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Becoming the Turning Point of the Family
lessons.theme: I believe: in Christ I can begin a new family story

v: “What do you mean, that you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’?
“As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “you shall not use this proverb any more in Israel.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

lessons.still: Imagine a river bending at a certain spot. The water upstream is still what it was, but from here the river flows in a new direction. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I am willing to let you bend me.”
teach: In Ezekiel's day the Israelites had a popular saying: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.” It meant: my suffering was caused by the generation before, and I am doomed. But God swore, “you shall not use this proverb any more in Israel.” God doesn't deny that the previous generation's influence is real, but he refuses to let it become fate. Before him every person can turn around, and every generation can begin again.

The Ten Commandments say God visits iniquity “on the third and on the fourth generation”, but follow at once with “showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.” Three or four generations against thousands: a hugely lopsided ratio. God's love far outweighs the consequences of sin. Mrs. Li in Taipei is raising a son and a daughter on her own. Her family of origin was full of quarrels and separation, and she often feared she would repeat the pattern. One day she read this passage and wrote in her diary: “I am not the continuation of a tragedy. I am the beginning of a thousand generations of love.”

Paul says, “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Becoming a turning point for the family doesn't come from gritting your teeth with willpower, but from abiding in Christ and letting his life grow in you bit by bit. It also doesn't mean changing completely all at once. Old patterns may still appear, but the direction has turned. Today, let us declare: I believe.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint. From the human view, “I'm doomed to be this way”, to God’s view, “in Christ I am a new creation”; from temporary failure to eternal hope. Change your beliefs and your life changes, change your life and your daily living changes, and one person's change can bring change to a whole family line.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who shows “loving kindness to thousands”, and his grace is far greater than the family's past.
Who am I? — Have I ever believed, “This is just how I am, this is just how my family is, and it can't change”?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe in Christ I am…; I believe that starting with my generation…; I believe my children will one day…
lessons.jesus: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector, despised by everyone, and his family's name was probably already ruined. But Jesus took the initiative to stay at his house, and Zacchaeus repented. Jesus said, “Today, salvation has come to this house.” When one person meets Jesus, the story of the whole house turns a corner. He wants to enter our homes in the same way.
lessons.pray: Father, I believe that in Christ I am a new creation, the old things have passed away, and all things have become new. I believe my family's past cannot decide my children's future, because you show loving kindness to thousands. Make me the turning point of my family, so that the hurt stops with my generation and blessing flows from it. When I am weak and old patterns return, remind me: the direction has turned. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations, read them aloud, and share them with your spouse or spiritual companion
When an old pattern comes back, say to yourself, “In Christ I am a new creation,” and choose a new response
Pray for your children: “Lord, let him receive loving kindness to a thousand generations.”
lessons.noon: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” — Lord, let me live out the new creation today.

fam.key: In Jesus, we are all new.
