lamb.do: In the morning, dress your child in fresh clean clothes, let them look at themselves in the mirror, and kiss their cheek.
lamb.say: A new day, a new you! Jesus loves you.

sprout.story: Little Green, a caterpillar, crawled slowly on the leaves every day and thought she could only ever crawl. One day she went to sleep in a little house called a cocoon. After many days the cocoon opened, and Little Green stretched out a pair of beautiful wings and flew into the sky! She was so surprised. “I'm new!” The Bible says that in Jesus we become new people too.
sprout.ask: In what way would you like Jesus to make you more like him?
sprout.do: Fold or draw a butterfly together, and write on its wings, “In Jesus, I am new!”

soldier.story: The Israelites used to love saying, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.” It meant: if Dad does something wrong, the son is sure to suffer, and nothing can change it. But God said, “You shall not use this saying any more!” Because before God everyone can choose again. Paul also says that in Christ we are a new creation. It's like a satnav that has led you the wrong way. Just press “recalculate route”, and from where you are now you can head in the right direction.
ask: Have you ever felt “That's just how I am, I can't change”?
In what area would you like to ask Jesus to “recalculate the route” for you?
soldier.do: Each person in the family writes one “I believe” sentence, such as, “I believe Jesus can help me change my habit of getting angry.” Read them aloud at dinner and pray for one another.

youth.talk: You may have heard people say, “You're just like your dad,” or “Everyone in your family is like that.” Words like these can sound like a label that says you can't change. In Ezekiel, God says he doesn't want people to use the saying about fathers eating sour grapes any more. Mom and Dad are learning to believe that we don't have to repeat the hurts of the previous generation. We also want to tell you: you don't have to repeat our mistakes.
ask: Is there a saying like “People in our family always…” that you dislike and don't want to become?
What would you like your future home to have in common with ours now, and what would you like to be different?
youth.do: Parents say to the child, “Our mistakes are not your destiny.” Each writes a one-sentence blessing for the other, and sticks it on the bedroom door.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for making us new in Jesus. Help us become more like Jesus every day and pass on good love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Learning to Show Honor at Home
lessons.theme: Today, honor the older generation in action and teach the next

v: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.
Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, how can I honor my parents today?” Perhaps it is a phone call, a meal, a word of thanks, or a prayer of forgiveness. Write down the first thought that comes.
teach: Paul says that children and grandchildren should “learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.” Notice the word “learn”: honor is not natural. It has to be learned and practiced, and the first place to practice is “their own family”. It is easy to be polite to people outside, but being patient with your parents at home is the real test. Our children are watching, and they are learning in the same classroom.

On the cross, in terrible agony, Jesus still saw his mother standing nearby. He said to Mary, “Woman, behold, your son!” and to John, “Behold, your mother!” In the last hours of his life, Jesus arranged care for his mother. Honor is not only a feeling but concrete arrangements: who takes parents to the doctor? Who calls regularly? Who will look after them when they are old?

But some people's parents have passed away, and some have been deeply hurt by their parents, and may still not be safe. Honor doesn't mean placing yourself or your children in harm's way, nor does it mean pretending nothing happened. You can pray for them, forgive step by step before God, keep safe boundaries, and, if needed, seek the company of a pastor or a professional. For most families, start today with one small thing: a phone call, a meal, a hug, and do it together with your children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice turns conviction into daily life. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things: however busy we are, we make time for our parents. When parents honor the older generation first, children are right beside them, “learning to show honor”. The “2” in 920 is not only people outside; it is also the elderly parents beside us every day.
q: Who is God? — God says honor is “acceptable in the sight of God.” How does he regard each small thing you do for your parents?
Who am I? — Is my honor for my parents concrete action, or just guilt that stays in my heart?
How should I respond? — What concrete thing will I do with my children today for my parents (or the older generation)?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus entrusted his mother to the disciple John, and “from that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.” At the moment he bore the sin of all humanity, he still carried out his duty as a son. His honor was not a slogan. In the hardest hour he still remembered, still arranged, still loved.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for caring for your mother even on the cross, and for giving me an example of honor. I confess that I have often failed to honor my parents because I was busy or because of past hurts. Today give me strength to show love in one concrete action. If there is still pain in my heart, lead me step by step toward forgiveness, and give me wisdom to keep proper boundaries. Let my children learn from me how to show honor. Amen.
acts: Do one concrete thing with your children for your parents or in-laws: a phone call, a small gift, a meal together
Discuss with your siblings or spouse: when our parents are old, how can we share their care?
If your parents have passed away or the relationship is not safe, write a letter you will not send, telling God your thanks and your pain
lessons.noon: “let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents” — Lord, teach me today to love my parents in action.

fam.key: We learn to honor together.

lamb.do: On a video call or visit with Grandpa and Grandma, hold your child to wave and blow kisses, and let their little hand rest on the screen or on the older person's hand.
lamb.say: We love Grandpa and Grandma. Big hugs for you!

sprout.story: Xiaoru's grandma had a sore leg and walked very slowly. One weekend the whole family went to see Grandma. Xiaoru asked, “Mommy, what can I do to help Grandma?” Mommy said, “You can hold Grandma's hand and walk slowly with her.” So Xiaoru held Grandma's hand and walked step by step to the park, singing to Grandma on the way. Grandma smiled happily. “With you beside me, my leg doesn't hurt at all!”
sprout.ask: What can you do for Grandpa and Grandma?
sprout.do: Draw a picture or record a video of you singing, and send it to Grandpa and Grandma, saying, “I love you!”

soldier.story: Jesus was nailed to the cross in terrible pain. But he saw his mother Mary standing below, crying, and said to his closest friend John, “Please take care of my mother.” From that day John took Mary into his own home and looked after her. Even in his greatest pain, Jesus remembered to take care of his mom. The Bible also says to “learn to show piety” in our own homes. Honoring parents takes practice, just like practicing the piano. Practice a little every day from when you are small, and you'll get better and better.
ask: Why do you think Jesus remembered his mom even in such terrible pain?
What could you do every day to “practice” honoring your parents?
soldier.do: As a family, plan an “honor action” for Grandpa and Grandma (or an older relative): write cards, make a snack, do some cleaning, or go for a walk together. Complete one today.

youth.talk: Grandpa and Grandma are getting older day by day, and one day they will need more care. Mom and Dad are learning how to share this, and sometimes we get tired and grumble. On the cross Jesus still thought to arrange care for his mother, and Paul says to “learn to show piety” in our own family. We want you to see that honor is not only red envelopes at festivals, but little-by-little company and responsibility.
ask: What do you think is the biggest challenge for our family in caring for older relatives?
When Mom and Dad are old, what do you hope our relationship will look like?
youth.do: Invite your child to visit or video call the grandparents with you. Beforehand, discuss what you'd like to ask them, and afterward share how it felt.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for teaching us to love Mom and Dad and Grandpa and Grandma. Help us learn every day to honor them, and keep them safe and well. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Turning Hearts Toward the Children: A Family Health Check
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: look back over the relationship stage and give the family a health check

v: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

lessons.still: Remember these fourteen weeks, from secure attachment, listening, affirming and being present, through love languages, discipline, apologizing and forgiving, to siblings and three generations. Ask the Holy Spirit, like a doctor, to gently examine this family with you: “Lord, where are we healthy? Where do we still need your healing?”
teach: The last verse of the last book of the Old Testament says, “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” Luke records that before John the Baptist was born, the angel quoted these words, saying he would “turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” to prepare a people for the Lord. The bridge between the Old and New Testaments turns out to be the mending of family relationships. When God revives a generation, he often starts with the hearts of parents.

Weeks 31 to 44 were the “relationship” stage. We learned secure attachment, listening before speaking, words of affirmation, presence and children’s love languages; discipline as love, not exasperating our children, boundaries and natural consequences, parents apologizing first, forgiveness and repair; and then sibling love, peace in conflict, three-generation faith, honor and letting go. Fourteen weeks is like a long journey, and today we stop to look at the map: where have we got to?

Invite the whole family to do a “family health check”, rating each area from one to five stars. One, Connection: do the children feel loved and heard? Two, Words: are the words in our home mostly building up or tearing down? Three, Discipline: are our boundaries clear, consistent and loving? Four, Repair: do we apologize and forgive? Five, Siblings: do the children make up on their own? Six, Three generations: do we respect our elders and tell of God's works? Choose the lowest-scoring area as the focus of prayer and adjustment in the next stage.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Having walked through the stages of life and relationships, we now go on to “ministry”: leading children to live out character and calling. Review, adjust and repeat is the necessary path of change. A family health check is not a report card. It lets us see what God has already done and what he still wants to do.
q: Who is God? — God is the God who turns the hearts of fathers to their children. In these fourteen weeks, where have you seen him transform your heart?
Who am I? — Looking back over the relationship stage, what has been my biggest growth? What most needs continued adjustment?
How should I respond? — Which area scored lowest in the family health check? What is my first adjustment for it next week?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” When the disciples tried to send the children away, he was indignant and gathered them close. Jesus' heart is a heart turned toward children. He holds us in his arms in the same way, and when we review our shortcomings, he blesses us first.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for walking with us through these fourteen weeks of learning about relationships. Thank you for turning my heart more toward my children, and for every change you have made in our family. I confess there are still many areas that need your healing and adjusting. Keep turning the hearts of parents to their children and the hearts of children to their parents, three generations of one heart, preparing a family fit for the Lord. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Complete all six areas of the family health check with your spouse, score separately, then compare and discuss
Ask each child, “During this time, have Mom and Dad become more like Jesus? Where is it most noticeable?” Only listen, and don't defend yourself
Choose the area that most needs adjusting, write one specific action for next week, and put it up at home
lessons.noon: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers” — Lord, keep transforming every heart in our home.

fam.key: Our hearts are drawing close.

lamb.do: Hold your child to your chest so their ear rests against your heartbeat. Hold quietly for a minute, then kiss them.
lamb.say: Listen, Mommy's (Daddy's) heart is saying: I love you so much.

sprout.story: In a little garden, some flowers were blooming beautifully and some were a bit withered. Old Gardener looked at them one by one. “This one needs more water, this one needs sunshine, and this one is growing so well!” He didn't scold the wilted flowers. He just took good care of them. After a few days the whole garden was in bloom. Our family is like a garden, and God is the best gardener, helping us all grow better together.
sprout.ask: What do you think is the prettiest flower in our family? Which one needs a little more water?
sprout.do: Draw “Our Family Garden” together: each person draws a flower, then adds raindrops and sunshine, and you pray together, asking God to care for our family.

soldier.story: The last sentence of the Old Testament says God will “turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” God cares very much whether the hearts of family members are close. It's like going to the doctor for a health check: not because you are ill, but to find out what is healthy and what needs care. Our family has learned a lot these months: listening, speaking kindly, discipline, apologizing, forgiving, brothers and sisters making up, and respecting Grandpa and Grandma. Today we will give our family a “health check” together.
ask: Over these months, in what area do you think our family has improved the most?
What do you think our family most needs “more water” on?
soldier.do: Do a family health check together: give one to five stars for each of six areas (being loved, speaking kindly, discipline, apologizing, making up, three generations), and choose one area to work on together next week.

youth.talk: For these months we have been learning to be better family members: listening to you, affirming you, being with you, disciplining with love, and learning to apologize and forgive. Honestly, in some areas we have improved, and in some we're the same as ever. Today we'd like to do a family health check, not to grade anyone but to hear how you truly feel. Your opinion matters a lot to us.
ask: In this time, what change in Mom and Dad has been most noticeable? What are you still waiting for?
If our family were a person, do you think it is “healthy” now? Where does it need to see a doctor?
youth.do: Parents invite the child to do the family health check together, letting the child score first and speak first. At the end, the family chooses one area as a shared goal for the next stage, writes it down and signs it.

fam.pray: Father, thank you for drawing our hearts closer. Thank you for helping us learn to love and make up. Please keep caring for our family and make us more like Jesus. In Jesus’ name, amen.

44.memT: Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.

mem.t: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

sat.d: Hide several cards around the house or in the park, each with one character quality written on it: honesty, courage, gentleness, patience, gratitude, responsibility. Search in teams, and whenever a card is found, name a true example of that quality in a family member, such as “Big Brother admitted last week that he broke the cup. That is honesty.” When all are found, each person chooses one card for “the quality I want to learn this month” and takes it home to stick by the bed. Finish by praying together, asking God to grow good character in our hearts.

sun: Growing up, did your parents care more about your grades or your character? How does that shape the way you raise your children today?
What unique temperament does your child have that you once wanted to change but are now beginning to appreciate?
What one way will you use next week to nurture a character quality at home? How could you encourage another parent who is anxious about grades?

lessons.title: In the Way He Should Go
lessons.theme: Parenting is dedicating a child to God and walking beside them on the right road

v: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”

lessons.still: Imagine you are holding your child's hand at the starting point of life's road. Many paths lie ahead, wide and narrow. Quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, I don't know where each road leads, but you do. Please lead us.”
teach: “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” This is one of the best-known verses for Christian parents. The Hebrew word for “train up” is also used for dedicating a temple or a new house, and carries the sense of “beginning, dedicating, setting a direction.” Raising a child is first of all not shaping him into what we want, but dedicating him to God and setting his direction at the start of life.

“The way he should go” can be understood on two levels. One is God's way: truth, righteousness and the fear of the Lord. The other is the child's own way: the unique design and temperament God has given each child. Good parenting lets the child walk in God’s way, using the temperament God gave him. A gardener does not ask a rose to grow into bamboo, but builds a frame and prunes the rose so it blooms at its loveliest.

When Samuel went to anoint a new king, he was drawn to Jesse's tall, handsome eldest son. But God said, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature,” and, “man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” Our society prizes a child's “outward appearance”: grades, top schools, talents, certificates. God prizes the child's heart: honest, brave, kind, God-fearing. A new stage begins. This week we turn from valuing grades to valuing character.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Having walked through life and relationships, we now enter “ministry”: bringing out our children's character and calling. Children are God’s inheritance and parents are stewards. A steward's job is not to design the child's life but to help the child find God's design and walk in God's way.
q: Who is God? — God looks at the heart, and he has a unique design for every child.
Who am I? — Do I care more about my child's “outward appearance” (grades, performance) or the child's “heart” (character, fear of the Lord)?
How should I respond? — Today, how can I affirm one of my child's character qualities, rather than one of their grades?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus saw Nathanael, he said, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!” What he noticed first was not Nathanael's education or achievements but his character. Jesus sees our children the same way: what he values is a sincere heart.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for entrusting my children to me. I confess that I often value their grades and performance above their hearts. Today I dedicate my children to you once more. Guide me to lead them in the way they should go, and help me see your unique design in each child. Make me like you, valuing the heart above appearance. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: For each child write a sentence: “Lord, I dedicate [name] to you.” and pray for them
Today find a chance to praise a child's character specifically, for example, “You shared without being asked. That is generosity.”
Notice the first thing you ask your child today: is it about grades, or about their heart?
lessons.noon: “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” — Lord, lead me to walk with my children in your way.

fam.key: God cares about our hearts.

lamb.do: Gently put your hand on your child's chest, then on your own chest, then give them a hug.
lamb.say: God looks at your heart, and your heart is so precious.

sprout.story: Samuel was looking for a new king. Jesse's oldest son was tall and handsome, and Samuel thought, “It must be him!” But God said, “Not him. I look at the heart.” All seven of Jesse's sons walked past, and God said no to each one. Finally the youngest, David, came running from the sheep, his cheeks rosy and his eyes bright. God said, “That's the one!” Because David had a heart that loved God.
sprout.ask: What kind of heart do you think God likes?
sprout.do: Cut out a paper heart and let your child draw “a heart God likes” on it: perhaps a smile, helping hands, or a child praying.

soldier.story: Samuel went to Jesse's house to anoint a new king. He saw Eliab, the oldest son, tall and handsome, and thought it must be him. But God said not to look at his appearance, because “man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” The one chosen was the youngest, David, who was out looking after the sheep. Today's world also looks at outward things: who has the best grades, who performs best, who has the most followers. But God values whether you are honest, brave, kind and loving toward him. Grades pass, but character stays with you for life.
ask: What do you think people at your school value most? What does God value?
Which character quality would you like others to use to describe you?
soldier.do: Each person writes down the one character quality they most want to grow, and sticks it on their desk. Each night this week before bed, think: did I practice it today?

youth.talk: Honestly, Mom and Dad sometimes care too much about your grades. Perhaps it is because we were brought up that way, or because we worry about your future. But the Bible says God looks at the heart, not at outward appearance. We want to think again about what matters most in your life. Of course you should work hard at school, but if you get good grades and are not honest or kind, that is not what we truly want.
ask: What do you think Mom and Dad value most about you? What do you wish we valued?
Among your classmates, is there anyone whose character you really admire?
youth.do: This week a parent says to the child just once, “Even if you don't do well in the exam, what we care about most is who you are,” and names one character quality in the child that you admire.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for caring about our hearts. Give us honest, kind hearts that love you, so that every day we walk in your way. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Whose Ruler Am I Using on My Child?
lessons.theme: Seeing my own expectations, and my child's unique temperament

v: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.

lessons.still: Imagine you are holding a ruler. What is marked on it? Grades, talents, good behavior, other people's children? Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light gently: “Lord, whose ruler am I using to measure my child?”
teach: David says, “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Every child is a work God has woven with his own hands, and no two are alike. Yet parents often hold a ruler. Sometimes it is marked with “my relatives' children”, sometimes with “what I was like as a child”, sometimes with “my ideal child”. Paul says that those who measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves “are without understanding.”

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine a light: what kind of parent am I? The Grades type, whose child's worth depends on scores; the Comparing type, always using other people's children as the standard; the Replica type, hoping the child will fulfill my unfinished dreams; the Hands-off type, who thinks respecting temperament means doing nothing; or the Gardener type, who knows the child's temperament, nurtures along its grain, and prunes when needed.

Mrs. Chen in Singapore has two sons. The elder is quiet and loves books, and the younger is energetic and loves taking things apart. She always held the elder's standard up to the younger and thought he was “distracted and couldn't sit still.” Then one day she watched her younger son spend two hours repairing a broken fan. She realized that he was not unfocused. He just focused in a different way. Raising a child “in his own way” begins with putting down someone else's ruler.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled parent shapes the child by personal expectations, trying to take God's place in deciding who the child will be. The self-emptied parent lets God be God and the child be a child, humbly discovering God's design. Move from the human viewpoint to God's: the child is not my work but God's masterpiece.
q: Who is God? — God wove each child with his own hands in the womb, and says they are “fearfully and wonderfully made.”
Who am I? — Am I more of a Grades, Comparing, Replica, Hands-off or Gardener parent?
How should I respond? — Which “ruler” do I need to put down? How will I appreciate my child's unique temperament today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus dealt with each disciple differently. To impulsive Peter he kept giving fresh chances. To doubting Thomas he said, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands.” He did not want every disciple to become the same, but led each one according to his temperament toward the same faith.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for making my children with your own hands, fearfully and wonderfully. I confess that I often measure them with other people's rulers, shape them with my expectations, and even feel disappointed when they are not what I imagined. Forgive me. Open my eyes to see your unique design in each child, and help me nurture them like a gardener, not carve them like a craftsman. Amen.
acts: Write down the “ruler” you most often use to measure your children, confess it to God and put it down
For each child, write three “unique temperament traits God gave them”, including the one you once wanted to change
Today avoid saying anything like “Look at other people's children…”
lessons.noon: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” — Lord, help me see my children through your eyes today.

fam.key: God made me special.

lamb.do: Hold your child's little hand and count their fingers one by one, then gently kiss their palm.
lamb.say: God made you so special, one of a kind.

sprout.story: The forest held a sports day. Monkey won the tree-climbing race, Rabbit won the running race, and Fish won the swimming race. But if you told Fish to climb a tree, she could not. If you told Monkey to swim, he would squeal with fright. Wise Old Owl said, “Every animal is wonderful, because God made each one different.” Little Tortoise nodded slowly. “I may run slowly, but I'm very patient!”
sprout.ask: What is special about the way God made you?
sprout.do: Play the “I'm Special” game with your child: take turns naming something special about the other, such as “Your laugh sounds lovely” or “You're so good with the puppy.”

soldier.story: David wrote in a psalm: “God, you made me with your own hands in my mother's womb. I thank you, because I am fearfully and wonderfully made!” It means everyone is a carefully designed work of God. Some people are good at math, some at drawing, some at comforting friends, some at fixing things. Paul said that comparing yourself with others is not wise. It's like asking whether an apple is better than a banana. They are different from the start, and each is good in its own way.
ask: Has there been a time you felt sad because you compared yourself with someone else?
What do you think is special about how God made you?
soldier.do: Make a “God's Masterpiece Card” for everyone in the family: write three special things about them, and give it to them at dinner.

youth.talk: You may often have heard us say, “Look at other people's children…” or felt that we wanted you to be a certain kind of person. We want to admit that sometimes we used the wrong ruler: other people's grades, dreams we never finished, relatives' opinions. The Bible says you are God's work, fearfully and wonderfully made, and Paul says comparing ourselves with one another is without understanding. We want to get to know you again, and the temperament God placed in you.
ask: What standard do you think we use most often to measure you? How does that make you feel?
What parts of your temperament do you think we haven't really seen yet?
youth.do: This week a parent arranges a one-to-one time with the child, asks, “What kind of person am I?”, and only listens and asks. At the end, name one quality you hadn't seen before and now appreciate.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for making me so special. Help me not to compare myself with others, but to thank you and to appreciate how each person in our family is different. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Character Is a Staircase for Life
lessons.theme: I believe: character matters more than grades and goes further

v: Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge;
and in knowledge, self-control; and in self-control, perseverance; and in perseverance, godliness;
and in godliness, brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love.

lessons.still: Imagine a long staircase, with a word carved on each step: faith, moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, love. You are holding your child's hand, and the two of you are standing on the first step. Say to the Lord, “Lord, we are willing to climb, one step at a time.”
teach: Peter says, “in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge.” Then comes self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. It is like a staircase: the bottom is faith and the top is love. Notice that “knowledge” is just one step, and it comes after moral excellence. Knowledge matters, but knowledge without moral excellence can become a tool for hurting people.

Chinese parents often invest most of their energy in the “knowledge” step: tutoring, talents, exams, schools. There is nothing wrong with that in itself, but if only that one step is built, the child is like a building with one very tall floor and the others empty, which is very unstable. Mr. Lin in Taichung says his biggest realization came on the day his son got into his first-choice school, when he saw how impatiently his son spoke to Grandma. In that moment he asked himself, “What kind of person have I raised?”

Today, let us change our viewpoint: from “temporary” to “eternal”: grades decide a few years, character decides a lifetime. From “earthly” to “heavenly”: people value performance, but God values the shape of a life. From “my face” to “my child's life”. Character is not the rival of grades but the foundation that carries all abilities a long way. Write your declaration: I believe.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your beliefs and your life changes; change your life and your daily living changes. Character is the shape of a life, the fruit the Holy Spirit grows in the heart. Parents must climb this staircase themselves first, and then the children will follow. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on scores or other people's opinions.
q: Who is God? — God calls us to “all diligence” in pursuing character, because he wants us to be like him.
Who am I? — In our home, which step of the staircase do I invest most time and money in?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe character matters more than…; I believe my child…; I believe our family should…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his life?” He placed the value of a life above every achievement. Jesus had none of the degrees or status the world admires, yet he lived out the most perfect character: honest, gentle, brave, self-giving. He is the example of our character.
lessons.pray: Father, I believe character matters more than grades, and I believe you value the shape of my children's lives. I confess that I often put too much energy into their knowledge and performance and neglect moral excellence, self-control, perseverance and love. Help me adjust our family's priorities, to climb this staircase myself first, and to walk beside my children one step at a time. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations and read them to your spouse or a spiritual companion
Check this week's family calendar: how much time goes to “knowledge” and how much to building character?
Choose one character quality for each child to nurture this month
lessons.noon: “in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge;” — Lord, let our family's character grow step by step.

fam.key: Good character matters more than a hundred out of a hundred.

lamb.do: When your child shares a toy or helps tidy up, crouch down at once, look into their eyes, and give them a big hug.
lamb.say: You shared. How gentle! God is so pleased.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu and Xiaojie were having a block-building contest to see who could build the tallest tower. Xiaoyu's tower was about to win, but Xiaojie's came crashing down, and he cried sadly. Xiaoyu stopped, walked over, and said, “I'll help you build it!” In the end nobody came first, but the teacher said, “What Xiaoyu won today is better than first place, because he has a heart that helps others.”
sprout.ask: What do you think Xiaoyu won that is better than first place?
sprout.do: Build a “Character Tower” with blocks. With each block, name a good quality, such as honesty, helping, saying thank you, or waiting.

soldier.story: Peter wrote to Christians: in your faith supply good conduct, then knowledge, then self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. It is like leveling up in a video game. You can't train just one skill. Every skill needs to level up for your character to grow strong. If you only get high exam scores but can't control your temper, aren't patient and don't know how to love, you're like a character with great attack but no defense, who falls easily.
ask: Of the qualities Peter lists, which level do you think is your highest? Which needs leveling up most?
Why do you think God values character more than grades?
soldier.do: Everyone in the family writes one “I believe” sentence, such as “I believe honesty matters more than a hundred out of a hundred”, and sticks it at their desk. Read it once a day this week.

youth.talk: Your generation is under great pressure: exams, school places, comparison, the perfect images on social media. Mom and Dad have sometimes added to that pressure. We want to say honestly that we valued your grades too much because we were afraid you would suffer later. But Peter says character is a staircase, and knowledge is only one step. We are beginning to believe that who you are matters more than what marks you get.
ask: In society today, do you think character really matters more than grades? Tell us what you honestly think.
Have you seen someone very capable who failed because of a character problem?
youth.do: Parent and child each choose one of the eight qualities in 2 Peter as a shared goal for the month, and remind and encourage one another.

fam.pray: Dear Father, help us not only to study hard but to have good character: honesty, patience, gentleness and love for others. Make us more and more like Jesus. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: A Child Makes Himself Known by His Doings
lessons.theme: Nurturing character: model, name, story, practice, reflect

v: Even a child makes himself known by his doings, whether his work is pure, and whether it is right.
In all things show yourself an example of good works. In your teaching, show integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility,

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and think: what character will my child see in me today? Say to the Lord, “Lord, before I teach my children, let me live it out first.”
teach: “Even a child makes himself known by his doings, whether his work is pure, and whether it is right.” A child's character does not appear only after he grows up. It can be seen in everyday small actions: how he treats his brother, how he handles winning and losing, how he treats other people's things. Character is like a muscle: the earlier you start and the more often you train, the stronger it grows. Parents don't need to wait until a child is “sensible.” Start from one small thing today. So how do we nurture character at home?

Here are five ways. One, Model: Paul says, “In all things show yourself an example of good works.” Children watch what we do first. Two, Name: when you see good behavior, name the quality: “You kept your promise. That is being trustworthy.” Three, Story: use Bible characters and life stories to give character a picture. Four, Practice: through chores, caring for a pet and keeping agreements, let character be exercised in daily life. Five, Reflect: at bedtime, think together, “Where was I honest today? Where do I need God's help?”

In Kuala Lumpur, the Zhengs have four children and both parents work long hours, so Grandma helps look after them. They came up with a simple idea: each month they pick one “family virtue” and write it on a whiteboard. During the day Grandma “catches” the children showing this virtue, and when Mom and Dad come home in the evening, Grandma announces the day's “Character Hero.” Three generations together turned character into daily conversation at home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is the key step in changing beliefs. When parents live out character themselves, they are the best teaching material; people matter more than tasks, and character matters more than grades. 920: when we live the self-emptied life and bear the fruit of the Spirit at home, children grow up among that fruit.
q: Who is God? — God sees each of a child's small actions, and he is also at work in the child's heart.
Who am I? — Of the five ways, which do I use most? Which do I use least?
How should I respond? — Which way will I use at home today to nurture which character quality in my child?
lessons.jesus: Jesus washed his disciples' feet, and then said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” He did not first give a lesson on humility. He first picked up the towel and bent down. Jesus' way of nurturing character in his disciples was to model first, then name it, then invite them to do it.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for showing me humility and love. I confess that I often ask my children for good character while not living it out myself. Today help me to be the example first, to see my children's good behavior and name the quality, and to practice patiently with them. Make our home a school of character. Amen.
acts: As a family, choose this month's “family virtue” and write it on a whiteboard or the fridge
Today “catch” your children showing good character at least three times, and name the quality
At bedtime, reflect with your child: where did I live out this quality today?
lessons.noon: “Even a child makes himself known by his doings, whether his work is pure, and whether it is right.” — Lord, help me see my children's goodness today, and first live out a good example.

fam.key: We practice good character every day.

lamb.do: Tidy up the toys together with your child, saying “Thank you for helping” with each one, and give a hug when you finish.
lamb.say: You helped put away the toys. That's being responsible! Well done!

sprout.story: Jiajia promised her puppy Bobo that she would feed him every day. One day Jiajia wanted to keep playing and did not want to go and feed Bobo. But she heard Bobo barking at the door and remembered, “I promised Bobo!” She ran at once to pour out his food. Mom saw and said, “Jiajia, you kept your promise. That's called being ‘trustworthy’!” Jiajia was so happy. She had learned a new quality.
sprout.ask: Did you keep a promise today?
sprout.do: Make a “character sticker chart”: whenever your child shows a good quality, name it and let them put on a sticker.

soldier.story: Proverbs says that every move a child makes shows what kind of person he is. That is good news, and also a reminder: character does not begin when you grow up. You are practicing now! It's like learning basketball. You have to shoot every day to get more accurate. Character is the same: every time you tell the truth, honesty grows; every time you wait, patience grows; every time you help someone, love grows. God sees each of your small choices.
ask: What character do you think your actions showed today?
Which quality would you most like to practice every day?
soldier.do: Choose this month's “family virtue” together. At dinner each day, take turns giving an example of seeing someone show it that day.

youth.talk: We often ask you to be responsible, honest and polite, but honestly, you can also see where we fall short: promises not kept, impatience with people on the phone, gossip behind people's backs. Paul says to “show yourself an example of good works” in all things, and we want to start with ourselves. This month we would like to choose one quality to practice with you, and we ask you to hold us accountable too.
ask: What quality do you think our family most needs to practice together?
In which quality have you seen Mom and Dad be inconsistent? You can tell us honestly.
youth.do: Parent and child choose one quality as the goal for the month, and agree to share each week about progress and failures, with the parent going first.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for seeing each of our small actions. Help us practice good character every day, honesty, responsibility and love, so that others see Jesus in us. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Increasing in Wisdom and Stature
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: walking beside the whole child as they grow

v: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

lessons.still: Think back over this week. In what way did you see your child grow? A sensible word, an unprompted act of help, a brave choice? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and thank God for this growth.
teach: Luke sums up Jesus' growth in Nazareth in one sentence: “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.” It is a picture of whole-person growth: wisdom (mind), stature (body), favor with God (spirit) and favor with men (relationships). All four grew together, not just one. The Son of God, in an ordinary carpenter's home, went through full and balanced growth, and this is also God's desire for each of our children.

In many families, parenting is like a table with four legs of different lengths: the wisdom leg is very long (tutoring, talents), the stature leg is fairly good (nutrition, exercise), but the “favor with God” and “favor with men” legs are very short, so the table wobbles. This week we learned that parenting is dedicating children to God, putting down the ruler of comparison, believing character matters more than grades, and nurturing character in five ways. Today we look back: is our family's table balanced on all four legs?

Notice that Luke first says Jesus “was subject to them,” and only then that he grew in all four ways. Growth in character happens in obedience, in the everyday, at home. Review is not to blame the child for falling short, but for parents to ask themselves first: does the environment I give my child let all four areas grow? Choose the one area that most needs strengthening as next week's adjustment.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjust and repeat is the necessary path of change. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: character growth starts with life, is seen in relationships, and finally bears fruit in service. Parents first review themselves, then walk with the children as they adjust. Humility draws out humility.
q: Who is God? — God delights in Jesus, and in our children too. He cares about every area of their growth.
Who am I? — Among wisdom, stature, favor with God and favor with men, which do I value most? Which do I neglect most?
How should I respond? — Next week, how will I help my child grow in the weakest area?
lessons.jesus: Hebrews says of Jesus, “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” The Son of God also went through a process of learning and growing. He understands how hard it is for children to grow, and how tiring it is for parents to walk beside them. He is the example of whole-person growth, and the one who walks with us as we grow.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for walking with us through this week. Thank you for letting me see my children grow, which is all your grace. I confess that I often value only their grades and neglect their relationship with you and with others. Help our family grow in balance, like Jesus, increasing in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: in which of the four areas has each child grown best? In which does each most need strengthening?
Ask your child, “This week, did Mom/Dad value your character more, and not only your grades?” Only listen, and don't defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as a weekly family exercise time or serving others together
lessons.noon: “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.” — Lord, let our children grow in every way like this.

fam.key: We want to grow up like Jesus.

lamb.do: Measure your child's height against the wall, draw a line, then hold their hand and say thank you to God together.
lamb.say: You've grown! God watches over you as you grow bigger every day.

sprout.story: When Jesus was little, he was just like you. He had to learn to walk, learn to talk, and learn to help. In his home in Nazareth he helped his father Joseph with carpentry and listened to his mother Mary. The Bible says Jesus grew bigger every day, wiser and stronger, and God liked him, and everyone liked him too. You are growing bigger every day too, and God likes you very much!
sprout.ask: What new thing did you learn to do this week?
sprout.do: Measure everyone's height and mark it on the door frame. With each mark, say, “God, please help [name] grow up like Jesus!”

soldier.story: When Jesus was twelve, he talked with the teachers in the temple, and everyone was amazed at how clever he was. But when he went back to Nazareth, he was still obedient to his parents and grew bigger day by day at home. The Bible says Jesus grew in wisdom, in body, in his relationship with God and in his relationships with people, all together. It's like a table that needs four legs the same length to be steady. If you are brilliant at study but don't exercise, pray or make friends, the table will wobble.
ask: Among wisdom, body, your relationship with God and your relationships with people, which do you think you have grown best in?
Which would you like to grow in more next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person draws “My Growth Table” with four legs, marks the longest and shortest legs, and chooses one to strengthen together next week. Mom and Dad draw first.

youth.talk: This week we have been talking about character and temperament. Honestly, changing the habit of focusing on grades is not easy, and this week we probably still asked too much about “How did you do?” Luke says Jesus grew in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and men. We would like to hear your view: in your life, are these four areas balanced? How can we support you, and not just add pressure?
ask: This week, did you feel Mom and Dad valued your character more, and not only your grades?
Of the four areas, which one do you most need our support in?
youth.do: A parent first apologizes to the child for one moment this week when they put too much weight on grades, and then together they make a small plan to bring the four areas into better balance.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for letting us grow bigger every day. Help us be like Jesus: wiser, healthy, loving you more, and loving others more. In Jesus’ name, amen.

45.memT: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

mem.t: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

sat.d: Turn the living room into a little carnival with four or five stalls: a drawing corner, a building-blocks workshop, a kitchen helper station, a storytelling or singing stage, and a fix-it-and-take-apart area. Each family member takes a turn at every stall for fifteen minutes. The parents don't instruct, but only observe: who lights up where, who concentrates most, who doesn't want to leave? Afterward, each person gives another family member an “I noticed you're really good at…” Finish by praying together, offering each person's gifts to God and asking him to use them to serve others.

sun: As a child, which of your gifts was noticed and nurtured? Which was overlooked or pushed down?
What gift did you discover in your children this week? Is there a “Saul's armor” you need to take off your child?
How will you give your child a chance to serve others with their gift next week? How could you help another family see their children’s gifts?

lessons.title: Good Managers of God’s Many-Sided Grace
lessons.theme: Every child carries a gift from God, to serve others

v: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;

lessons.still: Imagine each child holding a gift that God has wrapped with his own hands. Some are still unopened, and some have just been unwrapped at one corner. Quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for the gifts you have given my children. Teach me how to help them open them.”
teach: Peter says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” There are three key points. First, “each” has a gift: no child came into the world empty-handed. Second, the gift is “received”. It is given, not earned, so there is no room for pride or for feeling small. Third, the purpose of the gift is “serving one another”: not to stand out, but to bless others.

The “various forms” of grace carries the sense of many-colored, like a gem that throws different colors when you turn it in the light. One child speaks well and another listens well. One is good with numbers and another with colors. One has clever hands, and another has a tender heart that notices when others are sad. Paul also says, “having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us.” God never mass-produces children.

The parent's role here is that of a manager, not an owner. A manager does not own the master's goods, but looks after them carefully and puts them to work so they bring the greatest value. It is the same with nurturing a child's gifts: the gifts belong to God, not to the parents' reputation. Our task is to discover and nurture them, and guide the child to use them to serve others, “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two core aims: let Jesus reign; let Jesus receive all the glory. A child's gifts are not for the parents' pride but for Jesus to be glorified. A manager's heart is self-emptied: not possessive, not showing off, just faithfully nurturing what God has entrusted.
q: Who is God? — God gives grace “in its various forms”, and he gives each child different gifts.
Who am I? — Do I treat my child's gifts as God's trust, or as my report card as a parent?
How should I respond? — Today, how can I let my child use their gift to serve one person?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” He had all power and wisdom, yet he used it all to serve, heal and save. Jesus shows the true purpose of gifts: not to be noticed, but to bless people and glorify the Father.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for the many gifts you have given my children, and for letting me be their manager. I confess that sometimes I treat my children's talents as my own reputation, or value only certain gifts. Open my eyes to see the gift you placed in each child, and help me guide them to use their gifts to serve one another, so that you are glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write down three gifts or talents you see in each child
Tell your child today, “God has given you a gift: it is…, and it is for blessing others.”
Pray for your children's gifts, asking God to use them in serving others
lessons.noon: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” — Lord, let our family serve others with your gifts.

fam.key: God gives everyone a different gift.

lamb.do: Set out a few different things: a rattle, crayons, blocks, a picture book. Let your child choose, notice which one they like best, and play with them.
lamb.say: You like this so much! God has given you so many good gifts.

sprout.story: Mother Bird had three little birds. The eldest sang beautifully, the second flew very fast, and the youngest had short wings and couldn't do anything. The youngest was sad. “Don't I have a gift?” One day Little Rabbit got lost in the forest and was crying. The youngest bird flew down, sat quietly beside Little Rabbit and gently patted her. Mother Bird said, “Your gift is comforting others!” So every little bird has a gift from God.
sprout.ask: What gift do you think God gave you?
sprout.do: Wrap an empty box as “God’s gift” and let your child open it. Inside, put a note saying one gift you have seen in them, and read it aloud.

soldier.story: Peter wrote that everyone has received a gift from God and should use it to serve one another, as good managers of God's various gifts. Gifts are like tools from God: one person gets a paintbrush, another an instrument, another a heart that cares about people. These tools are not for showing off but for helping others. It's like a soccer team, with goalkeeper, defenders and strikers. Every position matters, and without any one of them the team can't play well.
ask: What do you think you are best at? How can you use it to help others?
How can the gifts of everyone in the family work together?
soldier.do: This week use one of your gifts to do something for the family: someone who draws makes a card, someone who cooks helps make a dish, someone funny makes everyone laugh.

youth.talk: When people talk about “gifts”, many think of singing hymns, preaching, or exceptional grades. But Peter speaks of grace “in its various forms”, which is wonderfully varied. Your gift might be coding, making videos, caring for friends, organizing events, or even being very good at noticing others' feelings. Mom and Dad admit that sometimes we only affirm a few talents that “look promising”. We want to get to know your gifts again.
ask: What gift do you think you have that we haven't noticed yet?
How could these gifts be used to serve others?
youth.do: Parent and child together list three gifts of each person in the family, and discuss how the family could use their gifts together this month to serve one person or one family.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for giving each of us a different gift. Help us use it well to help others, so that people see your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Taking Off Saul’s Armor
lessons.theme: Discovering a child’s gifts, not imposing a parent’s expectations

v: Saul dressed David with his clothing. He put a helmet of bronze on his head, and he clad him with a coat of mail.
David strapped his sword on his clothing and he tried to move, for he had not tested it. David said to Saul, “I can’t go with these, for I have not tested them.” Then David took them off.

He took his staff in his hand, and chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag which he had. His sling was in his hand; and he came near to the Philistine.

lessons.still: Think: each talent class and each tutoring session you have arranged for your child, does it come from their gift or from your expectation? Ask the Holy Spirit to shine gently: “Lord, have I put my armor on my child?”
teach: When David went to face Goliath, King Saul kindly dressed him in his own clothing, a bronze helmet and a coat of mail. This was the best equipment in the land, and it stood for the king's experience and expectations. But David took a few steps and said, “I can’t go with these, for I have not tested them.” So he took them off, and picked up his shepherd's staff, five smooth stones and his sling. These were the skills he had practiced while looking after sheep, when he rescued lambs from the mouths of lions and bears.

Many parents are like Saul. Out of love, we put on our children what we think is the best equipment: “Piano is good for you,” “Medicine is the most secure career,” “All the children in our family go to that school.” These are not necessarily wrong, but if the child “can't move” in them, we need to stop and think. Mr. Su in Kaohsiung always wanted his son to learn the violin. After six years of practice his son grew more and more miserable. Later they discovered that his son's real passion was the kitchen, and his cooking amazed the whole family.

Ask the Holy Spirit to shine a light: what kind of parent am I? The Imposing type, who decides what the child should be good at; the Anxious type, who has the child learn everything for fear of falling behind at the start; the Hands-off type, who thinks not interfering is respect; or the Discovering type, who gives chances, watches and listens, and nurtures along God's design. Saul’s armor was good, but it did not belong to David. What God gave David was a sling and stones.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled parent wants to decide the child's road in place of God, taking their own expectations as God's will. The self-emptied parent lets God be God and humbly discovers what God has placed in the child. Pride grabs power; humility lays power down and returns to the place of a steward.
q: Who is God? — During David's shepherd days, God had already prepared him for facing Goliath. He prepares our children in their everyday lives too.
Who am I? — Am I more of an Imposing, Anxious, Hands-off or Discovering parent?
How should I respond? — Is there a piece of “Saul's armor” I need to take off my child?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus called the fishermen Peter and Andrew, he said, “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.” He did not ask them to throw away their fishing experience and put on a rabbi's robe, but turned the skills they knew into a heavenly calling. Jesus discovers people. He does not remake them into someone else.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often put my expectations on my children and think it is for their good. Sometimes it is my regrets, sometimes my anxiety, sometimes other people's opinions. Forgive me, and help me take off the armor that does not belong to my children, see the sling and stones you have prepared for them, and nurture them according to your design. Amen.
acts: List all your child's current talent classes and tutoring, and honestly write beside each one: is this their gift or my expectation?
Ask your child, “Of these classes, which do you like best? Which do you least want to go to? Why?” Only listen, and don't defend yourself
Notice what your child most often does of their own accord when nobody asks them to
lessons.noon: “I can’t go with these, for I have not tested them.” — Lord, let me see the equipment that truly fits my child.

fam.key: What God gave me fits me best.

lamb.do: Let your child try on your big shoes, take a few steps, then swap back to their own little shoes and laugh together.
lamb.say: Daddy's shoes are too big! Your shoes fit you best.

sprout.story: David was going to fight the giant Goliath. King Saul said, “Wear my armor!” David put on the big, heavy armor and walked with a clank, clank, and nearly fell over. David said, “I'm not used to this. I can't walk!” He took off the armor and picked up his own sling and five little stones, the ones he knew how to use best. He trusted God, and with one stone the giant fell!
sprout.ask: Why do you think David took off the armor?
sprout.do: Let your child try walking in Mom's or Dad's big coat or shoes, then swap back to their own, and talk about which is easier to walk in.

soldier.story: When David was going to fight the giant Goliath, King Saul gave him his own armor, helmet and sword. These were the king's best equipment! But after David put them on he said, “I can't go with these, for I have not tested them.” He took them off and picked up the sling and stones he was used to from looking after sheep. While caring for the flock he had rescued lambs from the mouths of lions and bears, and God had been training him all along. Everyone has the “sling” God has given them, and does not have to force on someone else's armor.
ask: Is there something others think you should be good at but you feel it doesn't suit you?
What do you think your “sling and stones” are?
soldier.do: Draw two figures: one wearing “what others want me to do” and one holding “the sling God gave me”, and write down what you really love and are good at. Share it with Mom and Dad.

youth.talk: Sometimes the talents, tutoring and even future direction we have arranged for you are really our own expectations, or regrets from our childhood. It's like Saul putting his armor on David: kindly meant, but not necessarily a good fit. We want to admit that honestly. David took off the armor and picked up the sling he knew. We would like to know what you think truly belongs to you.
ask: Of the things we arrange for you, is there anything that feels like wearing armor that doesn't fit?
If you could freely choose, what would you most like to spend time developing?
youth.do: Parent and child look together at all the child's current classes and activities, honestly discuss what each one means, and decide together which to keep, adjust or pause.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for giving me the gift that fits me best. Help me not to envy others, and help Mom and Dad see the good things you have placed in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: I Have Called by Name
lessons.theme: I believe: every gift is from the Holy Spirit and can glorify God

v: “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
to devise skillful works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in bronze,
and in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood, to work in all kinds of workmanship.

lessons.still: Think of the one thing your child does with the most absorption: perhaps drawing, building, cooking, or caring for animals. Picture God standing beside them, smiling and saying, “I put that in him.” Quietly let that picture rest.
teach: When the tabernacle was to be built, God said, “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship.” The first person in the Bible said to be “filled with the Spirit of God” was not a priest or a prophet, but a craftsman, one who could carve, set stones, and work gold, silver and bronze.

This breaks the ranking that many Chinese parents hold: studying first, and everything else “won't amount to much.” But God says the ability to design, craft and carve is also the result of being filled with the Spirit, and can also be used to build God's house. In Sydney, the Cais, a first-generation immigrant family, insisted that their daughter study business, but she loved design. Later she took charge of all the visual design at church, and many young people came into the church because of the posters she made.

Today, let us change our viewpoint: from “only some talents have a future” to “every gift is from God”; from “my child's gift should bring honor to the family” to “my child's gift is for building for God”; from “I decide for my child” to “God has already called him by name” (see Exodus 31:2). When parents are convinced first, children dare to believe the gift in their hands is also valued by God. Write your declaration: I believe.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of viewpoint, from the human view to God's, from worldly values to God's values. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he not only leads in spiritual things but also fills the hands of a craftsman. Gifts are not higher or lower; what matters is faithfulness. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means every gift returns to his hand.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who “calls by name”, and he fills even a craftsman’s hands with his Spirit.
Who am I? — Do I have a ranking of gifts in my mind? Which gifts do I look down on?
How should I respond? — Write your “I believe” declaration: I believe my child's gift is…; I believe every gift…; I believe God will use my child to…
lessons.jesus: In Nazareth Jesus was known as “the carpenter”. For most of his years on earth the Son of God worked with his hands, sawing wood and planing boards, serving his community. His life tells us that work with the hands is holy too, and every honest labor and gift can glorify the Father.
lessons.pray: Father, I believe every gift is given by you, and I believe you have already called my child by name. I confess I have a ranking of gifts in my heart and often look down on some of my children's talents. Forgive me. Let me cherish every gift in my children as you do, and believe that your Spirit will fill them and use their hands and minds to build your kingdom. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” declarations and read them to your children
Find one gift in your child that you used to look down on, and affirm it specifically today
Pray for each child: “Lord, you have called him by name. Fill him with your Spirit.”
lessons.noon: “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,” — Lord, fill my children with your Spirit.

fam.key: God calls me by name and gives me gifts.

lamb.do: Gently say your child's name while holding their little hand, and stroke their palm and fingers.
lamb.say: [Name], God knows your name. God gave you such wonderful hands.

sprout.story: God wanted the Israelites to build a beautiful tent. God said, “I have chosen Bezalel. His hands are clever, and I will let him do it!” Bezalel could make a lampstand from gold, carve beautiful gems, and carve wood. God put cleverness and wisdom in his heart so that he could make the most beautiful things for God. Your hands are wonderful too. They can draw, build with blocks, and make beautiful things for God!
sprout.ask: What would you like to make for God with your hands?
sprout.do: Make a “gift for God” out of clay, paper or blocks. When it's done, pray together and offer it to God.

soldier.story: In the wilderness the Israelites were to build the tabernacle, the tent where God would be present. God named one particular person: Bezalel. God said, “I have filled him with my Spirit, with wisdom and skill to do all kinds of fine work.” Bezalel could carve, work gold and set gems. It's interesting that the first person in the Bible said to be filled with God's Spirit was a craftsman! This tells us that whether you are good at study, drawing, making things, sport or caring for people, all of these can be gifts from God.
ask: Do you think Bezalel's work was as important as the priests' work? Why?
How could what you're good at be used to “build God's house”?
soldier.do: Everyone in the family writes one “I believe” sentence, for example, “I believe that I can draw is a gift from God”, and writes one way they could use it to serve this month.

youth.talk: In Chinese society there is often a ranking: study comes first, doctors, lawyers and engineers are the ones who “amount to something”, and art, crafts and sports seem second. Honestly, Mom and Dad are influenced by this thinking too. But the first person in the Bible said to be filled with the Spirit of God was a craftsman, Bezalel. This makes us rethink: the gifts God values may be far wider than we imagined.
ask: How does the “ranking of talents” in society affect you?
Is there a field you're very interested in but fear we'd think has “no future”?
youth.do: A parent invites the child to introduce a field they love, listens seriously for ten minutes, and asks, “How could God use this gift?”

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for knowing my name and giving me special gifts. Fill me with your Spirit, and let me use the ability you gave me to do good things for you. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: Stir It Up Like a Fire
lessons.theme: Give chances and practice, so that gifts grow in serving

v: For this cause, I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

lessons.still: Imagine a pile of embers about to go out. Someone blows on them gently and adds some wood, and the fire blazes up again. Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, how can I add a stick of wood to my child's gift today?”
teach: Paul reminds Timothy, “you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.” A gift is like a fire: it can burn bright, and it can die down. When it isn't used, or is criticized, or is suppressed by fear, the fire shrinks. When it is encouraged, used and seen, it burns brighter. The parent's role is to keep adding wood and blowing gently. A sentence like “I love watching you do this” is often the breath that makes the fire catch again.

In the parable of the talents Jesus told, the servants who received five and two talents both “traded” and doubled their money, but the servant who received one was afraid and buried his in the ground. Gifts do not grow by being protected; they grow only by being used. Many children's gifts are buried, not because they are not good enough, but because of fear of failure, fear of being laughed at, or parents saying, “Take care of your homework first.”

Do three things today. One, give chances: let children try different things at home, at church and in the neighbourhood. Two, practice with them: gifts need training. Walk with them through the low point of “I don't want to practice any more,” but never force with shame. Three, serve: give the gift an outlet. The Lius in Kuching have five children. Their parents let the one who plays the piano accompany at Sunday school, the one who draws help paint the church noticeboard, and the chatty one keep an elderly neighbor company. In serving, their gifts were fanned into flame.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice is the key step in changing beliefs. Gifts are not display pieces but tools of service; the “2” in 920 is exactly who the gifts are meant to serve. When parents first serve with their own gifts, children will follow. Let Jesus receive the glory, not ourselves the applause.
q: Who is God? — God is the master who says to the faithful servant, “Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Who am I? — Am I adding wood to my child's gift, or often accidentally pouring cold water on it?
How should I respond? — What chance will I give my child today to serve others with their gift?
lessons.jesus: In the parable of the talents, the servant who received one said, “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” Jesus told this parable so that we would see that fear buries gifts, and trust makes them grow. In his own days on earth, Jesus gave all that the Father had given him, holding nothing back.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving my children gifts, and for giving me the chance to help fan this fire. I confess that sometimes I have poured cold water on them, out of worry, because of homework, or fear my child will fail. Today help me be someone who adds wood: give my children chances, practice with them, lead them into serving, and let their gifts burn brighter in your hands. Amen.
acts: Give your child a chance today to serve others with their gift, such as making a card for a neighbor or singing a song for an older person
Recall a time you “poured cold water” on your child's gift, and find a chance today to put it right
Discuss with your spouse: is there a place at church or in the community that would suit our child to serve?
lessons.noon: “you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.” — Lord, let me add a stick of wood to my child's gift today.

fam.key: Use God’s gifts to help others.

lamb.do: When your child claps, sings or dances, join in with them and applaud warmly.
lamb.say: You sing so beautifully! Let's sing to God.

sprout.story: Xiaoyu was very good at drawing, but she hid every picture in a drawer for fear of being laughed at. One day Mom said, “Old Mrs. Lin next door is ill and lonely. Could you draw a picture for her?” Xiaoyu was a little shy, but she drew a big sunflower. When Mrs. Lin received it, she stuck it up by her bed and smiled every day when she looked at it. Xiaoyu was so happy. “So my pictures can make people happy!”
sprout.ask: Who could you make happy with something you can do?
sprout.do: Today, in the way your child likes best (drawing, singing, making a snack), make a small gift for a friend or an older person, and deliver it together.

soldier.story: Jesus told a story. Before going on a journey, a master gave money to three servants. The one who got five talents traded and earned five more; the one with two earned two more. But the one who got one talent was afraid and buried it in the ground. When the master returned, he praised the first two as “good and faithful”, but he was very disappointed in the servant who buried his. A gift is like a seed: if you bury it and never plant it, it will never grow, but if you take it out and use it, it multiplies.
ask: Is there a gift of yours that you've “buried” for fear of being laughed at?
How could you “take it out and use it” this week?
soldier.do: Plan a “Gifts Service Day” as a family: each person uses their gift to do one thing for the church, neighbors or friends, to be completed this week.

youth.talk: Paul reminded Timothy to stir up the gift God gave him “like a fire”. We want to admit that sometimes we have carelessly poured cold water: a “take care of your homework first”, a disapproving look, and you may not want to try again. In Jesus' parable, the man who buried the money did so out of fear. We don't want you to bury your gifts out of fear. We want to be the ones who help add wood to your fire.
ask: Was there a time we made you feel your interest or gift was dampened?
Where would you like to use your gift to serve others? How can we support you?
youth.do: Parent and child find a chance to serve together (church, community, online) where the child can take part with their gift, with the parent providing lifts and encouragement.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving each of us gifts. Give us courage not to hide them but to use them to help others. In Jesus’ name, amen.

lessons.title: There Are Various Kinds of Gifts
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: appreciating and building up one another at home

v: Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit.
There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord.
There are various kinds of workings, but the same God who works all things in all.
But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all.

lessons.still: Think back over this week: what new gift did you see in each child? And was there any moment when you accidentally compared them? Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, without condemning, simply being honest.
teach: Paul says, “Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord.” Then he says, “to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all.” The church is like a body, with each part having a different function, and the home is a little body too.
