The children in one home have different gifts, yet all are given by the same Spirit, for the profit of the whole family.

In a family with many children, differences in gifts often become a source of comparison: “Your brother is good at study. Why aren't you?” “Your sister plays the piano. Why don't you learn?” But Paul says the eye can't tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” and the parts that seem weaker are all the more needed. This week we learned that gifts are for serving, to take off Saul's armor, that every gift is from the Holy Spirit, and to fan gifts into flame.

Today review honestly: have I seen my children's gifts more clearly? Have I put down comparing? Have I given them chances to serve with their gifts? And what about me? Parents have gifts too. Have we used them faithfully at home and at church? Review is not about grading but about taking the next step as a better manager. Choose one thing as next week's adjustment, and remember with thanksgiving that God placed these different children in one home as part of his good plan.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “5” in 235 is the five-fold team of comrades in arms, with different gifts building up the body of Christ together. The family is the same: different gifts, serving with one heart. Review, adjust and repeat move us from comparing to building up, from competing to working together.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who “works all things in all”, and he puts different gifts in one home.
Who am I? — This week, did I put down comparing and appreciate each child's different gifts?
How should I respond? — What one thing will I adjust next week? How will I help the family build up one another?
lessons.jesus: Paul says, “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.” All gifts come from Jesus and must return to him. He is the head of the body, and every part is joined to him. Every gift in our home is also joined and used in the hand of this Head.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for walking with us through a week of discovering gifts. Thank you for letting me see so many new gifts in my children. I confess that sometimes I still compare them, and neglect my own gifts. Help our family be like one body, appreciating and building up one another, serving you with one heart through our different gifts. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what gifts have we seen in each child this week? Where are we still comparing?
Ask your children, “This week, did Mom/Dad appreciate your gifts more?” Only listen, and don't defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week, such as giving each child one chance a week to serve with their gift
lessons.noon: “Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit.” — Lord, let our family appreciate one another's differences and serve you with one heart.

fam.key: We are different, but we are one family.

lamb.do: Point to your child's eyes, ears, little hands and little feet, and gently kiss each one in turn.
lamb.say: Eyes to see, ears to hear, hands to clap, feet to jump. Every one is so important!

sprout.story: Hand said, “I'm the best! I can pick things up!” Foot said, “No, I'm the best! I can walk!” Eye said, “I can see!” Ear said, “I can hear!” They argued and argued. Then the body wanted to eat an apple. Eye saw the apple, Feet walked over, Hand picked it up, and Mouth went crunch! Everyone laughed. “So we have to work together!” Our family is like that. Everybody is important.
sprout.ask: Which part of the body do you think you are in our family?
sprout.do: Play a “body teamwork game”: one person is the eyes (can only talk), another is the hands (blindfolded), and together they work to pick up an object.

soldier.story: Paul said the church is like a body, with eyes, ears, hands and feet. Each part is different, yet each is important. If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If the whole body were an ear, how would it smell? Our family is the same. Someone can cook, someone can fix things, someone can make everyone laugh, someone can comfort people. We don't all have to be the same, and we don't need to compare who is better, because God put us together so we could help one another.
ask: This week, did you discover a gift in someone at home that you hadn't noticed before?
How would you like to use your gift to help the family next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting. Each person names one gift in another family member and says one thing they want to do for the family next week with their own gift. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we have been talking about gifts. Honestly, Mom and Dad still sometimes compare you with your brothers and sisters, or with other people. Paul says there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit, and everyone is different yet equally important. We want to ask: this week, did you feel we appreciated you more? Or was it just words? Your feedback helps us to really change.
ask: This week, did you notice any difference in how Mom and Dad appreciated your gifts?
Where would you like us to support you more next week?
youth.do: A parent first apologizes to the child for one time they compared them, and then together they make a small plan for next week to serve with their gifts.

fam.pray: Dear Father, thank you for making each person in our family different, and each one important. Help us appreciate one another, help one another, and shine for you together. In Jesus’ name, amen.

46.memT: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

mem.t: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,

sat.t: Family Day: Cook a Meal Together
sat.d: Today, prepare a lunch or dinner as a whole family. Start with a short meeting and share out the jobs by age: little ones wash vegetables and set the table, school-age children crack eggs and measure rice, teens chop and run the stove, and Mom and Dad act as helpers rather than commanders. Allow mistakes along the way; a bit of eggshell in the bowl is fine. Before you eat, let each person say, “Today I made ___, and I made it for the Lord.” Afterward, wash up together, thank one another, and pray, thanking God for hands that can work side by side.

sun: This week, in housework, work or money, what touched you most about the words “as for the Lord”?
Are you more likely to do too much for your children, or to ask too much of them? What is the heart behind that?
Next week, how could you help another parent turn chores and pocket money into a school of character for the children?

lessons.title: Work Is a Blessing from the Beginning
lessons.theme: Work is not a curse; it is the stewardship God entrusted to people from the beginning

v: The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.

lessons.still: Hold today's tasks quietly in your heart: work, housework, school runs, homework. Do not rush to begin. Say to the Lord, “Lord, whatever my hands do today, I want to do it for you.” Stay quiet a moment and let those words be the first thought of your day.
teach: Many people assume work is a punishment that came after sin, but it is not so. Before there was any sin, God placed the man in the garden of Eden “to cultivate and keep it.” Work was God's design from the start: the way people share in his creating and care for his world. Sin brought the sweat and toil, but it did not take away the dignity of work itself. God is a God who works. He made us, and he invites us to work alongside him, so work was always meant to carry his image.

When Paul wrote to the church in Colossae, his readers included slaves, the humblest people of the day. He told them, “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.” Washing dishes, taking out the trash, editing a report, lifting boxes: people rank these jobs, but in the Lord's eyes any of them can be worship. What gives work its worth is not what we do, but who we do it for. The same cloth can wipe the table with grumbling or with worship.

The home is a child's first school of work. Whether a child does chores looks like a life skill, but the heart with which he does them is character. A child who learns to work “for the Lord” will carry that same heart into the classroom, the sports field and the office. Today's chore chart is really laying a foundation for a lifetime. Parents need not wait until a child does it perfectly before letting him help. Simply letting him take part is how we grow his heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of view. Move from “I work to earn money and to be noticed” to “I work for the Lord.” To let Jesus reign is to let him be the boss of my work; to let Jesus receive all the glory is to do my best whether or not anyone applauds.
q: Who is God? — God himself works, and he hands the dignity of caring for the garden to people. What do you see of God in this?
Who am I? — When I do chores at home or go to work, who am I usually doing it for in my heart?
How should I respond? — Which job do I like least today, and will I try doing it “for the Lord”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus spent many years as a carpenter in Nazareth, and the townspeople asked, “Isn’t this the carpenter?” The Son of God planed wood and drove nails with his own hands, pleasing his Father in work no one noticed. He also said, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.”
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving people work, and for entrusting this home to my care. I admit that I often grumble about housework, grow weary of my job, or work only for others' eyes. Renew my heart, so that every small thing I do today is done from the heart for you, and let my children see in me the joy of working for the Lord. Amen.
acts: Do the chore you like least, and before you start whisper, “Lord, this is for you.”
Thank a family member today for a chore they did, saying exactly what they did
At dinner, share: when in my work today did it feel like I was serving the Lord?
lessons.noon: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” — Lord, whatever is in my hands right now, I want to do it for you.

fam.key: Everything I do, I do for the Lord.

lamb.do: Give your child a small cloth to wipe the table with you. You wipe once, he wipes once, and clap together when you finish.
lamb.say: You're helping, well done! We're doing it together for Jesus.

sprout.story: God made a beautiful garden with sweet-smelling fruit trees, pretty flowers and lots of little animals. God said to Adam, “I'm putting you in charge of this garden!” Every day Adam watered the plants, pulled up weeds, and gave every animal a name. He was so happy, because he was helping God look after the garden!
sprout.ask: What can you do to help God look after our home?
sprout.do: Give your child a small job, such as watering a house plant or lining up their shoes neatly. When it is done, let them say, “I helped God look after our home!”

soldier.story: Paul wrote a letter to a group of servants. In those days servants did the hardest work every day, and often nobody thanked them. Paul told them: whatever you do, do it from your heart, as if you were doing it for the Lord Jesus, not for people to see. That means even if the boss is away and nobody praises you, Jesus sees. Think of sweeping the floor when Mom isn't looking: would you secretly sweep the dirt under the sofa? A person who works for the Lord does a good job even where no one can see.
ask: What chore do you like least? How would you do it if it were for Jesus?
Is there anything you only do well when a grown-up is watching?
soldier.do: This week, pick one chore as a “gift for the Lord.” Do it every day, even when nobody reminds you, and report back to the family at the weekend.

youth.talk: To be honest, Mom and Dad sometimes hate work too: endless meetings, chores that never end, and often we are just pushing through for results and for what others think. Paul says whatever we do should be as for the Lord. That challenges me, because it means my motive has to change, not just getting the job done. I am still learning, and maybe more slowly than you.
ask: What do you think is different about working “for the Lord” and working for grades, for teachers or for parents?
At school or in a part-time job, have you had a moment when you had to do well even though nobody was watching?
youth.do: Parents and teens each share one thing they recently did “only to be seen,” then pray for each other, asking the Lord to help us do things with a new heart.

fam.pray: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that we can help with the work. Help us to do it happily for you, whether or not anyone is watching. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Am I Doing Too Much for My Children?
lessons.theme: A child who is faithful in small things is trusted and trained at home

v: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise;
which having no chief, overseer, or ruler,
provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest.
He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.

lessons.still: Think back to the mornings of the past few days before leaving the house: who was packing the school bags? Who was looking for shoes? Who was hurrying everyone along? Ask the Holy Spirit to walk through those scenes with you. Do not rush to blame anyone; just ask quietly, “Lord, what part am I playing in this?”
teach: Solomon sent the lazy person to watch the ant: “which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer.” The ant needs no one standing over her; she knows what to do herself. This self-starting sense of responsibility is just what parents hope to see in their children, yet it is the hardest character trait to “teach.” No amount of lecturing can match a child being trusted and trained at home, again and again.

Today the Holy Spirit may want to shine his light not on our children but on us. Some parents are “do-it-all” parents: afraid the child will do it badly or waste time, we simply do everything ourselves. Some are “pushers”: we ask the child to be responsible while nagging and checking without end. Some are “let-it-go” parents: too tired, so anything will do. All three love their children, yet all three quietly take away the child's chance to learn responsibility.

Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” Faithfulness is built bit by bit: packing your own bag, remembering your own water bottle, bearing the consequences when you forget. Meiling, a single mother in Kuala Lumpur, says her biggest change was holding back from taking her son's forgotten homework to school. That day the teacher reminded him, and from then on he checked his bag himself the night before.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Doing everything for them often comes from the self-ruled life: I want the home to run at my pace and by my standards. Letting people be who they are includes letting children do what is right for their age. When parents step back, it is not that they love less, but that they trust God's work in the child.
q: Who is God? — God hands the care of his world to imperfect people. How do you feel about being trusted like that?
Who am I? — Am I more of a do-it-all parent, a pusher, or a let-it-go parent?
How should I respond? — What is one thing I am willing to let my child take responsibility for, starting today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus sent his disciples out two by two to preach, when they still often misunderstood and failed. He did not do everything himself. He gave them the chance to experience and learn, then listened to their reports when they returned and helped them reflect. That is the best kind of parenting.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on me. I admit that sometimes I do too much for my children, because I am in a hurry, because I care about appearances, because I fear they will fail; and sometimes all I do is push and nag. Give me faith and patience to let go in small things, so that my child learns to be faithful, and so that I learn to trust your work in him. Amen.
acts: List three things your child could do but you are doing, and begin handing one over
When your child forgets something, first ask, “What are you going to do?” instead of rescuing at once
Tell your child, “I believe you can do it, and it's fine if you're slow.”
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” — Lord, help me let my children learn faithfulness in small things, and help me be faithful in small things too.

fam.key: Faithful in small things, God is pleased.

lamb.do: Let your child put one toy back into the basket by himself. When it is done, pat his hand and give him a big smile.
lamb.say: You put it away all by yourself! Even a little thing, you did so well.

sprout.story: One summer a little ant carried a grain of rice bigger than she was, carrying and carrying it all the way home. A grasshopper nearby sang, “Stop carrying! Come and play!” The little ant said, “Winter is coming. I must get ready first.” When winter came, the ant's home was full of food, and she even shared it with the cold, hungry grasshopper!
sprout.ask: Like the little ant, what is one thing you can do all by yourself?
sprout.do: Play “Little Ant Moves House”: let your child “carry” their toys and picture books back to where they belong, one by one, and when they finish let them say, “I'm a faithful little ant!”

soldier.story: Junjie, a ten-year-old boy in Singapore, spent every morning looking for things: his water bottle, his homework book, his PE kit. His mom always nagged while helping him look, and both of them got cross. One day Mom said, “From tomorrow I won't help you look. Work it out yourself.” In the first week Junjie forgot his PE kit and had to sit out the lesson. In the second week he made a checklist and stuck it on the door. Jesus said that whoever is faithful in the smallest things will be faithful in big things too.
ask: Do you think Mom not helping Junjie look for things was loving him or not loving him? Why?
What small thing would you like to start being responsible for yourself?
soldier.do: Make your own “leaving the house checklist” or “bedtime checklist,” stick it on your bedroom door, and check it yourself every day this week.

youth.talk: I notice I often say, “You need to learn responsibility,” and then do so many things for you: reminding you, fixing things for you, explaining to your teachers for you. Maybe it is because I fear you will fail, or maybe because I cannot let go of control. I want to admit that first, and I want to hear how you feel, whether thankful or frustrated. I am willing to listen to either.
ask: What are some things you think I could let you decide and be responsible for yourself?
If you take responsibility but don't do it well, how would you like me to respond?
youth.do: Together make a “handover list”: three things you will be responsible for from this week, and how your parents promise to stay out of them.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for trusting us to do things. Help us to be like the little ant and do even small things well on our own, faithful and pleasing to you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Money Is Entrusted by God
lessons.theme: I believe: all things come from God, and we are only stewards

v: Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.
Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all! In your hand is power and might! It is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all!
Now therefore, our God, we thank you and praise your glorious name.
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.

lessons.still: Open your wallet or the account on your phone, take a look, then close it. Put your hand on your chest and say, “Lord, all of this is yours.” Stay quiet for a moment, notice any worry or attachment about money in your heart, and hand it to him.
teach: In his last years David prepared great quantities of gold and silver to build the temple, and the people gave willingly too. By any measure this was the “richest” moment of David's life, yet he prayed, “But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” David saw that he was not the owner but a steward holding things for a time. A steward need not be proud of how much he has, nor afraid of how little, but only be faithful.

Chinese parents take money seriously. We fear our children will waste it, yet we seldom talk about money with them, as if it were a grown-up matter. But children mostly learn about money not from our words but from our anxiety, our comparing, our showing off or our stinginess. What they see is: do Mom and Dad trust God, or trust money? The look on our faces over a bill speaks louder than anything we teach at the table.

Pocket money is a fine school for stewardship. In Tainan, Grandma gave her grandson Xiaoyu three glass jars: giving, saving and spending. Each week he divided his pocket money first, then spent. Once Xiaoyu used up his spending jar on snacks, and at the weekend he had no money for the model he wanted. Grandma did not top it up, but sat with him to make a new plan. What Xiaoyu learned was not only money management but that money is entrusted by God, to be used faithfully.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Turn from the worldly to the godly, from the temporary to the eternal. Money is a good servant but a terrible master. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him be Lord of my wallet. When parents first become self-emptied about money, children will come to believe “all things come from you.”
q: Who is God? — Greatness, power, glory and riches all belong to him. How much does a God like this deserve your trust?
Who am I? — With money, am I showing my children trust in God or trust in money?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe”: I believe our family's money is…; I believe God will…; I believe my children need to learn…
lessons.jesus: Jesus looked up and saw a poor widow putting in two small coins, and said she had put in more than all the others, because she put in all she had to live on. Jesus looks not at the amount but at the heart. And though he was rich, for our sakes he became poor, that we through his poverty might become rich.
lessons.pray: Lord of all, I believe that all things come from you, and that our family's income, savings and home are all entrusted to us by you. I admit that I often worry about money and use it to measure success. Set me free, make me a faithful steward, and let my children learn from me gratitude, contentment and cheerful giving. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements and stick them inside your wallet or on the back of your phone
Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: how do we currently give pocket money, and what would we like to change?
Prepare three jars or envelopes for your children: giving, saving and spending
lessons.noon: “For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” — Lord, everything in my hands is yours; teach me to use it faithfully.

fam.key: Everything belongs to God; I am a steward.

lamb.do: Let your child hold a coin, then help him drop it into a piggy bank, and when you hear the “clink” say thank you to God together.
lamb.say: God gave us this, so we take good care of it.

sprout.story: King David wanted to build God a beautiful temple, and he and everyone else brought lots of gold and silver. Everyone happily gave gifts to God. But David prayed, “God, all these things were yours to begin with! We are only giving back to you what you gave us.” It is like Mom giving you money to buy her a present, and Mom is still so happy!
sprout.ask: What good things has God given our family?
sprout.do: Prepare three little boxes labeled “For God,” “Save” and “Can spend,” and let your child put one coin in each box.

soldier.story: David had prepared lots of gold, silver and precious stones to build the temple, and the people gave willingly too. If David had proudly said, “Look how generous I am!” it might have seemed fair enough. But instead he prayed, “All things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” It is like borrowing a classmate's pen to finish your homework: you would never say the pen is yours. Our money, our toys and our time are all lent to us by God to look after.
ask: If money is lent to us by God, how would you use your pocket money?
Do you think giving to God is losing or gaining? Why?
soldier.do: This week start managing your pocket money with “three jars”: giving, saving and spending. First decide with your parents how much goes in each, then keep a record at the weekend.

youth.talk: We seldom talk about money properly. Honestly I struggle with it too: I worry there won't be enough, I compare myself with others, and sometimes I use money to prove myself. David says all things come from God. I believe that, but my daily life often does not show it. I would like to learn together with you, because soon you will be earning and spending your own money, and I hope you will be freer than I have been.
ask: Where do you think our family's attitude to money looks like trusting God, and where does it look like trusting money?
If you had an income of your own, how would you divide it between giving, saving and spending?
youth.do: Look together at a month's family spending in outline (no need for details), ask your teen what they notice, and invite them to pray with you about the family's giving next month.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving our family so many good things. We know they are all yours. Help us to use them well and gladly share them with others. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Take Up the Towel Like Jesus
lessons.theme: Housework is loving service, shared by the whole family

v: So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.still: Picture that night: Jesus stands up, takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around his waist, and kneels at the disciples' feet. Let this picture stay in your heart, and say to the Lord, “Lord, teach me how to take up the towel at home today.”
teach: It was the night before Jesus was betrayed, and the disciples were still arguing about who was greatest. No one was willing to do the humblest job, washing feet. Jesus quietly stood up and knelt down to wash their feet himself. When he had finished he said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” In God's kingdom, greatness is not being served but serving. The Lord did not teach humility with a sermon, but with a basin of water and a towel.

In many homes housework is a quiet war: who does more, who has it easiest, who is slacking. Mr. and Mrs. Huang, both working, once argued over who should take out the trash until they stopped speaking. Then they read this passage, and the husband said, “The Lord was willing to wash feet; what is a bit of trash to me?” When chores turned from “fair shares” into “serving one another,” the air in the house changed. The children no longer saw parents keeping score, but parents racing to serve.

So let the whole family practice today. Share the jobs by age: two- and three-year-olds can tidy toys and put socks in the laundry basket; preschoolers can set the table and water the plants; school-age children can fold clothes, take out the trash and wash the rice; teens can cook a dish or clean the bathroom. What matters is not how well it is done, but learning together the heart of Jesus taking up the towel. Parents must show the way first, and sincerely thank every small act of service.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place. The one who takes up the towel at home is the one who lets Jesus reign. Pride provokes pride, and keeping score provokes keeping score; humility draws out humility, and service draws out service. The whole family benefits in the Lord, and the home becomes the first place to see God's kingdom.
q: Who is God? — The Lord and Teacher knelt down to wash feet. How does this God's humility touch you?
Who am I? — With housework, am I more often keeping score of fairness, or glad to serve?
How should I respond? — Which chore will I use today to serve my family like Jesus?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into his hands, yet he still took up the towel and washed the disciples' feet, even those of Judas, who would betray him. His service did not come from lacking status but from being full of love. He said, “You also ought to wash one another’s feet.”
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for washing my feet and giving your life for me. I admit that at home I often keep score and feel I do the most and am treated unfairly. Today I am willing to take up the towel as you did and gladly serve my spouse and children. Teach our whole family to serve one another and to experience your love in our chores. Amen.
acts: Hold a ten-minute family chore meeting today and make a chore chart by age
Quietly get in first and do a chore your spouse usually does, without saying anything
Write at the top of the chore chart: “You also ought to wash one another’s feet.”
lessons.noon: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” — Lord, today let me take up your towel at home.

fam.key: We serve one another like Jesus.

lamb.do: When you wash your child's hands, rub his little hands slowly and gently, singing a simple song as you go.
lamb.say: Jesus loves us and washed our feet; Mommy and Daddy love you and wash your hands.

sprout.story: One evening Jesus was having dinner with his friends. Their feet were dirty and smelly from walking all day. Jesus stood up, took a basin of water and a towel, knelt down, and washed his friends' feet one by one. Peter was shocked: Jesus is our teacher, how can he wash my feet? Jesus said, “I'm showing you what to do, so you can help one another like this too!”
sprout.ask: How can you help someone at home today?
sprout.do: Play “Hand-Washing Service” as a family: one person takes a towel and dries another's hands, saying, “I love you, I serve you!” Take turns.

soldier.story: The night before Jesus was betrayed, the disciples were still arguing about who was greatest. In those days foot-washing was a servant's job, and nobody wanted it. But Jesus stood up, tied a towel round his waist, knelt down and washed every disciple's feet, even Judas, who was about to betray him. When he had finished, Jesus said, “I have given you an example,” and “you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” In our home, “washing feet” could be helping your little brother tidy his toys, helping Mom hang out the washing, or taking out the trash without complaining.
ask: In our home, who do you think most often “washes other people's feet”?
What kind of service is hardest for you? Why?
soldier.do: Make a family chore chart together, with each person choosing one “foot-washing task.” Each day this week that you do it, draw a little towel on the chart.

youth.talk: Our household chores are often very unfair, and I admit that sometimes I hand you a lot of jobs, or grumble while doing them, so that chores feel like a punishment to you. When Jesus washed the disciples' feet, he did not count who should have done it. I would like to start again, not dividing chores by “who owes whom” but learning together to serve one another. I am willing to change first, and I ask you to give me the chance.
ask: Where does our present division of chores feel unfair to you?
If chores are “washing one another's feet,” which one would you take on more? Which one would you like me to take on more?
youth.do: Redesign the family's chores together. Let your teen put forward a plan, and parents first accept at least one of their suggestions.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for kneeling down to wash your friends' feet. Help us to help one another at home without grumbling or keeping score, because we love you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Faithful in a Few Things
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: a steward does not seek to be great, only to be faithful

v: “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

lessons.still: Slowly look back over this week's chores, work and spending, like turning the pages of an account book. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you: where was I faithful? Where did I cut corners? Do not be afraid; the Lord's gaze is a gaze of grace.
teach: In the parable of the talents, when the master returned he did not ask how much was earned, but said to the two servants, “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things.” The one given five and the one given two received the very same praise. God values not scale but faithfulness. A child setting a pair of shoes neatly and an adult finishing a big project can be equally welcome before God.

Paul also says, “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” This week we have talked about work, responsibility, money and chores. When we review, we should not only look at whether the children did their chores or wasted money, but also at ourselves: Did I let go? Did I set an example? Did I use threats in place of company? Review is not to find out who is worst, but to come back together to the Lord and see how to do better next step.

The servant who buried his talent had a problem not of ability but of heart. He said, “I knew you that you are a hard man,” and “I was afraid.” If a child does chores only because he fears a scolding, he learns fear, not faithfulness. The direction for adjustment is to make home a place where mistakes can be tried again and good work is noticed. A child who learns responsibility in love will grow into a willing and cheerful steward.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition are the daily life of a steward. Deal with your own heart first, then with the children's behavior: when parents admit where they have not been faithful, children learn to face themselves honestly. Humility draws out humility, and faithfulness draws out faithfulness.
q: Who is God? — God is the master who says, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” How does he see your week?
Who am I? — This week, in work, chores and money, where was I faithful? Where was I like the servant who buried his talent?
How should I respond? — What is one thing I will adjust next week, and how exactly will I do it?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished!” He completed fully the work his Father gave him, leaving nothing out. He is the most faithful servant, and also the Lord who gives us grace and a fresh start. Our faithfulness flows from his.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking back through this week with me. I admit that I cut corners on some things, and sometimes used nagging and scolding in place of company, so that my children were afraid instead of willing. Forgive me, and thank you for your grace to me in small things. Help me to be more faithful in a few things next week, and let my children learn responsibility in love. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what good changes have there been in this week's chores and pocket money? What needs adjusting?
Ask your child, “This week, was Daddy/Mommy more like Jesus in doing chores?” Just listen, and do not defend yourself
Write down one specific adjustment for next week and tell your family
lessons.noon: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things” — Lord, I do not seek to be great, only to be faithful in the small things you entrust to me.

fam.key: Faithful in small things is great.

lamb.do: Remember one small thing your child helped with this week, hold him, kiss his little hand, and say thank you once more.
lamb.say: Thank you for helping this week. Your little hands are so clever!

sprout.story: A master was going on a long journey, and he left his money with three servants to look after. Two servants worked hard, put the money to work, and earned more. The third servant was very afraid and buried his money in the ground. When the master came back, he praised the hard-working servants: “Well done! You are good and faithful servants!” God is pleased when we use well what he has given us.
sprout.ask: What did you do this week that made God happy?
sprout.do: Sit in a circle as a family. Each person names one chore they managed this week, and the others say, “Well done! You're a faithful servant!” and give them a hug.

soldier.story: Jesus told of a master who, before leaving, gave money to three servants. The first received five talents and earned five more; the second received two and earned two more; the third received one, but out of fear buried it in the ground. When the master returned, he said exactly the same words to the first two: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” The master did not compare who earned more; he only looked at who was faithful.
ask: This week, were you faithful with your chore job or your pocket money jars?
What would you like to improve next week? How can your family help you?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: check the chore chart and the pocket money jars, and let each person name one thing done well and one thing to adjust next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we talked about chores, responsibility and money, and I want to review myself first: Have I really let go? Have I said I trust you and then not been able to keep from stepping in? The servant who buried the money did it out of fear. I do not want you to do things because you fear me, but because you know you are trusted and loved. If I have made you afraid, I want to hear it from you.
ask: Was there a time this week when I stepped in too much or nagged too much, so that you felt I did not trust you?
In responsibility or money, what would you like to challenge yourself to do next week?
youth.do: Parents first apologize to their teen for one time this week they stepped in or nagged too much, then decide together on a new “handover” item for next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for walking with us this week as we learned to work, manage money and serve one another. Some things we did well, and some not. Help us to be more faithful next week, pleasing to you. In Jesus' name, amen.

47.memT: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,

mem.t: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.

sat.t: Family Day: Visit Someone Who Works for the Lord
sat.d: Visit together an older Christian or church friend who works in a different field, such as a nurse, a plumber or electrician, a teacher, a street vendor or an engineer. Before you go, let the children prepare three questions: “How did you find this job?” “How do you serve God in your work?” “In the hardest time you have faced, how did God lead you?” Afterward, share a snack together. On the way home, let each person tell the one thing that stayed with them most, and finish by praying for that person and their work.

sun: This week, which passage helped you see again that “God has a plan for children”? How is that plan different from the plan you have made for your children?
Is there a life script you have already written for your children in your heart? Where did it come from?
Next week, how could you walk beside your own child, or a teenager in another family, in seeking God's will?

lessons.title: God Has a Plan for the Children
lessons.theme: God's thoughts toward every child are thoughts of peace, giving hope and a future

v: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.
You shall call on me, and you shall go and pray to me, and I will listen to you.
You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

lessons.still: Picture each child's face and name them one by one before the Lord. Do not rush to ask for their future; first grow quiet and say, “Lord, you knew him before I did, and you love him more than I do.” Let this peace sink into your heart.
teach: Jeremiah 29:11 is often printed on graduation cards as a kind of “bright future” blessing. But it was first written to people carried off captive to Babylon. God told them first: build houses, marry and have children, seek the peace of the city, for only after seventy years would he visit them. God's plan was not quick success, but hope even in a hard place.

“For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.” This is God's heart toward his people, and it is his heart toward our children. A child's future does not rest on the school system, the state of the economy or a parent's connections, but in the hands of a God whose thoughts are of peace. An anxious parent can breathe deeply at this.

Paul says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” The word “workmanship” carries the sense of “masterpiece.” Every child is God's own handiwork, and God has already prepared good works for him to do. A parent's task is not to design the child's life but to walk with the child in discovering God's design. When life planning begins with God, it is no longer a gamble but a search.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Move the view from the temporary to the eternal. The earthly eye asks only, “How much will my child earn, how high will he rise?” The heavenly eye first asks, “What did God make him for?” Only when Jesus reigns over the child's life can a parent move from anxious planner to restful companion.
q: Who is God? — Even in a land of captivity, God says, “to give you hope and a future.” What kind of God is he?
Who am I? — Do my worries about my child's future come more from God's promises, or from circumstances and comparison?
How should I respond? — In what way can I let my child know today that “God has a good plan for you”?
lessons.jesus: At twelve, in the temple, Jesus said to his anxious parents who had been looking for him, “Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” He knew clearly that he had come for his Father's will. Later he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” He is our example of a life lived in calling.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that your thoughts toward my children are thoughts of peace. I admit I am often anxious about their future, and I count school and jobs as more important than knowing you. Today I place each child's future in your hands. Fulfill your plan in them, and make me a parent who walks beside them as they seek your will. Amen.
acts: Write a one-line prayer for each child: “Lord, fulfill your good plan in ___.”
Find a chance today to tell your child, “You are God's masterpiece, and God has good things prepared for you.”
Write Jeremiah 29:11 on a small card and put it by your child's desk
lessons.noon: “For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil” — Lord, my children are in your hands, and I can rest.

fam.key: God has a good plan for me.

lamb.do: Hold your child and look at photos or a video of him as a baby, gently stroking his little hands and feet.
lamb.say: God made you, you are God's treasure, and God has a good plan for you.

sprout.story: A painter was painting on a big canvas. First he painted blue, then yellow, and a child beside him couldn't make it out: “What is it?” The painter smiled and said, “Wait till I'm finished and you'll see.” In the end, a lovely sunrise over the sea appeared! God is like that painter. He is painting you now, and he knows how beautiful you will be when you grow up.
sprout.ask: What do you think God is painting you to become?
sprout.do: Give your child a sheet of paper and let him draw “me when I'm grown up.” When he is done, Mom and Dad write beside it: “God's masterpiece.”

soldier.story: The Israelites were defeated and taken far away to Babylon. Everyone was discouraged and felt God didn't want them any more. Then the prophet Jeremiah wrote them a letter. It said: live well there, build houses and plant fields, because after seventy years God will bring you home. God also said, “For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.” Even in the hardest place, God's plan is still good.
ask: Have you ever had something that seemed terrible, but later you saw God leading?
What would you like to ask God about his plan for your life?
soldier.do: Write a short “letter to me in ten years' time,” with your dreams today and one prayer, and ask Mom or Dad to seal it and keep it.

youth.talk: Your generation is under great pressure: exams, choosing a course, a hard job market, and even adults can't say what the future will be. Honestly, I am often anxious about your future myself, and sometimes I turn my worry into nagging. Jeremiah 29:11 was first written to people who were captive and could see no way out. I would like to believe with you that when we can't see clearly, God's thoughts are still thoughts of peace.
ask: When you think about the future, what worries you most?
Does “God has a plan” feel like comfort to you, or a bit like a slogan from adults?
youth.do: Parents and teens each write down one worry about the future, swap and read them, then pray for each other's worry, without rushing to give advice.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for having a good plan for each one of us. Whatever the future holds, please keep leading us and be with us. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Am I Writing the Script for My Child?
lessons.theme: Parents are not the screenwriters of a child's life, but Eli, who helps him hear God's voice

v: The LORD called Samuel again the third time. He arose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” Eli perceived that the LORD had called the child.
Therefore Eli said to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”

lessons.still: Say softly in your heart, “Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.” Repeat it a few times and let your breathing slow. Then ask the Lord, “Among my expectations for my children, which are your voice and which are only mine?”
teach: Young Samuel was sleeping in the temple when he heard a voice calling him, and three times he ran to Eli. In those days “the LORD’s word was rare,” and Samuel did not yet know God's voice. The third time, old Eli understood. He did not answer for Samuel, nor push his own ideas on the boy, but taught him to say, “Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.” Eli's greatest contribution was to bring a child to God.

Today the Holy Spirit wants to shine his light on us: what kind of parent am I? Some are “screenwriters”: while the child is still small, the script is written: which school, which course, which career, preferably doctor or lawyer. Some are “audience”: you decide for yourself, I don't understand and don't want to interfere. And some are “Eli”: not hearing on the child's behalf, and not leaving him to listen alone, but walking with him as he learns to discern God's voice.

Mr. Chen in Vancouver had always hoped his son would study business and carry on the family firm. But his son loved music, and the two gave each other the cold shoulder for a year. Then, in prayer, Mr. Chen found that what he really cared about was his own face and sense of security. He apologized to his son and said, “Let's ask God together.” The script was set down, the father and son were reconciled, and the son began to seek God in earnest.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Writing a script for your child is often an extension of the self-ruled life: wanting to fulfill my own dreams or make up for my regrets through my child. Pride grabs power and leaves its place; humility returns to its place, letting God be God, the child be himself, and the parent be the companion.
q: Who is God? — God himself called a small child by name. Is he calling my child now?
Who am I? — Am I more a screenwriter, an audience member, or an Eli?
How should I respond? — Which expectation of my child do I need to bring back to God for a fresh look?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” Even the Son of God laid down his own wishes and obeyed his Father's will. When we pray for our children's futures, we too must learn to pray this way and hand our own scripts to the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on me. I admit I often write scripts for my children, laying my dreams, my regrets and my pride on them. Forgive me, and teach me to be an Eli who brings my children to you and teaches them to say, “Speak; for your servant hears.” And please call my children yourself. Amen.
acts: Write down the “script” you have for each child, and beside each line ask: is this God's voice or mine?
Today ask your child an open question: “What have you found most meaningful lately?” Just listen, and don't comment
Teach your child a simple prayer: “Lord, please speak, I'm listening.”
lessons.noon: “Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.” — Lord, let me listen to you first, and teach me to help my children listen to you.

fam.key: Lord, please speak, I'm listening.

lamb.do: In a quiet moment, softly call your child's name, wait for him to turn his head, then give him a smile and a hug.
lamb.say: God knows your name too, and God loves you very much.

sprout.story: One night while little Samuel was sleeping, he heard someone call, “Samuel! Samuel!” He ran to old Eli the priest: “Did you call me?” Eli said, “I didn't call you.” After this happened three times, Eli realized it was God calling Samuel! Eli taught him to say, “Speak, for your servant is listening!” So Samuel lay down and quietly listened to God.
sprout.ask: If God called your name, what would you like to say to him?
sprout.do: Play the “Listening for the Voice” game: your child closes his eyes and family members take turns whispering his name while he guesses who it is. At the end say together, “Lord, please speak, I'm listening!”

soldier.story: Samuel lived in the temple from childhood and learned from old Eli the priest. One night God called Samuel, but he did not yet know God's voice and thought it was Eli. The third time Eli understood, and taught Samuel to answer, “Speak; for your servant hears.” Eli did not say, “Let me tell you what God is saying.” He let Samuel hear for himself. Later Samuel grew up, God was with him, and he became a great prophet of Israel.
ask: How do you think God speaks to children today?
Has a grown-up ever helped you know God better? How did he do it?
soldier.do: Every night this week before bed, be quiet for a minute and say, “Lord, please speak, I'm listening.” Then tell Mom or Dad one thing that came to your mind.

youth.talk: I want to admit first that in my heart I have actually written a script for you: I hope you will study certain subjects and take a certain safe path. Some of it is because I love you, and some may be my own worry and pride. Eli did not hear God's voice for Samuel; he only taught Samuel how to listen. I want to learn from Eli, and I want to know how my expectations have affected you.
ask: Do you sense expectations I have about your future that I haven't said out loud?
If you didn't have to think about anyone's opinion, what direction would you most like to explore?
youth.do: A parent writes down one expectation for their child and reads it aloud to them, then says, “I'm willing to hand this to God, and let's seek him together.”

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that you know each of our names. Teach us to be quiet and listen to you, and to follow you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Calling Is Bigger Than a Career
lessons.theme: I believe: a child is first called to belong to Christ, and then to live for him in any post

v: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.
Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

lessons.still: Think about your own work or post right now, whether you go out to work, care for children at home, or are retired. Say to the Lord, “Lord, am I here because you called me?” Wait quietly and let him remind you that you first belong to him.
teach: Many people use the word “calling” only for pastors and missionaries, as if everyone else merely “goes to work.” But Paul says to all believers, “present your bodies a living sacrifice,” and “whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” Calling is not just an occupation but an identity: we are first called to belong to Christ, then to live him out in every post. Jobs change, but identity does not.

Calling has three layers. The first is “whom to follow”: every child is first called to follow Jesus. The second is “who to become”: God wants to shape Christ's character in him. Only the third is “what to do”: in which field, with which gifts to serve others. Parents often care only about the third layer, asking the child, “What will you be when you grow up?” and forgetting that the first two are the foundation. Without the first two, even the most dazzling career can turn out empty.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” The world's view of careers asks which field pays well and which has status. God's view of calling asks where light is needed, where your gifts fit, and where God can be glorified. A plumber who loves the Lord and a doctor who loves the Lord are equally called in God's eyes. Today we move from having heard to being convinced.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Living out the three foundations in calling: Jesus is my example; Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide. Whatever the child does in future, one purpose does not change: that Jesus receives all the glory, and that what belongs to God is built in that field.
q: Who is God? — God calls people first to belong to him, then sends them into every kind of work. How does this God see ordinary work?
Who am I? — I often ask my child, “What will you be when you grow up?” Have I also asked, “What kind of person do you want to be?”
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe”: I believe my child is first called to…; I believe his worth is not in…; I believe God will…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to the fishermen Peter and Andrew, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.” He first called them to follow him, and then changed the direction of their work. Jesus' call always begins with relationship: first follow him, and only then what to do.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I believe my children are first called by you and belong to you. I believe their worth lies not in grades, degrees or salary. I believe you will fulfill your will in them. Renew my mind so that I do not copy the world's measures of success, and let my children and me prove your good, well-pleasing and perfect will. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements and read them to your family at dinner
Today replace “What will you be when you grow up?” with “What kind of person do you want to be?” when you ask your child
Share which part of your own work feels like serving God
lessons.noon: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” — Lord, renew how I see my children's future, and let me look first to your will.

fam.key: I belong to Jesus first, then I do things.

lamb.do: Hold your child in your arms, hold his little hands, and help him make an “offering to God” gesture: both hands lifted up.
lamb.say: You are Jesus' treasure, and your little hands belong to Jesus too.

sprout.story: One day Peter and Andrew were fishing by the sea, their nets wet and the fish jumping. Jesus came along and said, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.” They put down their nets right away and followed Jesus. Later they didn't catch fish; they helped lots and lots of people get to know Jesus.
sprout.ask: If Jesus asked you to follow him, what would you say?
sprout.do: Play “Follow Jesus”: one person acts as Jesus and walks in front, everyone follows and copies the movements, and at the end say together, “I want to follow Jesus!”

soldier.story: In an essay, twelve-year-old Xin'en from Singapore wrote, “When I grow up I want to be a cleaner.” Her teacher frowned, but her mom asked her why. Xin'en said, “Because I see the cleaning auntie working so hard every day, yet she always smiles at everyone. I want to make people happy like her.” Her mom said, “Whatever you do, the most important thing is that you belong to Jesus, and use that work to love people and glorify God.” The Bible says, whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
ask: Do you think any kind of job is “not good enough” to glorify God? Why?
What kind of person do you want to be?
soldier.do: Each family member writes a card: “I want to be someone who ___.” Write no job, only character. Stick them on the fridge and encourage one another this week.

youth.talk: Our generation was taught that “you study to get a good job,” and a good job means high pay and status. I lived by that standard myself for many years. But the Bible says calling is bigger than a career: you are first a person who belongs to Christ, and whatever you do in future, you live for the Lord there. I am learning to look at my own work this way too.
ask: Do you think our family's “standard of success” is more like the world's, or God's? How can you tell?
If your calling is “what kind of person to become,” how would you describe it?
youth.do: Parents share honestly how they chose their work, including what they weighed then and what they think now, then invite their teen to say what direction is on their heart.

fam.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling us to follow you. Whatever we do when we grow up, we want to belong to you first and do everything to glorify you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Walking with Children as They Seek God's Will
lessons.theme: Acknowledge God in all your ways, and he will make your children's paths straight

v: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps.

lessons.still: Think of a choice your child is facing right now: choosing a club, a course, friends, or just how to plan next week. Place it before the Lord and say, “Lord, I don't know, but you do.”
teach: “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps.” The Bible does not tell us not to plan; it reminds us that planning is our responsibility and directing is God's sovereignty. Seeking God's will is not looking for a note with the answer written on it, but learning, step by step, to “in all your ways acknowledge him.” It is like driving at night: the headlights only light up a few dozen meters ahead, yet that is enough to get us all the way to our destination.

To walk with a child in seeking God's will, you can use five simple questions. One: What does the Bible say? Does this go against God's word? Two: Do I have peace in my heart as I pray? Three: Does this use the gifts and passion God has given me? Four: Are there signs of doors opening or closing in my circumstances? Five: What do the spiritual elders who love me think? These five are not a formula but a framework for helping children think in God's presence.

So let the whole family practice today. Pick a real choice your child is facing, big or small, discuss it using these five questions, and pray together at the end. For a small child it may be just “which toy to share with a friend today”; for a teenager it may be choosing subjects or planning the summer. The point is not that the parent decides for the child, but that the child experiences: I can bring my choice to God, and he will make my path straight.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head. “Don’t lean on your own understanding” does not mean we should not think, but that we should not put ourselves on the throne. The eight steps for changing a mindset are also a process of seeking God's will: information, revelation, conviction, practice, then review and adjustment.
q: Who is God? — God promises, “he will make your paths straight.” How have you experienced him leading you step by step?
Who am I? — When my child faces a choice, do I give the answer first, or pray with him first?
How should I respond? — For which real choice will I walk with my child in seeking God today?
lessons.jesus: Before choosing the twelve disciples, Jesus went out to the mountain alone and “continued all night in prayer to God.” The Son of God spent time with the Father before an important decision. He shows us that seeking God's will is not a hurried question but quiet waiting within a relationship.
lessons.pray: Lord, I often lean on my own understanding to make decisions for my children, or turn my anxiety into orders. Today I am willing to learn to come before you together with my children, and to acknowledge you in all our ways. Direct the steps of our whole family, and let my children know from early on that you are a faithful, guiding God. Amen.
acts: Today discuss a real choice with your child using the five questions
Copy Proverbs 3:5–6 onto a card and give it to your child
Tell your child about a time you yourself experienced God's guidance
lessons.noon: “In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” — Lord, I hand every step of mine and my children's to your direction.

fam.key: God will lead me on the right path.

lamb.do: Hold your child's hand and walk slowly around the house. At each room stop and say, “Thank you, God, for leading us.”
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy hold your hand, and God holds your hand too.

sprout.story: Xiaomi was going to Grandma's house, but there were lots of forks in the road and she didn't know which to take. Dad held her hand and said, “Don't be afraid. I know the way, so just follow me.” At every junction Xiaomi asked, “Dad, which way?” and Dad pointed it out to her. In the end they arrived safely at Grandma's. God is like that dad: every time we ask him, he leads us the right way.
sprout.ask: What would you like to ask God about which way to go?
sprout.do: Set up a “maze” at home with chairs and pillows. Let your child close his eyes and be guided to the end by Dad's or Mom's voice.

soldier.story: Jiahao, an eleven-year-old boy in Kuala Lumpur, had to decide between joining the soccer team and the Chinese orchestra, and the times clashed. His dad didn't choose for him, but asked five questions with him: What does the Bible say? Do I have peace in my heart as I pray? Which one uses your gifts? Are time and travel workable? What do the coach and the teacher advise? In the end Jiahao chose the orchestra, because he found he could help others most there. The Bible says, in all your ways acknowledge God, and he will make your paths straight.
ask: Is there something lately you didn't know how to choose?
What do you think “acknowledge God” means?
soldier.do: Take a choice you are facing and discuss it with Mom or Dad using the five questions, then pray together at the end.

youth.talk: The choices you face are growing in number and importance. I would love to just tell you the answer, because I fear you will take a wrong path. But I know that if I keep choosing for you, you will never learn to decide in God's presence. I want to try another way: we pray together and think together, and in the end you decide before God while I stand beside you.
ask: Do you think God is part of it when our family makes important decisions?
When you are making a choice, do you need me more to give an opinion, or to listen to you?
youth.do: Pick a choice you are facing and discuss it with your parents using the five questions. Parents promise to respect the decision you make after prayer.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for always holding our hands. When we do not know, please guide us, so that we walk in your way. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Fearfully and Wonderfully Made
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: see your children as God sees them

v: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
My frame wasn’t hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth.
Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.

lessons.still: Recall the moments this week when you talked with your children about the future and calling. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you: where did I set down my own script? Where could I not help picking it up again? Do not rush to blame yourself; just see honestly before the Lord.
teach: David said, “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.” And, “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Every child, before his parents knew him, was known by God; his character, his talents, even his weaknesses are in God's sight. “In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.”

This week we talked about God's plan for children, parents' scripts, calling being bigger than a career, and walking with children in seeking God's will. In our review, let us not only ask, “Has my child found a direction?” but first ask, “Have I been seeing my child with God's eyes?” When parents see a child as only a report card or a CV, it is hard for the child to believe he is fearfully and wonderfully made. Children learn to see themselves through their parents' eyes.

The direction for adjustment is that children often hear at home: your worth is not in what you do in future, but in being made by God's own hands and loved by him. Mrs. Lin in Taipei has three children: the eldest does well at school, the second is strong at sport, and the third is slow. She noticed that her look toward the third child often came with a sigh. This week she began saying one sentence to him each day: “God made you, and it is truly wonderful.” The third child's smiles gradually grew.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review and adjustment are the necessary road of change. When parents first admit before God their comparing and their scripts, children can see the Father's gaze in their parents' eyes. The focus is Jesus, not the child's performance and not other people's children.
q: Who is God? — God saw the child before he took shape, and wrote his days in his book. How does this God see your children?
Who am I? — This week, when did I see my child with God's eyes? When did I see with comparing eyes?
How should I respond? — What is one thing I will adjust next week, and how exactly will I do it?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus finished his work he said to the Father, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” He spent his life not chasing people's expectations but fulfilling the Father's commission. He also saw every person others overlooked: Zacchaeus, the Samaritan woman, the little children brought to him.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for making my children with your own hands; they are fearfully and wonderfully made. I admit that this week I still compared, was disappointed, and wanted to decide for them. Forgive me, and give me your eyes to see my children. Fulfill your plan in them, and let me walk beside them more humbly next week as they seek you. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: how has our view of the children's future changed this week? What are we still unable to let go of?
Ask your child, “This week, was Daddy/Mommy more like Jesus when talking about your future?” Just listen, and do not defend yourself
Write down one adjustment for next week, such as saying one thing each day that is uniquely good about one child
lessons.noon: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” — Lord, thank you for making me, and for making my children.

fam.key: I am God's wonderful work.

lamb.do: While you gently massage your child's hands and feet, touch each one and say, “These are God-made hands, God-made feet, God-made eyes.”
lamb.say: God made you so wonderfully, and we thank God so much.

sprout.story: Even while the baby was still in Mommy's tummy, God was already looking after him. God made his little hands, little feet, little nose, and the mouth that would laugh and sing. God said, “This baby is something I made with my own hands!” Every child is different: some love to draw, some love to run, some love to sing, and God likes every one of them.
sprout.ask: What did God make most special about you?
sprout.do: Take turns around the family saying, “Thank you, God, for making ___ so ___!” For example: “Thank you, God, for making my little brother laugh so well!”

soldier.story: David wrote a poem saying that God knew him and made him while he was still in his mother's womb. David said, “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” As a boy David was only a shepherd. His brothers were all bigger than him, and even his father didn't take much notice of him. But God saw David and chose him to be king. God does not look at appearance or grades; he looks at the heart.
ask: This week, what part of yourself do you think is God's wonderful design?
Next week, which of the strengths God gave you would you like to use more at home?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person in turn hears everyone say “what is wonderful about you,” then names one thing they want to improve next week. Mom and Dad receive everyone's feedback first.

youth.talk: This week we talked a lot about the future and calling. I want to review myself first: sometimes I still compare you with others, or when you share your thoughts my first reaction is worry instead of curiosity. I want to learn again to see you with God's eyes: you are God's fearfully and wonderfully made work, not mine. Thank you for being willing to let me learn again.
ask: This week, was there anything I said about your future that made you feel compared or pressured?
How would you like us to carry on talking about this next week?
youth.do: Parents first apologize to their teen for one comparison or bit of pressure, then together agree a time and way for the next “future conversation.”

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making each one of us so wonderfully. Help us to appreciate one another, not to compare, and to follow you together. In Jesus' name, amen.

48.memT: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says the LORD, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.

mem.t: From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

sat.d: Prepare beads and string in five colors: gold, black, red, white and green. Thread the bracelets together as a family, and as you add each bead say a line: gold is God and heaven, black is sin, red is the blood Jesus shed for us, white is being washed clean, green is growing with Jesus. Mom and Dad can also share how they came to know Jesus. When they are finished, each person wears one, then makes another to give to a friend who does not yet know Jesus. End by thanking God together for his salvation.

sun: How did you come to know Jesus yourself? What does that story teach you about raising your children today?
Are you more likely to “outsource” your children's faith to Sunday school, or to push them too quickly toward a decision?
Next week, how could you share the gospel clearly with your own children, or with the children of another family?

lessons.title: Knowing the Scriptures from Childhood
lessons.theme: Parents are a child's first evangelists

v: having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, in you also.
But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them.
From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Remember who first introduced Jesus to you: parents, a friend, a Sunday school teacher, or perhaps a book or a meeting. Thank God for that person. Then say to the Lord, “Lord, I want to be the one who introduces you to my child too.”
teach: When Paul wrote to Timothy he spoke of his “sincere faith,” which “lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice.” Timothy's father was a Greek, and the Bible does not say he believed; it was a grandmother and a mother who passed the faith on to Timothy. God often uses ordinary family members, at the dinner table and at bedtime, to sow the gospel into a child's heart a little at a time.

Paul also says, “From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.” The purpose of Scripture is not merely to make a child well-behaved, but to bring him to salvation “through faith which is in Christ Jesus.” It is good to teach children to keep the rules, memorize verses and attend Sunday school, but the most important thing is that they know the Savior who gave his life for them and trust him personally. Good deeds are the fruit; trusting Christ is the root.

Many parents feel that sharing the gospel is for pastors or Sunday school teachers, and that they are not qualified. But the gospel a child hears first comes from his parents' lips, and the gospel he sees first is seen in his parents. Grandma Lin in Penang, Malaysia, raised two grandsons on her own, and every night she did just one thing: she read them a passage of Scripture and prayed. Years later both grandsons said that was where their faith began.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Leading a child to know Jesus is not a ministry to complete but the overflow of a life. When parents first live in Christ, the gospel flows naturally out of relationship; when Jesus reigns in the home, children find it easiest to know this King.
q: Who is God? — God passed faith to Timothy through a grandmother and a mother. Is he willing to use you too?
Who am I? — In my child's faith, am I a present evangelist or an absent bystander?
How should I respond? — At what moment this week can I tell my child about Jesus?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” He is the good shepherd, willing to cross the hills for one lost lamb. A child's salvation is the Father's heart, and he longs for every child to come home to him even more than we do.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for bringing the gospel to me through others. I admit I often leave my children's faith to the church and seldom speak about Jesus myself. Forgive me, and give me courage and wisdom to be my children's first evangelist at home, so that they know the Scriptures from childhood and are saved through faith in Christ Jesus. Amen.
acts: Write down how you came to know Jesus, in three to five sentences, ready to tell your children
At bedtime tonight read your child a passage from a Gospel, and when you finish say, “Jesus loves you so much.”
Pray for each child's salvation, naming them one by one
lessons.noon: “the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” — Lord, let my children know you from childhood and be saved by trusting you.

fam.key: Jesus loves me, and he is my Savior.

lamb.do: Hold your child and sing a song like “Jesus Loves Me” in a gentle voice, giving him a soft kiss when you sing “Jesus.”
lamb.say: Jesus loves you so much, and Jesus is your good friend.

sprout.story: Timothy was a little boy. His grandma was called Lois and his mom was called Eunice. Every night Grandma and Mom held him close and told him stories about God: how God made heaven and earth, and how God loves people. Timothy heard lots and lots of stories, and slowly he came to love God too. When he grew up, he became someone who helped many people know Jesus!
sprout.ask: Which Bible story do you like best?
sprout.do: Let your child choose his favorite Bible story book. Tonight Mom or Dad reads it to him, and afterward you say together, “Jesus loves me!”

soldier.story: Timothy's father was a Greek and perhaps did not believe in God, but his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice loved God very much. From the time Timothy was very small, they taught him to read the Scriptures. Later Paul wrote in a letter that from childhood he had known the Scriptures, which are able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Jesus. When Timothy grew up, he became Paul's most trusted co-worker. It turns out that a person's faith in Jesus often begins at home.
ask: How do you think Mom and Dad, or Grandpa and Grandma, have helped you know Jesus?
What would you like to know more about Jesus?
soldier.do: Ask Mom or Dad to tell you how they came to believe in Jesus. You may ask three questions, then draw the story you heard as a four-panel comic.

youth.talk: I rarely tell you properly how I came to believe, maybe because it feels awkward, or because I assumed you had already heard. My own journey of faith was not perfect, with doubts and stumbles along the way. Timothy's faith came from his grandmother and mother.
