I hope your faith is not only something you “inherit” from us, but that you really know Jesus for yourself.
ask: Does your faith right now feel more like “a family habit” or “your own choice”?
Which part of my faith journey would you like to hear about?
youth.do: This week find a quiet time when parents honestly share how they came to faith, including their lowest moment, then invite your teen to ask anything.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for loving each one of us. Help us to know you and believe in you from childhood, and to follow you all our lives. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Let the Little Children Come to Me
lessons.theme: Parents must not hinder children from coming to Jesus

v: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

lessons.still: Picture Jesus with his arms open and the children running to him, laughing. Look quietly at that scene, then ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Lord, in our home, is there anything that is keeping the children from coming to you?”
teach: Some people were bringing little children to Jesus, but the disciples rebuked them, probably thinking the Teacher was too busy for children to matter. When Jesus saw it, “he was moved with indignation.” This is one of the few times the Gospels record Jesus being angry. He said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” Then he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. In Jesus' eyes, children are not an audience for the gospel but the stars of the kingdom.

Today the Holy Spirit wants to shine his light on us: what kind of parent am I? The “outsourcer” hands the child's faith wholly to Sunday school and seldom talks about Jesus at home. The “waiter” says he will wait until the child grows up and chooses for himself, and so gives him nothing. The “pressurer” is in a hurry for the child to raise a hand and make a decision, pushing with fear of hell or with prizes. And there is the “leader,” who, like those who brought the children to Jesus, naturally and steadily brings his child to the Lord.

Sometimes what holds a child back is not harsh words but our way of life: a faith that says one thing and does another, a home too busy for prayer, a Sunday that is treated as a social event. From these a child learns that Jesus does not seem very important. At other times the obstacle is a knot in the parent's own heart, a disappointment with God that has never healed. May we come back to Jesus first, so that our children can run to him without hindrance.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep the focus on Jesus, not on ourselves. The disciples thought they were protecting Jesus, but they were replacing his heart with their own judgment. Parents too can hinder children in the name of “what is best for them.” Humility is laying down power and letting the children go straight to Jesus.
q: Who is God? — Jesus was indignant that children were held back, and he took them in his arms himself. What heart do you see in him?
Who am I? — Am I more an outsourcer, a waiter, a pressurer, or a leader?
How should I respond? — What in our home is keeping the children from Jesus? Which one can I remove today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.” He did not merely welcome children; he held them up as an example for adults: trust simply, receive openly. He took them in his arms and blessed them, just as the Father longs to embrace every child who comes home.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, shine your light on me. I admit that sometimes I hand my children's faith to others, sometimes I am in a hurry for them to make a decision, and sometimes my own life makes you seem unimportant to them. Forgive me, remove everything in our home that gets in the way, and let my children run freely to you and be held in your arms. Amen.
acts: Write down one thing in your home that may be keeping your child from Jesus, and pray about it
Today lay your hand on your child's head and speak a word of blessing over him
Ask yourself: when did I last truly worship God in front of my children?
lessons.noon: “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them” — Lord, I want to bring my children to you and stop hindering them.

fam.key: Jesus welcomes every child.

lamb.do: Open your arms and let your child run to you, or lift him up and spin him round, then lay your hand gently on his head and bless him.
lamb.say: Jesus opens his arms to welcome you, just like Mommy and Daddy hold you.

sprout.story: One day lots of moms and dads brought their children to see Jesus. But Jesus' friends said, “Go away, go away, Jesus is busy!” The children were so sad. Jesus saw it and said, “Let the little children come to me, and don't stop them.” The children ran to him happily, and Jesus picked them up, stroked their heads, and blessed them.
sprout.ask: If you ran to Jesus, what would you like to say to him?
sprout.do: Play “Run to Jesus”: Mom or Dad stands at the other end of the room with open arms, your child runs over to be hugged, and you say together, “Jesus welcomes me!”

soldier.story: Once, grown-ups brought children to Jesus, hoping he would touch them. The disciples thought the children would be noisy and bother the Teacher, so they sent them away. Jesus saw it and was very angry. He said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.” Jesus took the children in his arms and blessed them. In Jesus' heart you are not a “small” person at all; you are someone he values and likes very much.
ask: What do you think might make a child not want to go to Jesus?
Why do you think Jesus said grown-ups should be like little children?
soldier.do: Every day this week find a time to say three things to Jesus yourself: one thank you, one sorry, and one please help me.

youth.talk: Sometimes I wonder whether our family has, without meaning to, made Jesus seem far away from you. Maybe I say I trust the Lord but live anxiously; maybe I too often talk about faith as “be good and go to church” rather than about Jesus himself. If so, I want to say sorry first. Jesus never found children a bother, and he has always welcomed you.
ask: On your way to knowing Jesus, what do you think has been the biggest obstacle?
Is there a question about Jesus you have always wanted to ask but never dared?
youth.do: Parents invite their teen to write down one real doubt or feeling about Jesus, and agree to find time this week to read a passage from a Gospel together and talk, without rushing to give standard answers.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for welcoming every child, and welcoming me. We want to run to you, to be held in your arms and blessed. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: A Gospel Children Can Understand
lessons.theme: I believe: the gospel is simple enough for a child to understand, and a child can truly believe

v: that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.
For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

lessons.still: Quietly say the gospel to yourself once: God loves me; I have sinned and left God; Jesus died for me and rose again; I trust him, and I receive new life. Say it slowly, and let each line touch your heart afresh.
teach: Paul says, “if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” And, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.” The heart of the gospel is not complicated, and you do not need to finish seminary to understand it. When parents cannot explain the gospel clearly, it is often not because the gospel is too hard, but because we rarely practice saying it in simple words. It is like a song you hear often: only when you try to sing it yourself do you find you do not know all the words.

The gospel can be boiled down to four lines, with the words adjusted to the child's age. One: God loves you, he made you, and he wants to be your friend. Two: but we all do wrong, and sin separates us from God. Three: Jesus is God's Son; he died for us on the cross and rose on the third day, building a bridge back to God. Four: when we admit our sin, trust Jesus and invite him to be Lord of our lives, we become children of God.

Can a child really believe? Jesus said the kingdom belongs to such as these. A child's faith does not need a lot of knowledge, but it does need real understanding and his own response. Parents should trust that the Holy Spirit can work in a child's heart. At the same time, remember that believing is not something parents do on a child's behalf; it is between the child and God. Our role is to share clearly, invite gently, and leave the result to God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change the way you think and you change a life. The gospel is the most basic shift in thinking: from “I must be good by myself” to “I need a Savior.” Only when parents are first convinced of the gospel's power can they speak about it freely in front of their children, rather than feeling it is church jargon.
q: Who is God? — Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, children included. How generous is this God?
Who am I? — Can I explain the gospel in three minutes in words a child understands?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe”: I believe the gospel is…; I believe my child can…; I believe the Holy Spirit will…
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to Nicodemus, “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” He said this to a learned ruler, and he said the same to the woman at the well. Jesus' gospel can be understood by adults and children alike.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I believe your gospel is the power of God to save everyone who believes, my children included. I admit I often feel I cannot explain it clearly, or fear that my child is too young to understand. Help me share you in simple words and with a sincere heart, and please let the Holy Spirit open my children's hearts, so that with their mouths they confess you as Lord and in their hearts believe that you rose from the dead. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements, and write the four lines of the gospel on a card in your own words
Practice in front of a mirror or with your spouse, telling the gospel in three minutes
At dinner use a simple picture, such as a bridge, to tell your child why Jesus had to die
lessons.noon: “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.” — Lord, let my children also call on your name and be saved by you.

fam.key: Jesus is the bridge back to God.

lamb.do: Take a little cross charm or draw a cross on paper, let your child touch it, and softly say the name of Jesus.
lamb.say: Jesus loves you. Jesus did the very best thing for you.

sprout.story: God loves us so much and wants to live with us. But we do naughty things, like telling lies and hitting, and these are called sin. Sin is like a big river that separates us from God. Jesus is God's Son, and he loves us so much that he lay down and became a bridge so we could walk across and get back to God. Jesus died, and on the third day he came alive again! If we trust Jesus, we can walk over the bridge and come home.
sprout.ask: Would you like to walk across Jesus' bridge and get back to God?
sprout.do: Use two chairs as the two sides of a river and a plank or a pillow as “Jesus' bridge.” Let your child walk across, and Mom or Dad on the other side hugs him and says, “Welcome home!”

soldier.story: On a sheet of paper, draw a person on the left, write “God” on the right, and in between draw a deep crack and write “sin” on it. The Bible says, “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” However hard we try to be good, we cannot jump over this crack. But God loves us and sent Jesus to die on the cross and rise from the dead. Draw a cross over the crack and it becomes a bridge. When we believe in Jesus and receive him, we can cross the bridge back to God.
ask: Why can't we jump over the crack by trying hard?
What do you think is the difference between “believing in Jesus” and “knowing about Jesus”?
soldier.do: Draw your own “cross bridge” picture, and this week use it to tell the gospel to a family member or friend.

youth.talk: You have grown up in the church, and you may know the content of the gospel by heart. But I want to ask a more honest question: is the gospel for you a set of doctrines, or good news you really need? For a time, the gospel was for me only something I knew; it was when I stumbled in life that I really experienced my need of a Savior.
ask: If you had to explain the gospel to a friend in your own words, what would you say?
Which part of the gospel do you find hardest to believe, or most moving?
youth.do: Parent and teen each take three minutes to tell the gospel in their own words, give each other feedback, then pray together.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for dying for us on the cross and rising again, so that we can get back to God. We believe in you and love you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Inviting Children to Receive Jesus
lessons.theme: Invite gently and clearly, in a way that fits the child's age, without pressure and without delay

v: But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:
Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.

lessons.still: Picture Jesus standing outside your child's heart door, knocking gently. He does not break the door down, and he does not give up. Be quiet a moment and say to the Lord, “Lord, prepare my child's heart, and prepare my mouth.”
teach: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him.” Jesus is the Lord who knocks, not the Lord who breaks in. “As many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children.” To invite a child to receive Jesus is to help him hear the knock and to tell him: you can open the door yourself. Parents cannot open the door for a child, but they can bring him to it.

How to do it by age. From birth to three: not an age of decision but an age of sowing. Say the name of Jesus often, sing hymns, pray as you hold your child, so that he joins “Jesus” with love. From three to six: tell the gospel with pictures, colors or the “Jesus bridge,” and ask, “Would you like to ask Jesus to live in your heart?” If he is willing, let him repeat a short prayer after you, line by line. From six to twelve: use the “cross bridge” to explain sin and salvation, make sure he understands three things (I did wrong, Jesus died and rose for me, I want to let him be my Lord), and then invite him to pray for himself. From twelve to eighteen: replace preaching with conversation, share your own struggles, and leave the decision to him.

You can lead your child in a prayer like this: “Lord Jesus, I know I have done many wrong things. Please forgive me. Thank you for dying for me on the cross and rising from the dead. I want to open my heart's door and ask you to come in as my Savior and the Lord of my life. Help me follow you all my life. In Jesus' name, amen.” Three reminders: do not push your child with fear, prizes or comparison; when he says “I'm not ready yet,” respect that and keep praying; after your child prays, note the date as his “spiritual birthday.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus reign begins with the child opening the door himself. If parents win a child's decision by pressure, they may gain a ritual but lose the child's heart. Self-emptied parents only share clearly and invite gently, and leave the Holy Spirit's work to the Holy Spirit.
q: Who is God? — Jesus stands at the door and knocks, waiting for people to open it themselves. How does he respect a child's heart?
Who am I? — Am I in too much of a hurry for my child to decide, or have I never dared to invite him?
How should I respond? — In what way suited to my child's age will I invite him to receive Jesus today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus asked the blind man Bartimaeus, “What do you want me to do for you?” He knew the answer, yet he let the man say it with his own mouth. Jesus never forced anyone to follow him. When the rich young ruler went away sad, he did not run after him to press him. His invitation is always sincere, clear and full of respect.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for knocking at the door of my child's heart. Give me wisdom to share you in a way my child understands, and courage to speak the invitation. Keep me from pushing my child with pressure or fear, and help me trust the Holy Spirit's work. If my child is not ready, give me patience to wait and to pray without ceasing. Amen.
acts: Choose a way to share the gospel that suits your child's age, and say it today
If your child is willing, lead him in a prayer to receive Jesus and note the date as his “spiritual birthday”
If your child already believes, ask him to tell how he came to know Jesus, and give thanks together
lessons.noon: “But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children” — Lord, let my children receive you and become your children.

fam.key: I will open my heart's door and ask Jesus in.

lamb.do: Hold your child in your arms, rest his hand on his chest, and pray for him: “Lord Jesus, please live in my treasure's heart.”
lamb.say: Jesus really wants to live in your heart. He loves you so much.

sprout.story: Bobo the puppy lived in a little house. One day someone went “knock, knock, knock” at the door. It was Bobo's best friend! But the door handle was on the inside, so his friend couldn't open it and had to wait outside. Bobo ran over and opened the door, his friend came in, and they ate snacks and played together. Jesus is like that good friend, knocking at the door of our hearts and waiting for us to open it and invite him in.
sprout.ask: Would you like to ask Jesus into your heart?
sprout.do: If your child is willing, let him put his hand on his chest and repeat line by line after Mom and Dad: “Jesus, I love you. I'm sorry for the wrong things I've done. Thank you for dying for me and coming alive again. Please live in my heart. Amen.” Then give him a big hug.

soldier.story: Jesus said, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him.” The handle of this door is only on the inside. Jesus won't break in; he waits for us to open it. Opening the door means: admitting I have done wrong and need Jesus; believing he died for me on the cross and rose again; and inviting him to be the Lord of my life. It is not because Mom and Dad want you to, but because you yourself want to follow Jesus.
ask: Do you think you have already opened your heart's door and asked Jesus in? Or are you still thinking?
If you asked Jesus to be your Lord, what would be different in your life?
soldier.do: If you want to, ask Mom or Dad to pray with you to receive Jesus, then write today's date on the first page of your Bible: “My spiritual birthday.” If you want to think some more, that's fine; this week tell Mom and Dad your questions.

youth.talk: I don't want to pressure you, or make you feel that “making a decision” is just a form or a ritual. Jesus says he stands at the door and knocks, and you are the one to open it. I want to ask you honestly: what is your relationship with Jesus right now? Whether your answer is “I already believe,” “I'm not sure,” or “I don't want to right now,” I want to hear it, and my love for you will not change.
ask: Do you think you have ever truly responded to Jesus' invitation? When was that?
What makes you hold something back about believing in Jesus?
youth.do: After the conversation, parents say: “If one day you want to pray to receive Jesus, or to give your life to him afresh, I'm here any time.” If your teen is willing, pray together; if not, bless him and do not press.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for knocking at the door of our hearts. We want to open our hearts and ask you to come in as our Savior and Lord. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Assured of Salvation, Following for Life
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: help children be sure of salvation and grow in the Lord

v: The testimony is this: that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.
These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.
I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

lessons.still: Look back over every moment this week when you talked with your children about Jesus: the joyful ones, and the awkward or unanswered ones. Ask the Holy Spirit to be with you as you look, and whatever the outcome, say to the Lord, “Lord, my child is yours, and I place him in your hands.”
teach: John wrote his letter “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Salvation is not a vague feeling but an assurance built on God's promise: “He who has the Son has the life.” Jesus also said, “I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” When a child does something wrong, he often doubts whether God still loves him. Parents must tell him again and again: you are saved not because you are good enough, but because Jesus is.

This week we talked about parents as first evangelists, not hindering children, telling the gospel in words a child understands, and gently inviting a child to receive Jesus. In our review, let us not take whether a child has made a decision as the measure of success or failure. Some children prayed this week, some are still thinking, and some even said no. Our faithfulness lies in sowing and watering; it is God who makes it grow.

For a child who already believes, the next step is to help him grow in the Lord: celebrate his spiritual birthday, read a short passage with him every day, talk with the pastor about baptism at the right time, and give him spiritual friends at church. For a child who has not yet responded, keep loving him, keep praying for him, and keep living out the gospel in daily life. Leading a child to know Jesus is not a single conversation but a lifetime of walking beside him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition apply to the gospel too. Proud parents treat a child's decision as their own achievement; anxious parents treat a child's non-response as their own failure; humble parents only ask, “Have I been faithful?” and then hand the child over to God.
q: Who is God? — God promises that no one can snatch his children out of his hand. What comfort does this give you?
Who am I? — This week, when I shared the gospel with my child, was it out of love or out of anxiety?
How should I respond? — Next week, how will I help a child who believes to grow, or keep praying for one who has not yet responded?
lessons.jesus: Jesus prayed to the Father for his disciples, “While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name.” He not only calls people but keeps them, prays for them and holds them up all the way. Today he still stands at the Father's right hand interceding for our children. In a child's journey of faith, a shepherd more faithful than any parent is leading.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking through this week with me. If my child received you this week, I thank you, and ask you to keep him following you all his life; if my child has not yet responded, I place him in your hands and ask you to keep drawing him. Forgive any pushing I did out of anxiety this week, and let me live out the gospel more and walk beside my children with more patience. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: what did each of us see this week as we shared the gospel with the children? How will we walk with them next?
Ask your child, “This week, when Daddy/Mommy talked with you about Jesus, did you feel any pressure?” Just listen, and do not defend yourself
Plan a small spiritual birthday celebration for a child who believes, and write a prayer card for a child who has not yet responded
lessons.noon: “I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” — Lord, my children are in your hands, and I can rest.

fam.key: Jesus holds me tight.

lamb.do: Wrap your hands gently around your child's little hand, hold it a while, then kiss the back of it.
lamb.say: Jesus' hand holds you tight and will never let go.

sprout.story: Baa the little lamb followed the good shepherd everywhere. One day Baa fell down. His knee hurt so much, and he was afraid the shepherd wouldn't want him any more. But the good shepherd knelt down, picked Baa up and said, “You are my little lamb, and I will never leave you!” Jesus is our good shepherd, and he says no one can snatch his little lambs out of his hand.
sprout.ask: Do you know that Jesus will always hold you?
sprout.do: Play “Can't Snatch Me Away”: Mom or Dad holds the child tight while the other family members pretend to snatch him, but they can't. At the end say together, “Jesus holds me tight!”

soldier.story: Some children, after they believe in Jesus, worry whenever they do wrong: am I still God's child? The Bible says, “He who has the Son has the life.” Jesus also said he gives us eternal life and no one can snatch us out of his hand. It is like when you do badly in an exam: you are still Mom and Dad's child. When we do wrong we should say sorry to God, but we do not need to fear being thrown away, because it is Jesus who saves us, not how well we do.
ask: Have you ever worried about whether you are still God's child?
What would you like to do this week to take one more step in following Jesus?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: those who believe share their “spiritual birthday” or how they came to faith, and each person names one small action for drawing closer to Jesus next week. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we talked a lot about coming to faith. I want to review myself first: was there any time I spoke too fast, too much like a sales pitch, so that it made you uncomfortable? If so, I want to say sorry. I also want you to know that wherever you are in your faith right now, you are my child, and someone God has been looking for and loving all along.
ask: In the way we talked about faith this week, where did you feel respected? Where did you feel pressure?
If you already believe, how would you like me to support your growth in faith?
youth.do: Parents first apologize for one thing this week that was too hasty or too preachy in a conversation about faith, then ask the teen how they would like the next talk to go, and agree a time.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for placing us in your hands, where no one can snatch us away. Help us to know Jesus more and love Jesus more every day. In Jesus' name, amen.

49.memT: From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

mem.t: I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.

sat.t: Family Day: Picnic of Faith Questions
sat.d: Prepare a simple picnic and a “question box,” and spread out a mat in the park or the living room. Before you set out, let each person write on a slip of paper a question they have about God, the Bible or faith. They may leave their name off, and little ones can ask a grown-up to write for them. At the picnic, take turns drawing out a question and discuss it as a family. When Mom and Dad do not know, they honestly say, “I don't know either; let's find out together.” Finally, put the questions that still have no answer back into the box and pray together: “Lord, we want to know you for ourselves.”

sun: When did your faith change from “my parents' faith” into “my own faith”?
When your child raises a doubt or a question about faith, what is your first reaction? What is the heart behind it?
Next week, how could you walk with a child or teenager, not only your own, as they build a personal relationship with God?

lessons.title: Another Generation Arose
lessons.theme: Faith cannot be inherited automatically; every generation must come to know God for itself

v: After all that generation were gathered to their fathers, another generation arose after them who didn’t know the LORD, nor the work which he had done for Israel.
For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth.
I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.

lessons.still: Picture your children ten years from now: where are they? Are they still following the Lord? Do not let worry take hold of you, but say quietly to the Lord, “Lord, let them know not only my God but their own God.”
teach: Joshua's generation saw with their own eyes God part the Jordan and bring down Jericho. Yet the Bible records a heartbreaking line: “another generation arose after them who didn’t know the LORD, nor the work which he had done for Israel.” In a single generation the faith was broken. It was not that God had stopped acting, but that the older generation had not passed on what God had done, and the next had not come to know God for themselves.

Faith cannot be inherited automatically, like a house, savings or a family name. A child can grow up in the church, memorize many verses and never miss a Sunday, and still have only a “second-hand faith”: that is Mom and Dad's God, not my God. When he goes to university, goes abroad or starts work, with no parents beside him, second-hand faith often cannot stand. It is like a borrowed coat: it looks like a good fit on an ordinary day, and only when the wind blows do you find it is not warm enough.

John says, “I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.” John called these believers his “children”; he had not fathered them, but raised them in the faith. The greatest joy of a spiritual parent is not a child who is well-behaved or successful, but one who walks in the truth for himself. Moving from the parents' faith to the child's own faith is the most important turn in these last weeks of this year's course.
lessons.light: 321 Light: First with God, then with myself, then with others. Parents can give their children a great deal, but cannot take the place of the child's own relationship with God. Parents need to move from “believing for the child” to “walking with the child as he believes,” letting Jesus reign directly over the child, not indirectly through his parents.
q: Who is God? — God wants to build a personal relationship with every generation and every person. How has he shown himself to you personally?
Who am I? — Is what my child knows now more “my God,” or “his own God”?
How should I respond? — What is one thing God has done in my life that I can tell my child today?
lessons.jesus: At twelve, in the temple, Jesus was found “sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions.” He did not just follow his parents to the festival; he explored and asked questions in his Father's house for himself. Jesus shows how a child grows up in faith: not by passively receiving, but by actively seeking.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I fear my children will become a generation “who didn’t know the LORD.” I admit I often ask only that they keep the rules and go to meetings, and seldom tell of what you have done in my life. Help me pass on your story, and above all please show yourself to my children, so that they walk in truth. Amen.
acts: Write down one real thing God has done in your life, and tell it to your children tonight
Ask yourself: if my child left home tomorrow, whose faith would he take with him?
Pray for each child: “Lord, let ___ come to know you for himself.”
lessons.noon: “I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.” — Lord, let my children walk in the truth for themselves.

fam.key: I want to know God for myself.

lamb.do: Let your child fold his hands himself while you sit beside him, and when he makes any sound of his own, say “Amen.”
lamb.say: You can talk to God by yourself too. God loves to hear you.

sprout.story: Every day Little Rabbit heard Mommy say, “Carrots are so sweet!” But he had never eaten one himself. One day he took a bite of a carrot, and wow! It really was sweet! Little Rabbit said, “So Mommy was right!” Knowing God is like that. Mom and Dad tell you that God loves you very much, and you can talk to God yourself and discover for yourself that God really loves you.
sprout.ask: What would you like to say to God yourself?
sprout.do: Today let your child say grace by himself. It doesn't need to be long; “Thank you, God” is just right. When he finishes, the whole family says “Amen.”

soldier.story: Joshua led the Israelites into the land of Canaan, and that generation saw many miracles with their own eyes: the Jordan parted and the walls of Jericho fell. But the Bible says that later another generation arose who did not know the LORD, nor what he had done for Israel. Perhaps parents did not tell their children the stories of God, and the children did not get to know God for themselves. In the end the whole nation turned away from God. Faith cannot rest only on Mom and Dad; each person must know God for himself.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “Mom and Dad believe in God” and “I believe in God myself”?
Have you had a moment when you experienced God yourself?
soldier.do: Ask Mom or Dad to tell a story of “something God has done in our family,” then write it down or draw it, and put it in a “Miracles of Our Family” book.

youth.talk: I have been thinking about something lately: one day you will leave home to study or work, and then nobody will remind you to go to church or read the Bible. I fear that what you take with you will only be “our family's habits,” not your own relationship with God. Honestly, I also went through a time when I only believed because my parents did. I would like to talk with you about where your faith is right now.
ask: If you lived alone in another city tomorrow, do you think you would still seek God? Why?
Which part of your faith is truly “your own”?
youth.do: Parents share their own turning point from second-hand faith to their own faith, then invite their teen to say where they are now, listening only and not marking.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you are not only Mom and Dad's God but my God too. Let me know you and love you for myself, and follow you all my life. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: We Have Heard for Ourselves
lessons.theme: A parent's testimony is the starting point; a child's own meeting with Jesus is the destination

v: From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything that I have done.”
So when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to stay with them. He stayed there two days.
Many more believed because of his word.
They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”

lessons.still: Ask yourself quietly: is my relationship with God my own? Or do I also live on someone else's faith? Ask the Holy Spirit to shine in like a lamp, so that you see honestly.
teach: After the Samaritan woman met Jesus she ran back to town to testify, and many believed in him because of her word. Later they asked Jesus to stay, and heard him for themselves. Then they said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.” The woman's testimony brought people to Jesus, but what made them truly believe was meeting him themselves.

The Holy Spirit wants to shine his light on us: what kind of parent am I? The “believe-for-him” parent pushes the child's faith along entirely, praying for him, reading the Bible for him, and answering everything for him. The “indifferent” parent feels faith is a private matter and never talks about it. And there is the “guide” parent, who like the Samaritan woman speaks eagerly of the Jesus she has met, and then steps aside, letting the child listen, ask and experience for himself.

In a two-income family in Singapore, Mr. Wang drove his daughter to school every day and always prayed for her in the car. One day she said, “Dad, you always finish praying for me, and I never know what to say myself.” Mr. Wang was stunned. From the next day he first asked his daughter what she wanted to say to God today, let her pray first, and then added a blessing of his own. Three months later his daughter began writing her own prayers in her diary.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Parents often think they must be the center of their child's faith, which is actually a hidden form of the self-ruled life. Self-emptied parents are like John the Baptist, who said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The focus is Jesus, not the parents; the more parents step back, the clearer Jesus becomes in the child's heart.
q: Who is God? — Jesus was willing to stay two days in a Samaritan town so that people could hear him for themselves. Does he long to meet my child personally too?
Who am I? — Am I a believe-for-him parent, an indifferent parent, or a guide?
How should I respond? — In which spiritual habit can I step back so that my child meets God himself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” He was not content with the disciples repeating what others thought; he wanted each one to answer with his own mouth. Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” What Jesus longs for is each person's own confession, including our children's.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, shine your light on me. I admit that sometimes I am too quick to believe for my children, treating their faith as my responsibility and my achievement; and sometimes I say too little about you. Make me a guide who bears eager witness to you, then steps aside, so that my children hear you for themselves and know for themselves that you are the Savior. Amen.
acts: Today, in one spiritual habit, let your child go first: let him pray first and share his feelings first, and you add afterward
Say to your child, “You can ask God yourself, and God will answer you himself.”
Write down one experience of your own of “hearing for yourself” from God, ready to share when there is a chance
lessons.noon: “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves” — Lord, let my children hear you for themselves.

fam.key: I can hear Jesus for myself.

lamb.do: Let your child sit on your lap, be still together for ten seconds, then whisper softly in his ear, “Jesus is here.”
lamb.say: Jesus is right beside you. He can hear you, and you can talk to him.

sprout.story: A lady met Jesus by a well, and Jesus loved her so much. She was so happy that she ran back to her village and shouted, “Come and see! Come and see Jesus!” Everyone ran to meet Jesus and hear him speak. Afterward they said, “We believe now, not only because of what the lady said, but because we have heard Jesus ourselves!”
sprout.ask: What would you like to say to Jesus? What do you think Jesus would say back?
sprout.do: Play “Pass the Message”: Dad whispers a sentence to your child, who passes it on to Mom. Then say: messages passed along can change, but hearing it yourself is clearest, and we can talk to Jesus directly too!

soldier.story: A woman in Samaria met Jesus by a well. Jesus told her about her past, and told her that he himself was the Savior. She ran back to town to tell everyone, and many believed because of it. Later the whole town asked Jesus to stay, and they listened to him teach for two days. In the end they said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves.” Mom and Dad and your Sunday school teachers are like that woman, bringing you to Jesus; but the most important thing is that you come to know Jesus for yourself.
ask: What do you think is the difference between “hearing others talk about Jesus” and “knowing Jesus yourself”?
In what ways can you get to know Jesus better for yourself?
soldier.do: This week choose a passage from a Gospel and read it by yourself. When you finish, write one sentence, “Jesus is ___.” Don't ask a grown-up; write what you discovered yourself, and share it with the family at the weekend.

youth.talk: I notice I often want to decide for you what your faith should look like: when to read the Bible, how to pray, what you ought to feel. But those Samaritans said they believed not because of the woman's word but because they had heard for themselves. What I can do is tell you about the Jesus I have met, but I cannot meet him for you. I would like to learn to step back a little.
ask: In matters of faith, do you think I manage too much or push too much?
Have you ever had a moment of “hearing for yourself” from God? What was that like?
youth.do: Parent and teen agree that this week parents will not remind their teen to read the Bible or pray; the teen will arrange it himself. At the weekend, share what each of you experienced with God this week.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you are willing to speak with each one of us yourself. Let us hear your voice for ourselves and know you for ourselves. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Doubt Is Not the Enemy of Faith
lessons.theme: I believe: a child's questions can lead him to know Jesus more deeply

v: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days, again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

lessons.still: Remember a time when you yourself doubted or questioned God. Was anyone with you then? Be quiet a moment, and say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you that you did not leave me because of my questions.”
teach: Thomas is often called “Doubting Thomas.” When the other disciples said they had seen the Lord, he said, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.” But Jesus did not scold him or shame him, or drive him from the disciples. After eight days Jesus came again, especially for him, and said, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands.” Thomas's doubt in the end brought out the fullest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!”

When many Christian parents hear their child say, “I'm not sure God exists,” or “Why does God allow bad things?”, the first reaction is to tense up, even to get angry, as if the child's question were betrayal. But doubting is different from unbelieving: unbelief shuts the door, while doubt is often a knock at the door. When a child asks, it shows he is thinking seriously about faith, and not just treating it as a house rule.

Zhiming, a single father in Kuala Lumpur, had a fifteen-year-old son who said one day, “I think evolution makes more sense than Genesis.” Zhiming wanted to refute him at once, but held back and said, “That's a good question. I don't fully understand it either, so let's look into it together.” For the next month father and son read books, searched online and asked their pastor. Later the son said that because his dad didn't shout at him that time, it was the first time he felt faith could be taken seriously.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of view, from “my child's doubt is a threat” to “my child's question is an opportunity.” Proud parents want to win the debate; humble parents are willing to say “I don't know either.” The Holy Spirit is the guide; parents need not have all the answers, only walk with the child as he seeks.
q: Who is God? — Jesus came again especially for one disciple who had questions. How does he treat people's doubts?
Who am I? — When my child raises questions about faith, do I tense up, preach, or seek together with him?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe”: I believe my child's questions…; I believe God can…; I believe I can…
lessons.jesus: A father brought his sick son to Jesus and cried out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” Jesus did not turn away this faith mixed with doubt, but healed the man's son. Jesus accepts imperfect faith, and accepts us and our children coming to him with questions.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I believe my child's questions are not the enemy of faith; I believe you can answer every sincere doubt; I believe I do not need all the answers, only to walk with my child to you. Take away my tension and my need to control, and make our home a place where it is safe to ask, so that questions lead us to know you more deeply. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements and put them by your bed
Today take the first step and ask your child, “Is there anything about God or the Bible that doesn't make sense to you?”
Next time your child raises a hard question, start by saying, “That's a good question, let's find the answer together.”
lessons.noon: “I believe. Help my unbelief!” — Lord, my children and I come to you with our questions; help our faith.

fam.key: If I have a question, I can ask God.

lamb.do: When your child looks at things with curious eyes, look with him, and point and say, “God made that!”
lamb.say: You are so clever, you like to look and to ask, and God likes you to be like that.

sprout.story: Jesus came alive again, and many of his friends saw him. But Thomas didn't. He said, “I have to see it with my own eyes and touch it with my own hands before I believe!” Eight days later Jesus came again. He wasn't cross; instead he said to Thomas, “Come, touch my hands.” As soon as Thomas touched them, he knelt down and said, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus loves children who ask questions!
sprout.ask: Is there something you'd like to ask about God?
sprout.do: Prepare a “question box.” Let your child say a question about God, and Mom or Dad writes it down and puts it in. One day this week, find the answer together.

soldier.story: Thomas was one of Jesus' twelve disciples. On the evening Jesus rose again, he happened not to be there. The other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But Thomas said he would not believe unless he could touch the nail marks in Jesus' hands. After eight days Jesus appeared again specially, and told Thomas to touch his hands and his side. Thomas at once said, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus did not scold Thomas; he helped him to believe. When you have doubts, you can tell God and Mom and Dad honestly too.
ask: Is there anything about God, the Bible or faith that you can't quite work out?
Do you think asking questions makes God unhappy? Why?
soldier.do: Write down one real question you have about faith and give it to Mom or Dad. Agree a time this week to read the Bible, look things up or ask the pastor together.

youth.talk: At school and online you may hear many things that challenge faith, and perhaps there are questions in your mind you dare not tell me, afraid I will be tense or disappointed. I want you to know you can ask. I have doubted myself, and there are questions I still do not have complete answers to. Jesus did not scold Thomas, and I do not want to scold you for your questions.
ask: What is the biggest question mark in your mind about faith right now?
When you have doubts, how would you like me to respond?
youth.do: Agree a time when your teen can bring the hardest faith question he has. Parents promise not to preach or rush to a conclusion, but to read the relevant Scriptures together or find a trustworthy book, and if necessary ask the pastor together.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you did not scold Thomas, and that you are not angry when we have questions. Help our faith, and let us know you more. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Children's Own Devotions
lessons.theme: Help children build the habit of being alone with God, according to age

v: Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

lessons.still: Picture the wilderness before dawn, with Jesus kneeling alone in prayer. All around is quiet, only he and the Father. Pause in this quiet too, and say to the Lord, “Lord, I want to be alone with you, and I want to pass this quiet on to my children.”
teach: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” The day before he had healed the sick of a whole town and worked late into the night, yet the very next morning the first thing he did was be alone with the Father. For Jesus, fellowship with the Father was not an extra religious activity but the source of life. A child's own faith also needs his own time alone with God.

How to do it by age. Ages three to six: each night before bed use a picture Bible, let the child turn a page himself, tell the story from the pictures, and say one line of thanks. Ages six to nine: give him a children's Bible and a small notebook, read a few verses each day, and draw a picture or write a sentence. Ages nine to twelve: teach him to read with three simple questions: What does this passage say God is like? What does it say I am like? What can I do today? Teenagers can choose their own reading plan, record it on a phone or in a journal, and parents need only ask now and then how it is going.

“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” A lamp need not light the whole road, only the next step. A child's devotions need not be perfect either; five minutes, one verse and one line of prayer is a good start. Let the whole family practice today: prepare a devotion corner or tool of his own for each child, do the first time with him, and then slowly let go. The point is not that parents check whether it was done, but that children taste the sweetness of being with God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head. If a child's devotion is only an assignment, it becomes just another tick-chart; if it is a date with Jesus, it becomes the source of life. Only when parents have their own devotions will children believe it is real.
q: Who is God? — God longs to be alone with every child. How does he meet you in the quiet?
Who am I? — Does my child see me as someone who is often alone with God?
How should I respond? — How will I help each child begin a devotion habit that suits his age today?
lessons.jesus: One day the disciples saw Jesus finish praying, and one said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray.” It was not because of a lesson but because they had seen Jesus' life that they longed to pray. So Jesus taught them the Lord's Prayer. Children are the same: they first see their parents pray, and then want to learn to pray.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for showing us a life alone with the Father. I admit my own devotions are often on and off, and I often turn my children's devotions into a task to be checked. Renew me, let me first enjoy being with you, and give me wisdom to walk with my children, according to their ages, as they begin to spend time with you, so that your word becomes a lamp to their feet. Amen.
acts: Prepare one devotion tool for each child: a picture Bible, a notebook, or a reading plan
Today go with your child through his first “own devotion,” just five minutes
Let your children see your own devotions: read the Bible and pray while they are awake
lessons.noon: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” — Lord, let your word light the next step for me and my children today.

fam.key: Every day I have a date with Jesus.

lamb.do: At a fixed time each day, hold your child and turn through a picture Bible, pointing at a picture and saying one word or a short sentence.
lamb.say: This is God's word. God wants to talk to you every day.

sprout.story: It was not yet light, and everyone was asleep, but Jesus quietly got up and went to a quiet place. There he talked with his Father for a long, long time. Jesus loves being with his Father most of all! We can also find a time each day to talk with Jesus and listen to Bible stories, just like a date with a good friend.
sprout.ask: When would you like to have your date with Jesus each day?
sprout.do: Help your child make a “date-with-Jesus corner”: a little mat, a picture Bible and a small lamp. Tonight turn one page of the Bible there and say one “Thank you, God.”

soldier.story: Shiqi, a ten-year-old girl in Ipoh, Malaysia, used to read the Bible with her mom. This term her mom gave her a notebook and said, “From today, this is your secret notebook with God.” Shiqi read a few verses every day and wrote notes with three questions: What is God like? What am I like? What can I do today? One day she read “Your word is a lamp to my feet” and drew a lamp, and beside it wrote, “God, please light up my exam tomorrow.”
ask: What do you think is the difference between reading the Bible by yourself and reading it with the whole family?
How would you like to record your time with God?
soldier.do: Begin your own devotions this week: read a few verses each day and, using the three questions, write a line or two or draw a picture. At the weekend you can pick one page to share with the family, or keep it private.

youth.talk: I want to be honest: my own devotions also often stop when I get busy and forget. So I don't want to demand it of you by checking. But I sincerely hope you have your own time with God, not to hand in work but because it is the true source of your life. You can do it your way: a reading plan, a journal, even listening to worship songs and praying.
ask: How do you spend time with God now? What is hard about it?
How would you like me to support you without it becoming pressure?
youth.do: Together choose or design a reading plan that suits you, and parents start a plan of their own. Don't check each other, but at the end of each week each share one verse that touched you most.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you want to be with us every day. Help us to find time each day to talk with you and read your word. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Becoming Spiritual Parents to Our Children
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: from parents who gave birth to spiritual parents

v: For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.
I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.
But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.

lessons.still: Recall the moments this week when you talked with your children about faith. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you: where did I step back so my child could meet God himself? Where could I not help believing for him and answering for him? Do not rush to mark yourself; just be honest before the Lord.
teach: Paul says, “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers.” A tutor teaches knowledge; a father gives life. A tutor is responsible for one subject; a father walks beside you for a lifetime. Paul also says that among believers he was “gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children,” and was pleased to impart not the Good News only, but “our own souls.” A spiritual parent has both the guidance of a father and the tenderness of a mother.

We are all parents who gave birth to our children, but not necessarily their spiritual parents. Parents who gave birth care for the child's body, schooling and future; spiritual parents walk with the child to know God and grow in the Lord, until Christ is formed in his heart. The two roles can overlap, but they need deliberate practice. For some children, spiritual parents are grandparents, Sunday school teachers or youth mentors, and parents should thank them and work with them.

This week we talked about second-hand faith, hearing for ourselves, doubt and questions, and children's own devotions. In our review, ask yourself: what am I giving my child, a set of rules or a relationship? Have I lived out a faith worth imitating, as when Paul said, “I beg you therefore, be imitators of me”? The direction for adjustment is for parents first to be real in their faith, then to walk beside the child gently, until the child too can say: this is my own God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “3” in 235: spiritual parents and children. The home is the first place to practice being spiritual parents. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: parents first have a real life, and only then can they build a spiritual relationship with their children, until the children too become spiritual parents to others.
q: Who is God? — God is the Father who began a good work in us and will complete it. How has he walked beside you as you grew?
Who am I? — This week, was I more my child's “tutor” or his “spiritual parent”?
How should I respond? — What is one thing I will adjust next week, and how exactly will I do it?
lessons.jesus: After he rose again, Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and then said, “Feed my lambs.” Jesus entrusted the work of a spiritual parent to a man who had fallen. He does not ask for perfection, only for love for him. It is the same with us: with love for the Lord, we go to feed the lambs in our home.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you are the best spiritual Father in my life. I admit that this week I sometimes acted like a tutor, only teaching and checking, instead of walking beside my children and cherishing them. Forgive me, and teach me Paul's gentleness and honesty, so that I become my children's spiritual parent. Thank you also for placing other spiritual elders around my children; please bless them. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: in our children's faith, are we tutors or spiritual parents? How should we adjust next?
Ask your child, “This week, was Daddy/Mommy more like Jesus when talking with you about faith?” Just listen, and do not defend yourself
Write a thank-you card to a spiritual elder in your child's life, and write down one adjustment for next week
lessons.noon: “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers.” — Lord, let me be not only my child's tutor but his spiritual parent.

fam.key: Together we grow in the Lord.

lamb.do: Rock your child gently in your arms, humming a hymn as tenderly as a mother nursing her child, and bless him at the end.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy love you, and we will love Jesus together with you.

sprout.story: When baby ducklings are first born they can't swim. Mother Duck jumps into the water first and paddles slowly, and the ducklings follow behind one by one, learning how to paddle. Mother Duck never leaves them, and keeps swimming ahead to show the way. Mom and Dad are like Mother Duck too, leading the way in knowing Jesus, and when you grow up you can lead other children to follow Jesus too!
sprout.ask: Which way of loving Jesus would you like to learn from Mom and Dad?
sprout.do: Line up as a family to play “Ducklings Follow Mother”: the one at the front does an action, those behind copy it, and at the end say, “Let's follow Jesus together!”

soldier.story: Paul was not just a teacher who preached; he treated people who believed in Jesus as his own children. He said you may have ten thousand tutors in Christ, but not many who love you like a father. Paul cared for them as tenderly as a mother, and encouraged them like a father. Later Timothy, whom Paul had taught, became a spiritual father to others too. A spiritual family, it turns out, is passed down from one generation to the next.
ask: Besides Mom and Dad, who else has helped you know God like a spiritual parent?
This week, was there one thing in your faith that you did by yourself?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one thing about their time with God this week, then names one thing to adjust next week. Finally write a thank-you card together to a spiritual elder. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we talked a lot about your own faith. I want to review myself: have I often acted like a teacher, only caring whether you read the Bible and go to church, and rarely really walked the road of faith with you? I want to be your spiritual parent, and not just someone who manages you. I also thank the other spiritual elders in your life who help you.
ask: This week, was there a time in matters of faith when you felt accompanied rather than managed?
What role would you like me to play on your journey of faith?
youth.do: Parents first apologize for one thing that was more “managing” than “walking beside,” then discuss together a new way of walking with you next week.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us spiritual family. Help us to walk beside one another and grow in the Lord together, and to help others know you. In Jesus' name, amen.

50.memT: I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.

mem.t: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

sat.t: Family Day: A Day of Serving Together
sat.d: Choose together someone to serve: an elderly neighbor who lives alone, a church member who finds it hard to get about, or a family that has just moved in. Arrange it beforehand, and ask the church team to help you plan. Little ones draw cards, school-age children prepare a hymn or a short blessing, teenagers help with shopping and baking, and Mom and Dad keep company and chat. During the visit, listen more than you speak, and pray for them before you leave. Back home, share as a family: whom did our light reach today?

sun: This week, at what moment did you see your family's light shining before others?
What is making your family “pass by on the other side,” unable to see the people near you who need help?
Next week, which family would you like to invite to serve a person or family in need together with you?

lessons.title: The Lamp That Lights the Whole House
lessons.theme: Our home is a lamp God has lit, to shine before people

v: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.still: Turn off the light in the room and light a small candle or switch on your phone's little flashlight. Watch quietly how that one point of light brightens everything around it. Say to the Lord, “Lord, let our home also become a point of light like this.”
teach: Jesus said to his disciples, “You are the light of the world.” He did not say, “Try hard to become light,” but “You are.” Light is not a task but an identity. Then Jesus used a homely picture: no one lights a lamp and puts it “under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.” In Jesus' parable, whom the lamp lights first is the people of the house.

A Christian family is like a lamp on a stand. It first lights those inside: a husband and wife who love each other, a child who is forgiven, brothers and sisters at peace; then the light naturally spills out through the windows onto neighbors, classmates and colleagues. The world is seldom moved by what we say, but it is often curious when it sees a different kind of home: how come their family is like this? The way a family lives is its longest sermon.

“That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The purpose of serving is not for people to praise how good our family is, but for them to see how good the Father is. This year we have traveled from God's design, through parents' lives, the rhythm of the home and relationships of love, to ministry. Serving together as a family is when everything learned this year is set on the stand and shines out.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. A home's light does not come from running activities; it shines out of renewed lives and relationships. One purpose: build what belongs to God. Every shining home is an outpost of God's kingdom in the neighbourhood.
q: Who is God? — God himself lit our home and set it on the stand. What is his heart for your home?
Who am I? — Is our family's light now on the stand, or hidden under a basket?
How should I respond? — What small good deed can our family do today so that people see the Father?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” Our home does not shine by itself, just as the moon reflects the sun; we can light others because Jesus' light first shone into our home.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for lighting our home. I admit we often hide the light under a basket, caring only for what is inside our own walls, afraid of trouble and of our weakness being seen. Let our home first light one another, and then let the light shine out to neighbors, classmates and colleagues, so that what they see is not us but your glory. Amen.
acts: Think together as a family: among our neighbors, the building staff and our children's classmates, who needs a little light?
Do one small kindness for a neighbor today, such as a greeting or helping carry something
Stick this on the inside of your front door: “Even so, let your light shine before men.”
lessons.noon: “Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works” — Lord, let our home shine out your light today.

fam.key: Our family is Jesus' little lamp.

lamb.do: Switch on a small night light in a dim room, hold your child and look at the light together, pointing your finger and saying “light.”
lamb.say: Jesus is the light, and you are Jesus' little light too.

sprout.story: One night the power went out, and the house was pitch dark so nobody could see. Dad lit a little candle and put it in the middle of the table, and suddenly the whole room was bright. Everyone could see one another's faces, and everyone smiled. If you hide the candle under a bowl, will the room still be bright? No! Jesus says we are like that candle, and we should let our light shine so that others can see God's love.
sprout.ask: How can you let your light shine?
sprout.do: Play “Hide the Light”: light up the room with a flashlight, then cover it with a bowl and ask your child which is brighter. At the end say together, “I won't hide, I'll shine!”

soldier.story: Jesus was teaching everyone on the mountain and said, “You are the light of the world.” In those days there were no electric lights, and when people lit an oil lamp at night they always put it high on a stand so the whole house could see. No one lit a lamp and then covered it with a big bowl. Jesus said our good deeds are like light, to shine before others, so that when people see them they praise not us but our Father in heaven. Helping up a classmate who has fallen at school, or caring for your little brother or sister at home, is shining your light.
ask: Who do you think most needs to see a little light at school or in the neighbourhood?
What is the difference between shining and “doing it to be seen”?
soldier.do: This week be a “secret shiner”: each day do one kind thing for one person without letting them know it was you, and tell the family in the evening.

youth.talk: Our family is often so busy that we only manage to look after ourselves: homework, work, all sorts of activities. But Jesus says we are the light of the world, and light is meant to shine out. I have been reflecting on whether our family is too much like a closed castle, protecting itself and seldom letting others feel God's love. That is not your fault; we parents must change first.
ask: What kind of family do you think we look like in other people's eyes?
Is there a classmate or friend of yours who is going through a dark time?
youth.do: Together with your teen, list three people or families your family could light up together, and choose one to act on this week.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you that you are the light of the world. Let our home be your little lamp, lighting others so that everyone sees the Father's love. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: The Home That Passes by on the Other Side
lessons.theme: The Holy Spirit shines his light on us: has our home seen the people in need?

v: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.still: Think of the people you passed this week: an elderly person at the roadside, the cashier at the supermarket, a child left out in your child's class, someone at church who has not come for a long time. Ask the Holy Spirit to let one of those faces stay with you, and ask the Lord, “Lord, did I pass by on the other side?”
teach: In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the priest and the Levite both “saw him” and “passed by on the other side.” They were not wicked people. Perhaps they were hurrying to serve in the temple, perhaps they were afraid of becoming unclean, perhaps they were simply too busy. The “business” in their minds blocked the “person” in front of them. Only the Samaritan, despised by the Jews, “when he saw him, he was moved with compassion,” stopped, and cared for the man with his own oil, wine, animal and silver.

Today the Holy Spirit wants to shine his light on us: what kind of family are we? The “busy” family, like the priest, has a church calendar so full that there is no time to stop and look at the people near us. The “protective” family fears its children meeting people who are “different,” fears danger and trouble, and so takes a detour. And there is the “compassionate” family, willing to have its plans interrupted, willing to pay a price, and turning love into concrete action.

The Chen family in Taichung have two children in elementary school. One day their younger daughter said a classmate had no lunchbox every noon. Her mom's first reaction was, “That's the school's business.” But at evening prayers she felt uneasy. The next day she contacted the teacher, and afterward prepared one extra lunchbox each week for her daughter to “happen” to share with the classmate. Later that classmate's mother came to church too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. The priest and the Levite were tied up with “tasks” and could not see the “person.” Do not neglect people for the sake of tasks. 920 reminds us that everyone we meet on the road may be a “2” God has placed beside us.
q: Who is God? — God saw the wounded person at the roadside and was moved with compassion. How does this God see the overlooked?
Who am I? — Is our family more a busy family, a protective family, or a compassionate family?
How should I respond? — Whom has God brought to mind? How am I willing to stop?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.” Jesus is the true Good Samaritan: he saw us fallen in sin and half dead, did not pass by on the other side, but gave his own life to bring us back and care for us.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on our home. I admit we are often too busy and too afraid of trouble, and we see people in need and pass by on the other side. Forgive us, give us a compassionate heart so that we are willing to stop, and let our children learn from us to see and to show mercy. Amen.
acts: Write down one person you “passed by on the other side” this week, pray for him, and ask God what you can do
Today ask your child, “Is there anyone in your class who seems lonely or in need of help?”
Block out one hour in your diary, kept ready for someone in need
lessons.noon: “When he saw him, he was moved with compassion.” — Lord, open my eyes so that I no longer pass by on the other side today.

fam.key: When we see someone in need, we stop and help.

lamb.do: When your child falls over or a toy drops on the floor, crouch down with him, touch it, lift it up, and blow on it gently.
lamb.say: It hurts! We stop to take care of him, and Jesus takes care of us in the same way.

sprout.story: A man was walking along the road when robbers beat him up, and he lay by the roadside in terrible pain. A priest came along, took one look, and crossed to the other side of the road and went away. Then another man came along, and he also walked away. Finally a Samaritan came. He stopped, put medicine on the hurt man and bandaged him, lifted him onto his own donkey, and took him to an inn to look after him. Jesus said: you should do the same!
sprout.ask: If you saw someone fall over, what would you do?
sprout.do: Act out the story of the Good Samaritan with soft toys: let your child play the one who stops to help, and use a plaster to bandage the “injured” toy.

soldier.story: A teacher of the law asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” Jesus told a story. A man was beaten half to death by robbers and left by the road. A priest and a Levite came by, saw him, and passed by on the other side. Finally a Samaritan came by. Jews usually looked down on Samaritans, but he was moved with compassion, bandaged the wounded man, took him to an inn and paid for his care. Jesus asked, “Which one was a neighbor?” The answer: the one who showed mercy. Jesus said, “Go and do likewise.”
ask: At your school or tutoring center, is there anyone “lying by the road,” someone who is often overlooked or bullied?
Why do you think the priest and the Levite did not stop? Do you ever have similar reasons?
soldier.do: This week pick a classmate or neighbor who is often overlooked, and start a conversation, play together or help with something, then tell the family what happened at the weekend.

youth.talk: I notice our family is often the one that “passes by on the other side.” We are busy and good at protecting ourselves, and sometimes I have even told you not to get too close to certain classmates. Protection is needed, but I fear that what I have taught you is only how to avoid people who need help. I would like to learn again with you how to be moved with compassion, loving people in ways that are both wise and safe.
ask: Is there someone around you whom you know needs help but you have never stopped for?
In what situations do you think helping someone needs you to involve a grown-up or a professional first?
youth.do: Talk together about a need you have both noticed, such as a lonely classmate or neighbor, and decide on a safe, concrete way to care for him together. If it involves bullying, self-harm or violence at home, tell a teacher, pastor or professional together.

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, open our eyes to see people who need help. Give us courage to stop and help them like the Good Samaritan. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: A Home with an Open Door
lessons.theme: I believe: our home's door is opened for God's kingdom

v: contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.
Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” So she persuaded us.

lessons.still: Picture your front door. When did a guest last come in? Was your heart glad or tense then? Be quiet a moment and say to the Lord, “Lord, this home is yours, and the door is yours.”
teach: Paul says, “given to hospitality.” Hebrews says, “Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.” The early church had no great cathedrals; the gospel spread from one home to the next. When Lydia came to faith, the first thing she did was say to Paul, “come into my house and stay.” Her home became the beginning of the church in Philippi.

Many Chinese families are not used to inviting people home: afraid the house is too messy, the food not good enough, the children too noisy, afraid of being seen as we really are. But hospitality is not about holding a perfect banquet; it is opening the door and opening the heart. A pot of rice porridge, a few small dishes and sincere care are enough to let a lonely person feel the warmth of a home. Children also learn from such evenings: our home does not belong only to us.

Hospitality is also a child's most natural school of service: little ones can say welcome at the door, school-age children can help set the table and introduce their toys, and teenagers can play with the guests' children or help look after guests. The Huang family in Singapore invite a newly arrived immigrant family to dinner every month, and the children say it is the evening they look forward to most. Today we move from knowing to conviction: our home is opened for God's kingdom.
