lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of view, from “this is my home” to “this is God's home, and we are only stewards.” To let Jesus reign includes letting him decide who sits at our table. Relationships matter more than things: an imperfect meal pleases God more than a tidy but closed home.
q: Who is God? — God has spread the gospel everywhere through one open home after another. Does he want to use your home too?
Who am I? — What makes me reluctant to open my door? Is it pride, tiredness, or fear?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe”: I believe our home is…; I believe hospitality…; I believe God will…
lessons.jesus: As he passed through Jericho, Jesus looked up at Zacchaeus in the tree and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” Jesus went into the home of a man everyone despised, and that day “salvation has come to this house.” Jesus is the one who best knows how to receive, and he invites us too to open our doors so that salvation may come to more homes.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I believe our home is yours and that our door is opened for your kingdom. I admit that I often shut it for fear of what people think, tiredness and fear. Change my heart so that I gladly welcome people, and let my children learn through one welcome after another to love and to serve. Send those in need to our home. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements and share them with your spouse
Decide together as a family: which family or person will we invite this month for a simple meal at home?
Let the children take part in preparing for the guests, each taking one small task
lessons.noon: “Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers” — Lord, open my door, and open my heart too.

fam.key: Our door is open for love.

lamb.do: When a guest arrives, carry your child to the door, wave and say “welcome” together, then let your child hand the guest a cookie.
lamb.say: A friend has come, and we welcome him. Jesus likes us to love people like this.

sprout.story: Lydia sold purple cloth. One day she heard Paul tell the story of Jesus, and she was so moved that she believed in Jesus, and her whole family was baptized. Straight away she invited Paul: “Please come and stay at my house!” Paul and his friends stayed with her, and they prayed and ate together. Later lots of people got to know Jesus at Lydia's house!
sprout.ask: Whom would you like to invite to our home to play?
sprout.do: Let your child draw a “welcome card,” with our front door and a smiley face, ready to give to the next guest who comes to our home.

soldier.story: When Paul arrived in the city of Philippi, he met a group of women praying by the river. One of them, Lydia, was a dealer in purple cloth. She heard the gospel, the Lord opened her heart, and she believed in Jesus, and her whole household was baptized. Then she said to Paul, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” From that day, Lydia's home became the place where the church in Philippi met. An open home can become a place where many people get to know God.
ask: What do you think are the good things about inviting people to our home? What makes you nervous?
If guests came, what could you be in charge of?
soldier.do: Plan a time of hospitality together as a family: decide whom to invite and what to eat, and have each person choose a job, such as setting the table, preparing games or saying grace.

youth.talk: I know that when guests come you sometimes find it a nuisance: tidying up, making conversation, and being asked about your grades. I used to feel the same myself. But I increasingly feel that opening our door is a gift our family can give to the world. I would like to ask what kind of hospitality you would feel comfortable with and willing to join. Your thoughts matter to me.
ask: Whom would you like our family to invite? Is there a friend you would like to invite?
When we have guests, what do you like least? How could we change it?
youth.do: Let your teen invite a friend, or someone they care about, to dinner at home. Let them decide part of the menu and the activities, and parents go along with it.

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us a home. Help us gladly to open our door and welcome others, so that everyone feels your love in our home. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: The Five Loaves and Two Fish in a Child's Hands
lessons.theme: Let children take part in serving: a small offering in the Lord's hands can feed the crowd

v: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,
“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?”
Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
Jesus took the loaves, and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down, likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.

lessons.still: Picture the child with his lunch, handing five loaves and two fish to Jesus. Be quiet a moment and ask the Lord, “Lord, what do we have in our hands that we can give to you?”
teach: Five thousand hungry people sat on the grass, and the disciples did not know what to do. Andrew said, “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?” Grown-ups saw “not enough,” but a child was willing to hand over his lunch. Jesus took it, gave thanks and shared it out, and everyone ate and was full. The miracle began with a child's offering.

We often think serving is for grown-ups, and that children should simply study well and wait until they are older. But in the Bible little Samuel served in the temple, the little servant girl pointed Naaman to the prophet, and a child with a lunch became the start of a miracle. A child's service may look small, but in Jesus' hands it is never small. We let children take part in serving not to keep them busy, but so that they experience early on: I too can be used by God.

How to involve children by age. Birth to three: go along with parents to visit older people, smile at people, hand over a card. Three to six: draw cards, sing a hymn, help hand out snacks. Six to twelve: join the church's acts of kindness, pray for a sick friend, give away part of their pocket money. Teenagers can look after younger children, take part in music or technical ministry, and visit or volunteer with their parents. Let the whole family do one act of service today, so that every child has his own “five loaves and two fish.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. The child's five loaves and two fish fed five thousand, not because there were many loaves, but because they were in Jesus' hands. Self-emptied service does not look at how much we have, but at how much we give. When parents give first, children learn to give.
q: Who is God? — Jesus fed five thousand with a child's lunch. How does he regard a small offering?
Who am I? — Do I often use “the children are still small” or “we aren't capable enough” as a reason for not letting my family serve?
How should I respond? — Which “five loaves and two fish” will our whole family give to Jesus today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus took the child's loaves, “having given thanks, he distributed” them to those sitting down. He did not despise how few loaves there were, nor bypass the child to do the miracle directly, but received, gave thanks and broke. Jesus likes to use small people and small things to show his great glory.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for accepting a child's lunch and doing a great miracle. I admit I often see only “not enough,” and often think children are too small to serve. Today our whole family gives you the little time, talent and belongings in our hands. Please give thanks, break and use them, and let our children experience from early on the joy of being used by you. Amen.
acts: Decide together as a family on one act of service to do today, and give each person a role by age
Let each child say, “My five loaves and two fish are ___.”
After serving, pray together as a family for the people you served
lessons.noon: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish” — Lord, what we have is small, but we are willing to give it all to you.

fam.key: Even small me can be used by Jesus.

lamb.do: Let your child put a cookie in your hand. You take it and say “thank you,” then share half of it with another family member.
lamb.say: You shared with someone else, well done! Jesus likes you to share.

sprout.story: Lots and lots of people came to hear Jesus tell stories, and they listened until they were hungry, but there was nothing to eat. A little boy had brought five loaves and two fish, and he said, “My lunch is for Jesus!” Jesus took it and thanked his Father, and then he kept on sharing and sharing. Wow! All five thousand people were full, with twelve baskets left over! The little boy was so happy because Jesus had used his lunch.
sprout.ask: What do you have that you could give to Jesus, for him to use?
sprout.do: Let your child choose something of his own, such as a drawing, a sweet or a song, and take it to give to someone who needs encouragement.

soldier.story: Five thousand people followed Jesus all day, and everyone was hungry. Philip said that even two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them all. Andrew found a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, the lunch of a poor family. But the boy was willing to hand it over. Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and shared them out, and not only did everyone eat and was full, but twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered up. You may think you are too small and not capable enough, but Jesus likes best to use people who are willing to hand over what they have.
ask: What are your “five loaves and two fish”? Maybe a talent, a little time or a little pocket money?
Where would you like to serve others?
soldier.do: Complete a service task together with your family, such as making cards for older people at church, praying for a sick friend, or giving part of the money in your giving jar. You take charge of one part.

youth.talk: I used to feel that you were so busy with schoolwork that serving could wait until after exams. But now I think I may have taken away your chance to be used by God. The child with the five loaves and two fish, when the grown-ups had given up, handed his own things to Jesus. You have many abilities I do not: music, technology, ways of relating to young people.
ask: What abilities or time of yours do you think you could use to serve people?
What kind of service would you like our whole family to do together?
youth.do: Let your teen suggest a way of serving that interests them, and parents join in once. For example, help with children's Sunday school, church audio-visual work, performing at a care home, or volunteering together.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for using the little boy's five loaves and two fish to feed so many. We want to give you our small things too. Please use us. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Not Growing Weary in Doing Good
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: serving as a family, servants of all

v: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.still: Think back over this week's moments serving together as a family: there were moving times, and times of tiredness, grumbling or awkwardness. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you, and say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for using this imperfect family of ours.”
teach: Paul says, “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” Serving is often tiring: the elderly person we visit may complain, the guests we receive may be rude, and the children may start begging to go home halfway through. Paul knew people grow weary, so he reminds us that the harvest is not today but “in due season.” A sower must be patient, just as a farmer does not dig up the seed every day to see if it has sprouted.

Jesus said, “whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant,” and that he came “not to be served but to serve.” This week we have talked about the home as the light of the world, not passing by on the other side, opening the door in hospitality, and letting children take part in serving. In our review, ask: what is our motive for serving? Is it to make our children's CVs look good, or to make others think our family is spiritual? Or is it truly to love people and glorify God?

The direction for adjustment is to make serving a way of life for the family and not a one-off event. Hosting once a month, visiting once a term, praying each week for someone in need: a small rhythm lasts longer than one grand effort. Watch the family's load too: serving is not meant to wear the family out, but to let the family grow together in love. If a family member is tired, caring for that family member first is also serving.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review, adjustment and repetition: serving too must grow in this cycle. Proud service wants to be seen; self-emptied service seeks only God's pleasure. First with God, then with myself, then with others, then with tasks: the strength to serve comes from my relationship with God, not from zeal itself.
q: Who is God? — God promises, “we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” How does he see your service that seems to bear no fruit?
Who am I? — This week, was our family's motive for serving love for people, or wanting to be seen?
How should I respond? — What is one thing our family will adjust next week, and how will we build a rhythm of serving?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” The older people we visit, the guests we receive, the classmates we help: Jesus himself is in them. He remembers every cup of cold water and every time we stopped, and none of it is wasted.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for using our whole family to serve this week. I admit that sometimes our motives were not pure, and sometimes we were tired, grumbled, and even wanted to give up. Forgive us and renew our strength, so that we do not grow weary in doing good. Help us build a lasting rhythm of service, so that this home remains a servant of all. Amen.
acts: Talk with your spouse for ten minutes: in this week's family service, what was the most moving moment? Where does the rhythm need adjusting?
Ask your child, “This week when we served together, was Daddy/Mommy more like Jesus?” Just listen, and do not defend yourself
Decide together as a family on a regular monthly rhythm of service and write it in the family calendar
lessons.noon: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” — Lord, give our whole family strength to keep on doing good.

fam.key: We serve together and do not give up.

lamb.do: Remember a moment this week when your child shared or helped, act it out again as you hold him, then kiss him and say thank you.
lamb.say: You helped someone this week, and Jesus is so happy, and so are we.

sprout.story: A little farmer planted tiny seeds in the field and watered them every day, but on the first day nothing sprouted, and on the second day nothing either. The little farmer was a bit discouraged, but he kept on watering. After many days, wow! Little green shoots popped up, and later there were lots of delicious fruits. Helping others is just like that. Even if you can't see results at first, don't give up!
sprout.ask: Whom did you help this week? Do you think he was happy?
sprout.do: Plant a seed together in a small pot and water it every day, to remind everyone: do good and don't give up, and God will make it grow.

soldier.story: The disciples James and John wanted the best seats in Jesus' kingdom, and when the other disciples heard, they were angry. Jesus called them together and said that in the world great people like to boss others around; but among you, whoever wants to be great must be everyone's servant. For Jesus himself came into the world not to be served but to serve, and even to give his life for us. The truly great are those who are willing to serve others.
ask: When our family served this week, which part did you like best? Which part made you tired or not want to do it?
Whom would you like to keep serving next week?
soldier.do: Hold a ten-minute family meeting: each person shares one feeling from this week's serving, then together decide on one regular monthly act of service. Mom and Dad go first.

youth.talk: This week we did some serving together, and I want to review myself first: did I turn serving into another kind of pressure, or look very spiritual in front of others and come home impatient? If so, I want to say sorry. I hope our family's serving truly comes from love and can keep going, not heat up for a while and then stop.
ask: In this week's serving, which part do you think was sincere? Which part was only going along?
What rhythm do you think our family could keep up for serving without getting too tired?
youth.do: Parents first apologize for one impatient or showy moment in serving, then together design a rhythm of service the whole family can keep up over time, giving your teen part of the decision.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting our whole family serve together. Help us not to lose heart or give up, but to go on loving and helping people like Jesus. In Jesus' name, amen.

51.memT: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

mem.t: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.

sat.t: Family Day: An Ebenezer Thanksgiving Meal
sat.d: Bring to today's table what the family wrote yesterday about “what God has done in our family this year.” Let each person find a small stone and write on it, with a marker, one thing to give thanks for or a date. Stack the stones in a corner of the living room as your family's own “Ebenezer.” If you can, invite the family you hope to walk beside to share a simple meal. After the meal, ask each family member to say in a sentence or two what God has done this year, and little ones can show their drawings. Finally, the two families pray together and give the new year to God.

sun: Looking back over this year, what has changed most clearly in your home: mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships, or ministry? Give an example.
Is your family more like a pond that only receives, or a river that flows out? What is blocking the flow?
Which family would you like to walk with through this course in the new year? How do you plan to begin inviting them?

lessons.title: A Home Whose Heart Has Turned
lessons.theme: Revival begins when parents' hearts turn to their children, and then flows to another home

v: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, ‘to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children,’ and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to prepare a people prepared for the Lord.”

lessons.still: Go back to the morning of the first week a year ago, when you said before the Lord, “This home is yours.” Say it to him once more, adding this time: “Lord, please use this home to bless another home.”
teach: The last words of the Old Testament are a promise about the family: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” After that God was silent for four hundred years. At the opening of the New Testament, the angel announcing John the Baptist's birth to Zechariah quotes exactly these words: “to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.” At the hinge between the Testaments, God set the revival of the family. It turns out that God prepares people to welcome the Messiah beginning in the home.

A “turning of the heart” is not a passing emotion but a change of direction. Over this past year we began with the parents' own hearts: admitting the self-ruled life, returning to our place, abiding in the Lord, learning to bear the fruit of the Spirit at home, building the family altar, mending relationships, and then moving on to character, calling and leading children to know Jesus. All of this has been the process of fathers' hearts turning to their children and children's hearts turning to their fathers.

But Malachi's promise does not stop within one home. John the Baptist was to “prepare a people prepared for the Lord.” A home that has turned becomes a home that prepares others. Today is the start of the last week of the year, and we ask: how can what God has done in our home flow to another home? One home influencing another is the most natural way for God's kingdom to spread on earth. It is like one candle lighting another: its own light is not diminished.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The five-fold change from the inside out: mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships, ministry. This is just the road we have traveled this year. Ministry is not leaving home to do something great; it is letting a changed home flow out naturally to build what belongs to God, one home after another.
q: Who is God? — God kept the last words of the Old Testament for the revival of the family. How much does this God value your home?
Who am I? — This year, has my heart turned more toward my children? Have my children's hearts turned more toward me?
How should I respond? — What action will I take today so that my family feels “my heart is turned toward you”?
lessons.jesus: In the parable of the prodigal son Jesus said that “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” This is what a father's heart turned toward his children looks like. Jesus came to reveal the Father's heart to us, and to turn our hearts back to the Father.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for all you have done in our home this year. You turned my heart toward my children and have begun to turn my children's hearts toward me. I admit there is still much that is imperfect, but I thank you for your faithfulness. Keep working in our home, and use this imperfect home of ours to bring your heart to another home. Amen.
acts: Look through this year's notes or photos and find one thing by which God changed your heart
Tell each child today, “I've got to know you better this year, and thank you.”
Pray for a family who has come to your mind, and ask God whether he wants you to walk beside them
lessons.noon: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers” — Lord, keep turning our hearts, and let our home flow to other homes.

fam.key: God draws our hearts close together.

lamb.do: Let your child lie on your chest and listen quietly to your heartbeat together, then place his little hand over your heart.
lamb.say: Mommy and Daddy's hearts are always turned toward you, and God's heart is always turned toward you too.

sprout.story: There was a big tree whose roots gripped the earth deep down. When the fruit on the tree was ripe, it fell to the ground, and the seeds inside grew into little trees. The little trees grew up, bore fruit, and grew even more little trees. Later that place became a whole forest! Our family is like that big tree. God lets us love one another, and he wants our love to grow into other families' homes too.
sprout.ask: Whose home would you like our family's love to grow into?
sprout.do: Draw a big tree together with the name of everyone in the family on it, then draw a little tree beside it and write the name of a family we would like to bless.

soldier.story: In the very last words of the Old Testament, God said: I will send Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers. Then God was quiet for four hundred years. When the New Testament begins, an angel told Zechariah that his son John would turn the hearts of fathers to their children, to prepare the way for Jesus. So before God begins something great, he first draws hearts in the family close together. Our family has been learning to draw closer all this year too.
ask: This year, where do you think our family has grown closer?
How do you think our family could help other families draw closer too?
soldier.do: Write a short letter to Mom or Dad about the biggest change you have seen in our family this year, and read it aloud at dinner.

youth.talk: We have walked fifty-two weeks together this year, and honestly I don't know whether you have felt a change. What I have learned most is that it was not that I needed to change you first, but that my heart had to turn toward you first. There is still much I haven't done well, but I am very thankful for this year. I have also started to wonder whether what God has done in our family could help other families.
ask: This year, what do you think my biggest change has been? Where am I still the same as before?
Is there a friend's family that you feel really needs help?
youth.do: Parent and teen each write down one change they have seen in the other this year, swap and read them, and then pray together for a family you want to bless.

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for drawing our family's hearts close together. Let our love flow out too, to help other families know you. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: Pond or River?
lessons.theme: The Holy Spirit shines his light: does our home only receive, or does it also flow out?

v: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you.

lessons.still: Picture two scenes of water: a still pond and a flowing river. Ask the Holy Spirit quietly, “Lord, this year our family has received so much; which of the two are we more like?”
teach: Paul said to Timothy, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.” In this one verse there are four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. The gospel never stops in one person or one home, but is handed from one generation to the next, flowing from home to home. Jesus also said he chose us and appointed us “that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.”

Today the Holy Spirit wants to shine his light on our home: are we a pond or a river? The pond kind of home is good at receiving: listening to sermons, taking courses, reading spiritual books, and the home really does get better, but all the blessing stays inside, and over time it turns stagnant. The river kind of home receives just the same but lets the blessing flow out: walking beside a newly married couple, caring for a single-parent family, inviting another family to read the Bible together. Living water must flow to stay fresh.

321 uses “235” to describe the network of spiritual relationships: the 2 are spiritual companions, a couple or friends who support one another; the 3 are spiritual parents and children, with someone who leads me and someone whom I lead; the 5 are comrades in arms, a team that serves together according to the five-fold ministry. This year we have been learning to be spiritual parents to our children at home; in the new year God is also inviting our home to become a spiritual companion or spiritual parent to another home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last of the eight steps for changing a mindset is “multiplication.” Without multiplication, information, revelation, conviction and practice all stop with ourselves. A self-ruled home wants to hold on to its blessing; a self-emptied home is willing to entrust its blessing to others, because the blessing was God's all along.
q: Who is God? — God chose us and appointed us to go and bear fruit that remains. What is his expectation of your home?
Who am I? — This year, has our family been more like a pond or a river?
How should I respond? — In 235, who is currently a spiritual companion to our family? Who is a spiritual parent? Whose spiritual companion or parent can we become?
lessons.jesus: Of Jesus' three and a half years, he invested most in twelve disciples, eating, living and walking with them. After he rose he said to them, “Go and make disciples of all nations.” What Jesus showed was not building a huge organization but one life reproducing in another.
lessons.pray: Lord, shine your light on our home. This year we have received so much grace, and I admit we easily keep the blessing within our own walls and become a comfortable pond. Take away our selfishness and fear, and make our home a river, entrusting to others what you have given us, so that we bear lasting fruit. Amen.
acts: Draw your family's “235”: write who your spiritual companions and spiritual parents are, and the people you could walk beside
Ask your spouse, “Of what we've learned this year, which family would we most like to share it with?”
Pray every day this week for a family you might walk beside
lessons.noon: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.” — Lord, let what our home has received flow to others.

fam.key: God's love is meant to flow out.

lamb.do: In the bath or a basin, let your child pour water with a small cup into another cup, and when it is full, pour it into the next.
lamb.say: God gives us so much love, and we pour love out to others too.

sprout.story: In the forest there was a little pond. Hardly any water flowed out, and slowly it became dirty, so the little animals did not want to drink from it. Beside it was a little river whose water kept flowing and flowing, and wherever it flowed green grass and flowers grew, and the deer and the rabbits came to drink. The little pond said, “I want to be a little river too!” So it opened a little gap and let the water flow out, and it became clear and bright itself.
sprout.ask: What do you think our family can “flow” to other people?
sprout.do: Use two cups and a straw or tube to show it: which is better, water that stays in the cup and never moves, or water that keeps flowing? At the end say together, “God's love is meant to flow out!”

soldier.story: Paul trained a young man named Timothy, teaching him God's word. Paul said to Timothy: what I have taught you, teach to faithful people, so that they can teach others. Count them: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others, four generations altogether! It is like a relay race: the runner who gets the baton cannot hold it to his chest; he has to run a stretch and then hand it to the next person. Our family has received many batons from God this year, and now we must pass them on.
ask: What do you think is the most important thing you have learned this year from Mom and Dad or from church?
To whom could you “pass the baton” on this?
soldier.do: Make a “relay baton,” for example by rolling up paper, and write on it one truth you have learned this year. This week, tell it to a friend or a younger brother or sister.

youth.talk: I notice our family has received a great deal this year, but we seldom think of giving it away. We are a bit like a comfortable pond, with all the good things kept at home. I want to tell you about an idea called “235”: everyone needs spiritual companions and spiritual parents, and also to become a spiritual parent to others. At your age you can already become a spiritual older brother or sister to someone younger.
ask: Is there someone younger than you around whom you could walk beside to help them know God?
How do you think a teenager could become someone's “spiritual parent” or “spiritual older sibling”?
youth.do: Each of you, parent and teen, draw a “235” diagram of your own relationships and write in the names, then share them with each other and pray together for one person on the diagram who needs walking beside.

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving our family so very much love. Make us like a little river, letting your love flow to others. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: One Home Walking with Another
lessons.theme: I believe: our imperfect home can walk beside another home

v: He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them,
and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.
Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

lessons.still: Think of the family that has come to your mind: their names, their difficulties, their children. Be quiet a moment and say to the Lord, “Lord, we are not perfect, but if you want to use us, we are willing.”
teach: Priscilla and Aquila were a couple who made tents, and because the emperor “commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome,” they were forced to move to Corinth. They were immigrants and craftspeople, not apostles and not elders. Yet they opened their home to welcome Paul, living and working with him; and later in Ephesus they met Apollos, an eloquent man, mighty in the Scriptures, and “took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.” An ordinary home helped shape an important preacher.

This couple did not correct Apollos publicly in the synagogue; they took him home and explained gently at the table. This is the most beautiful picture of family companionship: not teaching from above, but acceptance, sharing and walking together in everyday life. Paul later said all the churches of the Gentiles gave thanks for them, and a church met in their house. A dinner table can often change a person more than a pulpit can.

Many parents will say, our own family isn't even sorted out, so how are we qualified to walk beside anyone? But Priscilla and Aquila were also displaced. We walk beside another home not because we are already complete, but because we have traveled part of the way, know where one stumbles, and know how God holds us up. Today we move from knowing to conviction: our imperfect home, in God's hands, can bless another home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility, so both win. A home willing to admit weakness is best able to walk beside another weak home; a proud home only puts pressure on others. The focus is Jesus, not our family's record, but what God can do through us.
q: Who is God? — God used a displaced couple of craftspeople to help shape Apollos. How does he see an ordinary home?
Who am I? — What makes me feel our family is “not qualified” to walk beside others?
How should I respond? — Write your own “I believe”: I believe our home…; I believe God can, through us…; I believe in the new year we will…
lessons.jesus: Jesus sent out seventy “two by two,” and said, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few.” He never sent perfect people, but people willing to go, and he gave them one another for company. Today he is still calling willing homes, to walk together two homes at a time.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I believe our imperfect home can bless another home in your hands. I believe you used Priscilla and Aquila and can use us too. I admit I often draw back because of my own weakness. Give us humility and courage to open our home and our lives, and to walk beside one family on the road of faith in the new year. Amen.
acts: Write three “I believe” statements and read them aloud together with your spouse
As a couple, list two or three families you might walk beside: newlyweds, new parents, a single-parent family, a family new to church
Pray for each family on the list, asking God to show you which to start with
lessons.noon: “When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.” — Lord, make our home also a home that welcomes people and walks beside them.

fam.key: Our family can walk beside other families.

lamb.do: Take your child to play with a child from another family, and let him hand a toy to the other child.
lamb.say: We play together and share together, and God likes us to be good friends.

sprout.story: Aunty Priscilla and Uncle Aquila made tents. When they met Uncle Paul, they asked him to come and stay at their house, where they worked and prayed together. Later they met Uncle Apollos, who was very good at preaching, but there were some things he didn't know yet. Priscilla and Aquila invited him to their home and slowly, gently told him more about Jesus. Their home became a home that helped lots of people!
sprout.ask: Which good friend's family would you like to invite to our home?
sprout.do: Make an invitation card with your child, drawing our family and another family holding hands, ready to give to a family we would like to walk beside.

soldier.story: Priscilla and Aquila were a married couple who were forced to leave Rome and move to Corinth to make tents. They welcomed Paul to stay in their home. Later in Ephesus they heard a man named Apollos preach, and he preached well, but some parts were not yet complete. They did not correct him in front of everyone, but invited him to their home and “explained to him the way of God more accurately.” Apollos later became a preacher who helped many churches. An ordinary married couple used their home to help one person, and so helped many churches.
ask: Why do you think Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos home instead of correcting him in front of everyone?
What do you think our family has to share with other families?
soldier.do: Write a list together of “things our family can share,” such as saying grace, family day activities, and how we say sorry to each other. Everyone writes at least one.

youth.talk: I often feel our family still has so many problems that we could not possibly help anyone else. But Priscilla and Aquila were themselves immigrants driven out of Rome, and they did not wait until life was settled before they began. I have been wondering whether, in the new year, our family could walk beside one other family. It need not be perfect: just eating together, praying together, and sharing what we have learned this year.
ask: What do you think our family is best able to share with others? What would you least like others to see?
If we were to walk beside a family, what role would you like to play?
youth.do: Discuss with your teen a list of families you might walk beside, let them give their view, and decide together which family to pray for first.

fam.pray: Dear Jesus, thank you for using ordinary homes. Please use our home too, to help another family know you better and love you more. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: A Threefold Cord
lessons.theme: Start today: invite a family to walk with God

v: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.still: Picture a rope made of three strands braided together: one strand is God, one is your family, and one is the family you will walk beside. Say quietly to the Lord, “Lord, be the strand in the middle, and braid us tightly together.”
teach: “Two are better than one,” and “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.” The Teacher saw that a person alone falls most easily, while those with a companion can hold each other up. He ends: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” Two homes walking together is already good, and with God in the middle they become a strong cord. Today we turn this week's conviction into concrete action.

Walking beside another home can start with very simple steps. First, pray: as a couple, pray for that family for a week. Second, invite: begin with a simple meal or an outing, without rushing to teach. Third, walk together: invite them to go through “321 Family Life,” meeting weekly or every other week, each doing the work at home and sharing the three Sunday small-group questions when you meet. Fourth, entrust: when they begin to change, encourage them to walk beside another family.

The attitude of walking beside matters more than the method: listen more, speak less, don't compare, don't preach, and be willing to share your own failures. The children can join in too: little ones play together, school-age children do family day activities together, and teenagers can become spiritual older brothers and sisters to the other family's children. If the other family is facing domestic violence, addiction or serious emotional or physical distress, gently help them seek help from the church's pastors and professionals, and do not carry it alone.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “2” in 235 is spiritual companions. A family cannot fight alone; it needs companions, and a mature family must also become a companion to others. The order of relationships is first God, then people: the most important strand of the three is God's, and both homes depend on him.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to be the strand in the middle of two homes. What confidence does this give you?
Who am I? — Am I used to going it alone, as one person or one family?
How should I respond? — What concrete action will I take today to invite a family to walk with us?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.” When two homes eat, pray and share God's word together, Jesus is there. His promised presence is not only in the temple and the church building but at every table where people gather in his name.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for promising to be with those who gather in your name. Today we are willing to take a step and invite a family to walk with us. Prepare their hearts and ours, so that we listen more and speak less, and share sincerely. Be the strand in the middle of the threefold cord, and braid the two homes tightly together in your love. Amen.
acts: Send a message or make a call today inviting the family on your heart to a meal
Agree with your spouse on a regular monthly time for walking beside them
Prepare to invite them to go through “321 Family Life” with you next year
lessons.noon: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” — Lord, be the strand in the middle of us, and braid two homes together.

fam.key: With God in the middle, together we are stronger.

lamb.do: Take three colored strands of wool or cloth and plait them into a braid in front of your child, and let him pull on it and feel how strong it is.
lamb.say: God is with us, and so we are so strong.

sprout.story: Little Bear tried to carry a big log by himself, but couldn't move it, and fell over. Little Rabbit ran over and helped him up, and together they carried it, and at last it moved! In the evening it was very cold, but when they snuggled up together they were warm. Little Bear said, “Two are better than one!” Little Rabbit said, “And it's even better if God is with us!”
sprout.ask: Who would you like to do good things with?
sprout.do: Play the “Can't Break It” game: first give your child a single thin string, which breaks with a gentle pull; then braid three strings together, and no matter how he pulls it won't break. Say together, “With God in the middle, we are stronger!”

soldier.story: King Solomon said, two are better than one. If one falls, the other can lift him up; if two lie together they keep warm; and if someone attacks, two can stand against him. At the end he said, “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” A single thread breaks easily, but three strands braided together are very strong. Our family and another family, with God in the middle, make a threefold cord.
ask: Do you have a good friend who has helped you up when you have fallen?
If our family walks with another family, what could you do?
soldier.do: With your family, braid a bracelet from three cords: one for God, one for our family, and one for the family we want to walk beside. When it's done pray together, and give it to a child in that family.

youth.talk: Today we are really taking a step: inviting a family to walk with us. Honestly, I am a bit nervous, afraid I will do it badly and afraid of being turned down. But I think that rather than wait for perfect, we should start now. I need your help very much too, because the other family's children may be more willing to listen to you than to me. Shall we give it a try together?
ask: If the other family has a child about your age, how would you like to get along with him?
What do you think we most need to watch out for when we invite others, so that nobody feels pressured?
youth.do: Let your teen take part in the invitation: write the message together, decide the first meeting's activity together, or let your teen invite the other family's child.

fam.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us good friends. Be with us, and let our family and other families follow you together, as strong as a threefold cord. In Jesus' name, amen.

lessons.title: The LORD Has Helped Us Until Now
lessons.theme: Review & adjust: look back over the year, do a family health check, write down your testimony, then set out again

v: Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
The LORD has done great things for us, and we are glad.
that this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’

then you shall tell them, ‘Because the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the LORD’s covenant. When it crossed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. These stones shall be for a memorial to the children of Israel forever.’”

lessons.still: Slowly leaf through this year's photos, notes or calendar, from the first week to today. Ask the Holy Spirit to look with you page by page: the laughter, the tears, the apologies, the reconciliations, the prayers. Do not rush to mark them; just say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for being here all along.”
teach: At Mizpah Samuel set up a stone and named it Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.” Joshua also told Israel to take twelve stones from the Jordan, so that “when your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’” parents could tell of God's work. Remembering is not nostalgia but carving God's faithfulness in stone for the next generation to see.

Today, let the whole family do a family health check together, using the five-fold change we have walked through this year. One: Mindset. Do we believe more that the family is God's design? Two: Life. Are the parents abiding more in the Lord and becoming more like Jesus? Three: Lifestyle. Have the family altar and spiritual rhythm been built? Four: Relationships. Are we better at apologizing, forgiving and loving one another? Five: Ministry. Have we started serving together and flowing out to others? Let each person give each item one to five stars, without arguing over the scores, just listening to one another's feelings, and then together choose the one you most want to grow in during the new year.

Jesus said to the man who had been healed, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.” Finally, let the whole family write down “what God has done in our family this year”: parents write a paragraph, children a sentence or a drawing, to be put up at home and taken to share with the family you will walk beside. Invite them to go through this course with us in the new year. The year has ended, but God's work in our home has not; he wants to flow through us to the next home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps end with review, adjustment, repetition and multiplication. A year of lessons is one complete cycle, and the new year is another. Let Jesus reign and let Jesus receive the glory: testimony is not boasting how good our family is, but telling how good God is.
q: Who is God? — “The LORD helped us until now.” Looking back over this year, for which of God's works are you most thankful?
Who am I? — Among the five-fold changes, which has our family grown most in? Which most needs continued practice?
How should I respond? — In the new year, what is one thing our family will adjust? Which family will we walk beside?
lessons.jesus: Before he ascended, Jesus said to his disciples, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” This year has traveled from the first week's “Unless the LORD builds the house” to today's “The LORD helped us until now.” The one who builds our home has promised to be with us for ever.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, until now you have helped us. Thank you for all you have done in our home this year: you changed my mindset, renewed my life, built up our lifestyle, mended our relationships, and have begun to use us to serve others. I admit there is still much that is imperfect; please keep building. In the new year we say once more as a whole family: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. Amen.
acts: As a family, complete the five-fold family health check and choose the one you most want to grow in during the new year
As a family, write down your testimony of “what God has done in our family this year”: parents write a paragraph, children a sentence or a drawing
Invite the family you want to walk beside to go through “321 Family Life” with you in the new year
lessons.noon: “The LORD helped us until now.” — Lord, thank you for your faithfulness this year; in the new year we still depend on you.

fam.key: Until now, God has helped us.

lamb.do: Open up this year's photos of your child and point to them one by one, saying “Thank you, God” with each one. At the end hold him and bless him for the new year.
lamb.say: You've grown so much this year, God has helped us all along, thank you, God.

sprout.story: After the Israelites won the battle, Samuel brought a big stone and stood it on the ground, and named it “Ebenezer,” which means: God has helped us all the way to today! After that, every time someone saw the stone, they remembered how good God is. God has helped our family so many, many times this year, so let's set up a stone to thank God too!
sprout.ask: What do you most want to thank God for this year?
sprout.do: Let your child find a small stone, and Mom and Dad help him write or draw on it what he wants to thank God for, then put it on the family's “thank-you stone pile.”

soldier.story: When the Israelites crossed the Jordan, the river stopped and everyone walked across on dry ground. Joshua told twelve men each to take a stone from the middle of the river and pile them on the bank. He said that when your children one day ask, “What do you mean by these stones?” you can tell them the great things God did. Many years later Samuel also set up a stone and said, “The LORD helped us until now.” Our family has had many miracles this year, some big and some small, and we want to write them down too.
ask: This year, what do you think is the greatest thing God has done in our family?
In the new year, in which area do you most hope our family will grow?
soldier.do: Take part in the family health check: give one to five stars for each of the five areas and say your reasons. Then write one sentence on the family's testimony sheet: “What God has done in our family this year.”

youth.talk: This year is ending, and I want to say honestly first: I am not a perfect parent, and this year there have been many times I let you down. But looking back, I really do see that God has done a lot in our family, and a lot in me. I would like to hear your honest score, good and not so good. I also want to ask whether you would be willing to join us in sharing this year's journey with another family.
ask: If you had to score our family's changes this year, how many marks would you give? Why?
What role would you like to play as we walk beside another family?
youth.do: Complete the family health check and testimony together: parents first apologize to their teen for the one thing most needing an apology this year, then ask the teen to write down what “God has done in our family” in their eyes, and finally invite another family together to walk with you next year.

fam.pray: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for helping our family all through this year. In the new year we want to keep following you, and to help other families know you. In Jesus' name, amen.

52.memT: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.
